- stomach ache
- feeling sick and diarrhoea

title: Fungal nail infection
section_path: Fungal nail infection > Treatment for a fungal nail infection
text:
You cannot take antifungal tablets if you have certain conditions, such as liver or kidney disease. They may also not be suitable if you're pregnant or breastfeeding.

Badly infected nails sometimes need to be removed. It's a small procedure done while the area is numbed (under local anaesthetic).

title: Fungal nail infection
section_path: Fungal nail infection > Preventing fungal nail infections
text:
You can get a fungal nail infection if your feet are constantly warm and damp.

You're more likely to get an infection if you wear trainers for a long time and have hot, sweaty feet.

There are some things you can do to help prevent fungal nail infections.

title: Fungal nail infection
section_path: Fungal nail infection > Preventing fungal nail infections > Do
text:
- treat athlete's foot as soon as possible to avoid it spreading to nails
- keep your nails short
- keep your feet clean and dry
- wear clean socks every day
- wear flip-flops in showers at the gym or pool
- wear shoes that fit well and do not have high heels or narrow toes
- throw out old shoes

title: Fungal nail infection
section_path: Fungal nail infection > Preventing fungal nail infections > Don’t
text:
- do not wear shoes that make your feet hot and sweaty
- do not share towels
- do not wear other people's shoes
- do not share nail clippers or scissors

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide
text: Furosemide is a medicine used to treat swelling caused by a build-up of fluid in the body. It can also be used for high blood pressure. It’s only available on prescription.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > What furosemide is for
text:
Furosemide is mainly used to treat a build-up of fluid in the body (oedema), which often affects your hands, arms, feet or legs.

It's a type of medicine called a diuretic, sometimes called water tablets because they make you pee more. This helps to get rid of excess fluid from your body.

You might be offered furosemide if you have oedema because of a condition that affects your heart, kidneys or liver, such as:

- heart failure
- chronic kidney disease
- severe liver damage (cirrhosis)

Furosemide is also sometimes used to help treat high blood pressure (hypertension).

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > How to take furosemide
text:
Furosemide usually comes as tablets or liquid that you swallow.

How much you need to take and for how long depends on why you're taking it.

Your doctor may prescribe a low dose to start with and increase it after a week or more. This reduces the chances of side effects.

You usually take it once a day at first, but if your doctor decides to increase your dose then you may need to take it twice a day.

Always check the packet or leaflet that comes with your medicine. Ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice if you're not sure how to take it or have any problems taking it.

When taking furosemide:

- try to take it at the same time each day – ideally every morning if you take it once a day, or at the same time every morning and late afternoon if you take it twice a day
- swallow tablets and capsules with water
- you can take it with or without food

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > How to take furosemide
text:
You may need to take furosemide for a long time if your swelling is because of a long-term condition like heart failure. If you take it for a long time, you'll be offered regular blood tests to check your health.

Taking furosemide can make you feel like you need to pee more urgently and frequently, so it may be useful to plan for this after taking it.

If you get ill with vomiting, diarrhoea or a high temperature (fever) when taking furosemide, there's a risk you'll get dehydrated.

Talk to a pharmacist or doctor for advice or follow the advice they've already given you.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > How to take furosemide > If you miss a dose of furosemide
text:
If you forget to take a dose of furosemide, take it as soon as you remember, unless it's nearly time for your next dose.

If it's nearly time for your next dose, skip the dose you missed and take your next dose at the usual time.

Do not take 2 doses to make up for a missed dose.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > How to take furosemide > If you take too much furosemide
text: Taking an extra dose of furosemide can be dangerous.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > How to take furosemide > If you take too much furosemide > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if:
text:
- you've taken more than your prescribed dose of furosemide

If you're told to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring the furosemide packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > Side effects of furosemide
text: Like all medicines, furosemide can cause side effects, but not everyone gets them.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > Side effects of furosemide > Common side effects
text:
Common side effects of furosemide can include:

- peeing more than usual
- feeling thirsty, with a dry mouth and lips (these can be signs of dehydration)
- dizziness
- headaches
- muscle twitches

If you feel dizzy or drowsy after taking furosemide, do not drive, ride a bike or use machinery until you no longer have these symptoms.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > Side effects of furosemide > Common side effects > Non-urgent advice: Speak to a pharmacist or doctor if:
text:
- you have any side effects that bother you or do not go away

They may be able to give you advice about how you can reduce the side effects. Keep taking your medicine unless you're advised to stop.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > Side effects of furosemide > Serious side effects
text:
Furosemide can sometimes cause serious side effects, although most of them are rare.

Possible serious side effects of furosemide can include:

- an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) - causing symptoms such as a swollen throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash and difficulty breathing
- blistering skin around the mouth, eyes, nose or genitals, with flu-like symptoms (Stevens-Johnson syndrome)
- pain in your lower back or side, feeling sick, a high temperature, and having problems with peeing or having blood in your pee – these could be signs of kidney problems
- becoming very dehydrated – causing symptoms like peeing less than usual, having dark yellow or brown coloured pee, feeling dizzy or lightheaded, feeling tired, sunken eyes and confusion

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > Side effects of furosemide > Serious side effects > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if:
text: - you're taking furosemide and think you might be having serious side effects

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > Side effects of furosemide > More about side effects
text:
These are not all the side effects of furosemide.

For a full list, see the leaflet that came with your medicine or search for your medicine leaflet on the electronic medicines compendium website.

You can report any side effects you get on the Yellow Card website.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > Who can and cannot take furosemide
text:
Most adults can take furosemide. Sometimes it’s suitable for children.

But furosemide is not suitable for everyone. For example, it may not be suitable if:

- you've had an allergic reaction or serious side effect from taking furosemide or another type of diuretic
- you have kidney or liver problems
- you have diabetes or Addison's disease
- you have or have had gout
- you have low blood pressure

Before taking furosemide, tell your doctor if you have any medical conditions.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > Who can and cannot take furosemide > Breastfeeding and furosemide
text: Tell your doctor if you're breastfeeding. Furosemide is not usually used while breastfeeding. Your doctor may offer a different treatment while you're breastfeeding.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > Who can and cannot take furosemide > Pregnancy and furosemide
text:
Tell your doctor if you're pregnant or trying to get pregnant. Furosemide is not usually used during pregnancy.

Find out more about taking diuretic medicines during pregnancy on the Bumps (Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy) website.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > Taking furosemide with other medicines, food and drink
text:
There are some medicines and supplements that may not mix well with furosemide.

This includes:

- other medicines used to treat high blood pressure, including aliskerin, beta blockers and ACE inhibitors like lisinopril
- medicines used to treat heart rhythm problems, including digoxin, amiodarone, flecainide and sotalol
- medicines or supplements that increase your potassium levels
- some non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
- medicines used to treat constipation (laxatives)
- fluconzanole (an antifungal commonly used to treat thrush)
- antidepressants, such as amitriptyline and sertraline
- antipsychotics, such as risperidone
- lithium (used to treat some mental health problems)

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > Taking furosemide with other medicines, food and drink
text: This is not the full list of medicines that may not mix well with. Before taking it, tell your doctor if you’re taking any other medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > Taking furosemide with other medicines, food and drink > Food, drink and alcohol with furosemide
text:
You can eat as normal while taking furosemide, but check with your doctor how much fluid you can drink while you’re taking it.

It’s important not to get dehydrated while taking furosemide, but how much you drink will depend on why you’re taking it.

It’s best not to drink alcohol because it can cause side effects like dizziness, feeling light-headed and dehydration.

title: Furosemide
section_path: Furosemide > Find out more about your medicine
text:
To find out more about your medicine, you can:

- check the leaflet that comes with it
- search for your medicine leaflet on the electronic medicines compendium website
- speak to a pharmacist or doctor for advice

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
text: Find out how fusidic acid treats skin and eye infections and how to use it.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > About fusidic acid
text:
Brand name: Fucidin

Fusidic acid is also sometimes known as sodium fusidate.

Fusidic acid is an antibiotic. It works by stopping bacteria from growing.

It's used to treat bacterial infections, such as

- skin infections including impetigo
- eye infections including conjunctivitis

Fusidic acid is only available on prescription. It comes as a cream, ointment, or eye drops.

It's also available with a steroid as a combined cream. Brand names include Fucibet (fusidic acid with betamethasone) and Fucidin H (fusidic acid with hydrocortisone).

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > About fusidic acid
text: It's also given by injection, as a liquid you swallow, or as tablets, but these are usually only used in hospital.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > About fusidic acid > Key facts
text: - You'll usually use fusidic acid eye drops twice a day, or fusidic acid cream or ointment 3 or 4 times a day. - Common side effects of fusidic acid eye drops include dry, sore, itchy or stinging eyes. It's unusual to get side effects with fusidic acid cream or ointment. - If you get blurred vision after using eye drops, avoid driving, cycling or using tools or machines until your vision is better. - Your condition should improve a few days after starting treatment. - It's important to finish your full course of treatment, to stop the infection coming back.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Who can and cannot use fusidic acid
text: Brand name: Fucidin

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Who can and cannot use fusidic acid > Who can use fusidic acid
text: Most adults and children can use fusidic acid cream, ointment and eye drops.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Who can and cannot use fusidic acid > Who may not be able to use fusidic acid
text: Fusidic acid is not suitable for some people. To make sure it's safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had an allergic reaction to fusidic acid or any other medicine.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid
text:
Brand name: Fucidin

Always follow the instructions from a pharmacist or doctor, or the leaflet in the medicine packet.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid > Dosage and how to use fusidic acid
text:
Fusidic acid comes as a cream, an ointment or eye drops.

The main difference between fusidic acid cream and ointment is how it feels. The ointment is greasier than the cream.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid > Dosage and how to use fusidic acid > Dose for cream and ointment
text:
Whether you're using cream or ointment, you'll usually put it on 3 or 4 times a day.

If you are using a cream which also contains a steroid, you'll usually put it on twice a day.

If you have been told to cover the infected skin with any dressings or bandages, including a nappy if you are using it on a baby, you may not need to use the medicine so often. Follow your doctor's advice.

Check with your pharmacist or doctor if you're unsure.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid > Dosage and how to use fusidic acid > Dose for eye drops
text:
Fusidic acid eye drops come as a gel in a tube. As the gel touches your eye it becomes runnier.

You'll usually put 1 drop into your eye twice a day, once in the morning and once in the evening.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid > Dosage and how to use fusidic acid > How to use cream or ointment
text: - Always wash your hands before using fusidic acid cream or ointment. Unless you're using the cream or ointment to treat your hands, always wash your hands afterwards, too. - Remove the cap. Check the seal is not broken before you first use the cream or ointment. There is a small spike in the top of the cap – push this spike through the seal on the tube. - Put a thin layer of cream or ointment onto the infected area and gently rub it on. - Be careful to avoid your eyes if you use it on your face.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid > Dosage and how to use fusidic acid > How to use cream or ointment
text:
If you get any medicine in your eye, wash it out with cold water straight away, then bathe your eye with eyewash if possible. Your eye may sting.

If you start to have any problems with your sight or your eye is sore, contact your doctor immediately.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid > Dosage and how to use fusidic acid > How to use cream or ointment > Important: Fire warning
text: Fusidic acid cream or ointment applied to the skin can dry onto your clothes and bedding. This makes them more likely to catch fire. Wash your clothes and bedding regularly to reduce build-up of fusidic acid, although this will not totally remove it. Avoid smoking or going near naked flames.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid > Dosage and how to use fusidic acid > How to use eye drops
text:
- Always wash your hands before using fusidic acid eye drops. - Take the cap off the tube when you're ready to use the medicine. Check that the seal is not broken before you first use the eye drops. - It's important that the tip of the tube does not touch your eye. - Tilt your head back. Pull your lower eyelid down gently. Hold the tube over your eye and look up. Squeeze 1 drop into your lower eyelid. It may help to use a mirror.

You might get some blurred vision straight after putting the drop into your eye, but this should clear after a few minutes.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid > Dosage and how to use fusidic acid > How to use eye drops
text:
If the eye drops are for a child, it might be easier to put the drops in while they're asleep or lying down.

If you normally wear contact lenses, wear your glasses instead until your symptoms have completely gone. Wait for 24 hours after the last dose of eye drops before using your contact lenses again. The eye drops can damage some contact lenses.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid > Dosage and how to use fusidic acid > How long to use it for
text:
Your condition should start to improve a few days after you start treatment.

But it's very important to use the medicine for as long as your doctor has told you to use it. There may still be some bacteria on your skin or in your eye, even if it looks normal again.

Treatment with fusidic acid cream or ointment is usually for 1 or 2 weeks, although you'll sometimes use it for longer.

If you're using fusidic acid eye drops, you'll usually carry on using them for at least 48 hours after you feel better and your eye looks normal. This will help make sure that all the bacteria have been killed.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid > Dosage and how to use fusidic acid > How long to use it for
text: Do not keep the eye drops for more than one month after you first open them. Ask your pharmacist how to dispose of the rest of the medicine correctly.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid > Dosage and how to use fusidic acid > How long to use it for > Important: Finishing your course of fusidic acid
text: Carry on using this medicine until you have finished the course, even if you feel better. If you stop your treatment early, the infection could come back.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid > If you forget to use it
text: If you forget to use fusidic acid, use it as soon as you remember. Then continue to use it at the usual time.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > How and when to use fusidic acid > If you use too much
text:
If you use too much fusidic acid cream, ointment or eye drops, or if you get some in your mouth, it's unlikely to harm you.

Talk to your pharmacist or doctor if you're worried, or if you or your child swallow a lot of the medicine.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Side effects of fusidic acid
text:
Brand name: Fucidin

Like all medicines, fusidic acid can cause side effects, although not everyone gets them.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Side effects of fusidic acid > Common side effects of fusidic acid > Common side effects of cream or ointment
text:
It's unusual to have side effects with fusidic acid cream or ointment.

Some people get skin irritation where they put the cream or ointment on. This happens in less than 1 in 100 people.

Keep using the cream or ointment, but talk to your pharmacist or doctor if skin irritation bothers you or does not go away.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Side effects of fusidic acid > Common side effects of fusidic acid > Common side effects of eye drops
text:
These common side effects of fusidic acid eye drops happen in more than 1 in 10 people. There are things you can do to help cope with them:

Burning, stinging, itching, soreness or dryness in the eye you're treating

Do not rub your eye as this can make things worse. Wet a clean flannel with cool water, close your eye and put the flannel over your eye for a few minutes to ease the symptoms.

Make sure you do not share the flannel with others, and wash it after you've used it.

Always wash your hands after touching your eyes to stop the infection spreading.

Blurred vision in the eye you're treating

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Side effects of fusidic acid > Common side effects of fusidic acid > Common side effects of eye drops
text:
Avoid driving, cycling or using tools or machines while this is happening. If it lasts for more than a day or two, speak to your doctor as they may need to change your treatment.

Keep using the eye drops, but talk to your doctor if the advice on how to cope does not help and these side effects bother you or do not go away.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Side effects of fusidic acid > Serious side effects
text:
Serious side effects of fusidic acid are rare and happen in less than 1 in 1,000 people.

Call a doctor or call 111 now if:

- your eye infection gets worse after using the eye drops
- you have burning or stinging in your eye that does not go away
- you get itchy, raised areas of skin that may look red, although the redness may be harder to see on brown or black skin – this could be a sign of hives (urticaria)

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Side effects of fusidic acid > Serious side effects > Serious allergic reaction
text: In rare cases, it's possible to have a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to fusidic acid.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Side effects of fusidic acid > Serious side effects > Serious allergic reaction > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
text:
- your lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly become swollen
- you're breathing very fast or struggling to breathe (you may become very wheezy or feel like you're choking or gasping for air)
- your throat feels tight or you're struggling to swallow
- your skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale (if you have black or brown skin, this may be easier to see on the palms of your hands or soles of your feet)
- you suddenly become very confused, drowsy or dizzy
- someone faints and cannot be woken up
- a child is limp, floppy or not responding like they normally do (their head may fall to the side, backwards or forwards, or they may find it difficult to lift their head or focus on your face)

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Side effects of fusidic acid > Serious side effects > Serious allergic reaction > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
text:
You or the person who's unwell may also have a rash that's swollen, raised, itchy, blistered or peeling.

These can be signs of a serious allergic reaction and may need immediate treatment in hospital.

Do not drive yourself to A&E.

The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Side effects of fusidic acid > Other side effects
text: These are not all the side effects of fusidic acid cream, ointment or eye drops. For a full list, see the leaflet inside your medicines packet.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Side effects of fusidic acid > Reporting side effects
text:
You can report any suspected side effect using the Yellow Card safety scheme.

Visit the Yellow Card website for more information about reporting side effects.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while using fusidic acid
text: Brand name: Fucidin

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while using fusidic acid > Fusidic acid and pregnancy
text:
It's safe to use fusidic acid cream, ointment or eye drops while you're pregnant.

Very little of the medicine gets to your baby, and the small amount that does will not harm them.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while using fusidic acid > Fusidic acid and breastfeeding
text:
It's OK to use fusidic acid cream, ointment or eye drops while you're breastfeeding. It's very unlikely that any fusidic acid will get into your breast milk.

Some fusidic acid creams also contain a steroid. It's still OK to use these creams while breastfeeding, but do not apply them directly to your breast.

When using the cream or ointment, be careful that your baby does not come into contact with the areas of your body you have put it on. Wash your hands after you have used it and before picking up your baby.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while using fusidic acid > Fusidic acid and breastfeeding
text:
If you're using fusidic acid for impetigo and you need to put the cream or ointment on your breasts or nipples, wash it off before feeding your baby. It's usually better to use cream rather than ointment when breastfeeding, as it's easier to wash off. If you're using fusidic acid for another condition, do not apply it to your breast without first speaking to your doctor or a pharmacist.

It's very rare for breastfed babies to have side effects from medicines you're using. But it's important to keep monitoring your baby if you're using any medicine while breastfeeding.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while using fusidic acid > Fusidic acid and breastfeeding
text: Contact your healthcare professional or call 111 as soon as possible if you notice that your baby is not feeding as well as usual, has any unusual symptoms, or if you're worried about them.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while using fusidic acid > Fusidic acid and fertility
text: There's no evidence to suggest that using fusidic acid reduces fertility in either men or women.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Using fusidic acid with other medicines and herbal supplements
text: Brand name: Fucidin

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Using fusidic acid with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines
text: There are no other medicines, herbal remedies or supplements known to cause problems if you take them at the same time as fusidic acid cream, ointment or eye drops.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Using fusidic acid with other medicines and herbal supplements > Important: Medicine safety
text: Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you're taking any other medicines, including herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Common questions about fusidic acid
text:
Brand name: Fucidin

How does fusidic acid work?

Fusidic acid is an antibiotic. It kills the bacteria causing the infection, by stopping it from growing and spreading.

When will I feel better?

Your condition should improve a few days after starting treatment.

It's very important to use the medicine for as long as your doctor has told you to, even if you feel better.

Carry on using fusidic acid until you have finished the course.

If your infection is no better after using fusidic acid for 7 days, make another appointment with your doctor.

Also tell them if you start to feel worse at any time.

Will it give me thrush?

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Common questions about fusidic acid
text:
No, you're unlikely to get thrush from using fusidic acid.

Some people get thrush after taking a course of antibiotic tablets. It happens because antibiotics kill the normal harmless bacteria that help to protect you against thrush.

But fusidic acid creams, ointments and eye drops only work on the area where you're using them (on your skin or in your eyes) so the medicine does not get into the rest of your body.

Will it affect my contraception?

Fusidic acid cream, ointment and eye drops will not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception.

Can I drive or ride a bike?

title: Fusidic acid (Fucidin)
section_path: Fusidic acid (Fucidin) > Common questions about fusidic acid
text:
After putting fusidic acid eye drops in, you might get some blurred vision for a short time.

If this happens to you, do not drive, cycle or use machinery or tools until your vision is clear.

Can I drink alcohol while using fusidic acid?

Yes, you can drink alcohol while using fusidic acid.

Is there any food or drink I need to avoid?

You can eat and drink normally while using fusidic acid.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
text:
Other brand names: Ispagel

Find out how Fybogel treats constipation and how to take it.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > About Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
text:
Other brand names: Ispagel

Ispaghula husk is a laxative taken to treat constipation (difficulty pooing). It's usually known by the brand name Fybogel. Other brand names include Ispagel.

It works by bulking poo up with fluid so that it's softer.

It comes as plain or fruit-flavoured granules that you mix with water to make a high-fibre drink.

Fybogel is available on prescription and to buy from pharmacies and shops.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > About Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Key facts
text: - Fybogel is a high-fibre drink that you take in the morning and evening, preferably after a meal. - It usually takes 2 or 3 days to work. - When taking this type of laxative, it's important to drink plenty of fluids. - The main side effects are wind and bloating. - It's possible to have a mild allergic reaction to Fybogel such as itchy eyes, nose or skin. To help avoid this, try not to breathe in the powder.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Who can and cannot take Fybogel
text: Other brand names: Ispagel

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Who can and cannot take Fybogel > Who can take Fybogel
text:
Most adults can take Fybogel, including while pregnant or breastfeeding.

Only give Fybogel to a child under 6 years old if it's been prescribed by a doctor.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Who can and cannot take Fybogel > Who may not be able to take Fybogel
text:
Fybogel is not suitable for some people. To make sure it's safe for you, tell your doctor or pharmacist before taking Fybogel if you have:

- ever had an allergic reaction to Fybogel or any other medicine
- any changes in your poo, such as having blood in it, or how often you need to poo, which are unusual for you and has lasted longer than 2 weeks
- tummy pain and you feel sick or are being sick, these could be signs of a blockage in your bowel
- muscle weakness of the bowel (colonic atony)
- difficulty swallowing or any throat problems
- a rare genetic condition called phenylketonuria

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > How and when to take Fybogel
text:
Other brand names: Ispagel

Fybogel comes as sachets of plain, orange- or lemon-flavoured granules.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > How and when to take Fybogel > Dosage and how to take Fybogel > Dosage
text:
The usual dose of Fybogel for constipation is:

- for adults and children aged 12 years and over – 1 sachet of granules twice a day
- for children aged 6 to 11 years – half to 1 level (5ml) teaspoonful of granules twice a day
- for children aged 5 years or under – half to 1 level (5ml) teaspoonful of granules twice a day, only if recommended by a doctor

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > How and when to take Fybogel > Dosage and how to take Fybogel > How to take Fybogel
text:
It's best to take Fybogel after a meal or snack and at least 30 minutes before or after you take any other medicine.

To make up the medicine, open the sachet and empty the amount of granules you need into a glass. Add at least 150ml of cold water to the glass.

Stir well until all the granules have dissolved and the Fybogel solution is clear or slightly hazy, then drink it immediately.

Try not to breathe in the powder when you make up the Fybogel drink, because there's a small chance this could trigger a mild allergic reaction.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > How and when to take Fybogel > Dosage and how to take Fybogel > How to take Fybogel
text:
Have your evening drink of Fybogel at least an hour before going to bed. Do not drink Fybogel just before you go to sleep because this can make it harder for your bowel to move the poo along.

It's important to drink extra fluid if you're taking Fybogel. Adults should try to drink more than 2 litres, or around 8 glasses, of fluid each day. If you do not drink enough fluid while taking Fybogel, your constipation may get worse.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > How and when to take Fybogel > Dosage and how to take Fybogel > How long to take it for
text:
Talk to a doctor if your constipation has not improved or it gets worse after 3 days or taking Fybogel.

For more serious constipation, or if you're taking Fybogel to increase the fibre in your diet, your doctor may recommend that you take it for many months.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > How and when to take Fybogel > If you forget to take it
text:
If you forget a dose of Fybogel, skip the missed dose and take the next dose at the usual time.

Never take 2 doses at the same time. Never take an extra dose to make up for a forgotten one.

If you often forget doses, it may help to set an alarm to remind you. You could also ask your pharmacist for advice on other ways to help you remember to take your medicine

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > How and when to take Fybogel > If you take too much
text:
Taking more than the usual dose of Fybogel may cause wind (farting) and tummy pain. If you take an extra dose, drink plenty of water.

If you have pain or symptoms that worry you, speak to your doctor or call NHS 111 for advice.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Side effects of Fybogel
text:
Other brand names: Ispagel

Like all medicines, Fybogel may cause side effects in some people, but many people have no side effects or only minor ones.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Side effects of Fybogel > Side effects of Fybogel
text:
Side effects of Fybogel include wind and bloating.

This sometimes happens because of the sudden increase of fibre in your diet.

It should get better after a few days. If the side effects continue, or you're worried, talk to your doctor or pharmacist.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Side effects of Fybogel > Side effects of Fybogel > Mild allergic reaction
text:
It's possible to have a mild allergic reaction to Fybogel, such as itchy eyes, nose or skin.

You're more likely to have a mild allergic reaction if you have had an allergic reaction before and if you're exposed to the powder regularly (for example, you care for someone who takes Fybogel).

If you think you're having a mild allergic reaction to Fybogel, stop taking it and ask your pharmacist or doctor for advice.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Side effects of Fybogel > Side effects of Fybogel > Serious side effects
text: In rare cases, it's possible to have a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to Fybogel.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Side effects of Fybogel > Side effects of Fybogel > Serious side effects > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
text:
- your lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly become swollen
- you're breathing very fast or struggling to breathe (you may become very wheezy or feel like you're choking or gasping for air)
- your throat feels tight or you're struggling to swallow
- your skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale (if you have black or brown skin, this may be easier to see on the palms of your hands or soles of your feet)
- you suddenly become very confused, drowsy or dizzy
- someone faints and cannot be woken up
- a child is limp, floppy or not responding like they normally do (their head may fall to the side, backwards or forwards, or they may find it difficult to lift their head or focus on your face)

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Side effects of Fybogel > Side effects of Fybogel > Serious side effects > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
text:
You or the person who's unwell may also have a rash that's swollen, raised, itchy, blistered or peeling.

These can be signs of a serious allergic reaction and may need immediate treatment in hospital.

Do not drive yourself to A&E.

The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Side effects of Fybogel > Side effects of Fybogel > Other side effects
text: These are not all the side effects of Fybogel. For a full list, see the leaflet inside your medicines packet.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Side effects of Fybogel > Reporting side effects
text:
You can report any suspected side effect using the Yellow Card safety scheme.

Visit the Yellow Card website for more information about reporting side effects.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking Fybogel
text: Other brand names: Ispagel

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking Fybogel > Fybogel and pregnancy
text: Fybogel is commonly taken during pregnancy and is not harmful to your baby.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking Fybogel > Fybogel and breastfeeding
text:
You can take Fybogel while breastfeeding.

It does not pass into breast milk so has not caused any side effects in breastfed babies.

It’s important to drink plenty of fluids while taking Fybogel, and this will also help with your breast milk supply.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking Fybogel > Fybogel and fertility
text:
There's no evidence to suggest that Fybogel reduces fertility in either men or women.

For more information about treating constipation and how laxatives can affect you and your baby during pregnancy, visit the Bumps (Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy) website

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Taking Fybogel with other medicines and herbal supplements
text: Other brand names: Ispagel

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Taking Fybogel with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines
text:
Fybogel can change the way some medicines work.

Tell your pharmacist or doctor if you're taking any other medicines before you start to take Fybogel, including:

- lithium, a medicine for mood problems
- carbamazepine, a medicine for epilepsy and mood problems
- digoxin, a heart medicine
- insulin or any other medicine for diabetes
- mesalazine, a medicine to treat bowel disease
- pain medicines that can cause constipation, such as codeine

These are not all the medicines that may cause problems if you take them with Fybogel. For a full list, see the leaflet inside your medicine packet.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Taking Fybogel with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines
text: Fybogel can affect how other medicines, vitamins and supplements are absorbed in your body. If you need to take another medicine or a supplement, take it more than an hour before or after you take Fybogel.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Taking Fybogel with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines > Taking Fybogel with other laxatives
text:
Sometimes you may need to take 2 different types of laxatives at the same time to get your bowel moving.

Only take 2 types of laxatives together if a doctor or pharmacist has recommended it because it can increase your chance of side effects.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Taking Fybogel with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines > Taking Fybogel with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) remedies
text: You can take Fybogel at the same time as IBS remedies such as Buscopan.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Taking Fybogel with other medicines and herbal supplements > Mixing Fybogel with herbal remedies and supplements
text: Take Fybogel more than an hour before or after taking any other medicines, remedies or supplements.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Taking Fybogel with other medicines and herbal supplements > Important: Medicine safety
text: Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you're taking any other medicines, including herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Common questions about Fybogel
text:
Other brand names: Ispagel

How does Fybogel work?

Fybogel is a type of laxative called a bulk-forming laxative. It makes your poo softer and bigger, so it's easier to pass.

When will I feel better?

It takes 2 to 3 days for Fybogel to work.

Talk to your doctor if you're still constipated after 3 days. They may be able to suggest a different medicine.

How does Fybogel compare with other laxatives?

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Common questions about Fybogel
text:
Other types of laxatives work in a different way from Fybogel, but are equally good at treating constipation. Which one works best for you will depend on how hard the poo is or how difficult it is to push out.

Some may work quicker than Fybogel.

Osmotic laxatives (for example, lactulose) draw water from the rest of the body into your bowel to soften poo and make it easier to pass. They take 2 or 3 days to work.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Common questions about Fybogel
text:
Stimulant laxatives (for example, senna and bisacodyl) speed up your bowel by stimulating nerves that control the muscles lining your gut. They work faster than other laxatives. If you take them at bedtime, they work overnight.

Poo-softening laxatives (for example, arachis oil and docusate) allow water to get into poo so it's softer and easier to pass.

Can I take Fybogel after an operation?

Yes, you can take Fybogel to relieve constipation after surgery.

Will it affect my contraception?

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Common questions about Fybogel
text:
Fybogel does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill, progestogen-only pill or emergency contraception.

Can I drive or ride a bike?

Taking Fybogel should not affect your ability to drive or ride a bike.

Can I drink alcohol while taking Fybogel?

Yes, you can drink alcohol while taking Fybogel.

Is there any food or drink I need to avoid?

You can eat and drink normally while taking Fybogel. Drink plenty of water to keep poo soft.

title: Fybogel (ispaghula husk)
section_path: Fybogel (ispaghula husk) > Common questions about Fybogel
text:
It might help to stop eating refined and processed foods or foods that do not contain much fibre, such as pastries, ice cream, cheese and meat for a while, as these foods can make constipation worse.

Can lifestyle changes help constipation?

You may be able to improve your constipation without using laxatives.

Before trying Fybogel, or to stop constipation coming back, it may help to:

- get more fibre into your diet – adults should aim for about 30g of fibre a day. High-fibre foods include fruit, vegetables and cereals. If you're not used to eating high-fibre foods, increase the amount of fibre you eat gradually
- try bulking agents, such as wheat bran, which can help make your poo softer and easier to pass (although this type of fibre can sometimes make bloating worse)
- drink plenty of water to keep poo soft
- exercise – being physically active helps to keep your bowel moving

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin
text: Read about how gabapentin treats epilepsy and nerve pain, and how to take it.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > About gabapentin
text:
Gabapentin is used to treat epilepsy.

It's also taken for nerve pain, which can be caused by different conditions, such as diabetes and shingles, or by an injury.

In epilepsy, it's thought that gabapentin stops seizures by reducing the abnormal electrical activity in the brain.

With nerve pain, it's thought to block pain by affecting the pain messages travelling through the brain and down the spine.

Gabapentin is available on prescription. It comes as tablets, capsules and a liquid that you swallow.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > About gabapentin > Key facts
text: - You'll usually take gabapentin 3 times a day. You can take it with or without food. - Most people who take gabapentin do not get any side effects, but some people may feel sleepy, tired and dizzy. Common side effects are usually mild and go away by themselves. - It takes at least a few weeks for gabapentin to work. - Most people do not have to stay on the same brand of gabapentin as there's very little difference between brands. - Some people can become addicted to gabapentin. When stopping gabapentin, you'll need to reduce your dose gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms. - If you take medicines for epilepsy, you're entitled to free prescriptions for all the medicines you take, not just your epilepsy ones. You can get an application form from your doctor's surgery.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Who can and cannot take gabapentin > Who can take gabapentin
text: Most adults and children aged 6 years and over can take gabapentin. It's sometimes prescribed for younger children by a specialist doctor.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Who can and cannot take gabapentin > Who may not be able to take gabapentin
text:
Gabapentin is not suitable for some people.

To make sure it's safe for you, tell your doctor if you:

- have ever had an allergic reaction to gabapentin or any other medicine
- have ever misused or been addicted to a medicine
- are trying to get pregnant or are already pregnant
- are on a controlled sodium or potassium diet, or your kidneys do not work well – gabapentin liquid contains sodium and potassium, so speak to your doctor before taking it
- have a condition that affects lungs and airways, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or severe asthma

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > How and when to take gabapentin
text: Gabapentin is a prescription medicine. It's important to take it as advised by your doctor.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > How and when to take gabapentin > Dosage and how to take gabapentin
text:
Each capsule of gabapentin contains 100mg, 300mg or 400mg of gabapentin. Each tablet contains 600mg or 800mg of gabapentin.

If you're taking gabapentin as a liquid, it usually contains 50mg in 1ml of liquid. Always check the label.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > How and when to take gabapentin > Dosage and how to take gabapentin > Dosage for epilepsy
text:
The usual dose for:

- adults and older children (aged 12 and over) is 900mg to 3,600mg a day, split into 3 doses
- younger children (aged 6 to 12 years) – varies depending on their weight

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > How and when to take gabapentin > Dosage and how to take gabapentin > Dosage for nerve pain
text: The usual dose to treat nerve pain in adults is 900mg to 3,600mg a day, split into 3 doses.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > How and when to take gabapentin > Dosage and how to take gabapentin > Changes to your dose
text:
To reduce the risk of side effects, your doctor will prescribe a low dose to start with and then increase it over a few days.

When you find a dose that suits you, it will usually stay the same.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > How and when to take gabapentin > Dosage and how to take gabapentin > How to take it
text:
Swallow gabapentin capsules and tablets whole with a drink of water or juice. Do not chew them.

You can take gabapentin with or without food.

Try to space your doses evenly through the day. For example, you could take it first thing in the morning, early afternoon and at bedtime.

If you or your child are taking a liquid, it will come with a plastic syringe or spoon to measure your dose. If you do not have a syringe or spoon, ask your pharmacist for one. Do not use a kitchen spoon, as it will not measure the right amount.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > How and when to take gabapentin > Dosage and how to take gabapentin > How long to take it for
text:
If you have epilepsy, it's likely that when your condition is under control you'll still need to take gabapentin for many years.

If you have nerve pain, when your pain has gone you'll continue to take gabapentin for several months or longer to stop it coming back.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > How and when to take gabapentin > If you forget to take it
text:
If you forget a dose, take it as soon as you remember, unless it's within 2 hours of your next dose. In this case, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the usual time.

Never take 2 doses at the same time. Never take an extra dose to make up for a forgotten one.

If you have epilepsy, it's important to take this medicine regularly. Missing doses may trigger a seizure.

If you forget doses often, it may help to set an alarm to remind you. You could also ask your pharmacist for advice on other ways to help you remember to take your medicine.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > How and when to take gabapentin > If you take too much
text: Taking too much gabapentin can cause unpleasant side effects.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > How and when to take gabapentin > Immediate action required: Go to A&E or call 999 now if:
text:
You take more than your prescribed dose of gabapentin and you:

- feel dizzy or sleepy
- have double vision
- start slurring your words
- pass out (faint)

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > How and when to take gabapentin > Urgent advice: Contact 111 for advice if:
text:
- you take more than your prescribed dose of gabapentin

You can call 111 or get help from 111 online.

If you need to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring the gabapentin packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > How and when to take gabapentin > Stopping gabapentin
text:
It's important you do not suddenly stop taking gabapentin, even if you feel better. Stopping gabapentin suddenly can cause serious problems.

If you have epilepsy, stopping gabapentin suddenly can cause seizures that will not stop.

If you're taking it for any reason and stop suddenly, you may have severe withdrawal symptoms, including:

- anxiety
- difficulty sleeping
- feeling sick
- pain
- sweating

It's possible to prevent withdrawal seizures and other symptoms by gradually reducing the dose of gabapentin.

Do not stop taking gabapentin without talking to your doctor first. You'll need to reduce your dose gradually.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin
text: Like all medicines, gabapentin can cause side effects, although not everyone gets them.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Common side effects of gabapentin
text:
These common side effects of gabapentin may happen in more than 1 in 100 people. They're usually mild and go away by themselves.

There are things you can do to help cope with them.

Feeling sleepy, tired or dizzy

Do not drive, cycle or use tools or machinery until you feel better.

As your body gets used to gabapentin, these side effects should wear off. If they do not wear off within a week or two, your doctor may reduce your dose or increase it more slowly. If that does not work, your doctor may suggest a different medicine.

Feeling sick (nausea)

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Common side effects of gabapentin
text:
Take gabapentin with or after a meal or snack. It may also help if you do not eat rich or spicy food. Take small sips of water or other fluids to avoid dehydration. Signs of dehydration include peeing less than usual or having dark, strong-smelling pee.

Being sick (vomiting)

Take small sips of water or other fluids to avoid dehydration. Signs of dehydration include peeing less than usual or having dark, strong-smelling pee. Do not take any other medicines to treat vomiting without speaking to a pharmacist or doctor.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Common side effects of gabapentin
text:
If you take the combined pill or the progestogen-only pill and you're being sick, your contraception may not protect you from pregnancy. Check the pill packet for advice.

Diarrhoea

Drink plenty of water or other fluids to avoid dehydration. Signs of dehydration include peeing less than usual or having dark, strong-smelling pee. Do not take any other medicines to treat diarrhoea without speaking to a pharmacist or doctor.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Common side effects of gabapentin
text:
If you take the combined contraceptive pill or the progestogen-only pill and you have severe, watery diarrhoea, or any diarrhoea that lasts for more than 24 hours, while taking gabapentin, your contraception may not protect you from pregnancy. Check the pill packet for advice.

Mood changes

If you feel this medicine is causing mood changes, talk to your doctor. They may be able to change you to a different medicine.

Swollen arms and legs

Try sitting with your feet raised on a chair or bed. When you stand up, try not to stand for too long. Gently exercising your arms might help. Talk to your doctor if this does not get better.

Blurred vision

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Common side effects of gabapentin
text:
Avoid driving, cycling or using tools or machinery while this is happening. If it lasts for more than a couple of days, speak to your doctor as they may need to change your treatment.

Dry mouth

Try chewing sugar-free gum or sucking sugar-free sweets. Brush your teeth twice a day and see your dentist regularly for check-ups.

Difficulty getting an erection

Speak to your doctor. They may be able to change your medicine or offer other treatments that might help with this problem.

Weight gain

Gabapentin can make you more hungry, so it can be easy to put on weight.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Common side effects of gabapentin
text:
Try to eat a healthy, balanced diet without increasing your portion sizes. Do not snack on foods that contain a lot of calories, such as crisps, cakes, biscuits and sweets. If you feel hungry between meals, eat fruit and vegetables and low-calorie foods.

Doing more exercise will also help.

Memory problems

If you're having problems with your memory, speak to your doctor. They may want you to try a different medicine.

Headaches

Make sure you rest and drink plenty of fluids. It's best not to drink too much alcohol. Ask your pharmacist to recommend a painkiller.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Common side effects of gabapentin
text:
Headaches should usually go away after the first week of taking gabapentin. Talk to your doctor if they last longer than a week or are severe.

Getting more infections than usual

If you notice this, speak to your doctor.

Keep taking the medicine, but talk to your doctor if this advice does not help and a side effect is still bothering you or does not go away.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Serious side effects
text:
Very few people taking gabapentin have serious side effects.

Call a doctor or call 111 now if you:

- have a high temperature, swollen glands that do not go away, your eyes or skin turn yellow (this may be less obvious on brown or black skin), unusual bruises or bleeding, severe tiredness or weakness, unexpected muscle pain or weakness, with or without a rash – these may be symptoms of a serious reaction
- have long-lasting stomach pain, are feeling sick or being sick – these may be signs of an inflamed pancreas
- have muscle pain or weakness and you're having dialysis treatment because of kidney failure
- are seeing or hearing things that are not there (hallucinations)
- have trouble breathing

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Serious side effects > Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E now if:
text:
- you have thoughts about harming yourself or ending your life

This can sometimes happen after only a week of taking gabapentin.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Serious side effects > Serious allergic reaction
text: In rare cases, it's possible to have a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to gabapentin.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Serious side effects > Serious allergic reaction > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
text:
- your lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly become swollen
- you're breathing very fast or struggling to breathe (you may become very wheezy or feel like you're choking or gasping for air)
- your throat feels tight or you're struggling to swallow
- your skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale (if you have black or brown skin, this may be easier to see on the palms of your hands or soles of your feet)
- you suddenly become very confused, drowsy or dizzy
- someone faints and cannot be woken up
- a child is limp, floppy or not responding like they normally do (their head may fall to the side, backwards or forwards, or they may find it difficult to lift their head or focus on your face)

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Serious side effects > Serious allergic reaction > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
text:
You or the person who's unwell may also have a rash that's swollen, raised, itchy, blistered or peeling.

These can be signs of a serious allergic reaction and may need immediate treatment in hospital.

Do not drive yourself to A&E.

The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Long-term side effects
text:
Some people can become addicted to gabapentin. If this happens, you'll have withdrawal symptoms after you stop taking the medicine.

When you stop taking gabapentin, you'll need to reduce your dose gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms. Do not stop taking gabapentin without talking to your doctor.

Talk to your doctor if you're concerned about becoming physically dependent on gabapentin.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Other side effects
text: These are not all the side effects of gabapentin. For a full list, see the leaflet inside your medicines packet.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Side effects of gabapentin > Reporting side effects
text:
You can report any suspected side effect using the Yellow Card safety scheme.

Visit the Yellow Card website for more information about reporting side effects.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking gabapentin > Gabapentin and pregnancy
text:
Gabapentin is not generally recommended in pregnancy as there's not enough information about whether it's safe for your baby.

However, from the small amount of information that is available, there's no clear evidence that it's harmful. It should only be taken if the benefits of the medicine outweigh the possible risks.

If you take gabapentin for epilepsy, it's important that this is well controlled during pregnancy, as seizures can harm you and your baby. Keep taking gabapentin, but talk to your doctor urgently. They may recommend you change to a different medicine.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking gabapentin > Gabapentin and pregnancy
text:
If you're trying to get pregnant or have become pregnant while taking gabapentin, it's recommended to take a high dose of folic acid (5mg a day). You can get this from your doctor or midwife.

Ideally, you'll take high-dose folic acid for 3 months before you start trying to get pregnant and for the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. Do not worry if you have not taken it before you get pregnant, but start taking it as soon as possible once you know you're pregnant. It helps your baby to grow normally.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking gabapentin > Gabapentin and pregnancy
text:
If you take gabapentin around the time of giving birth, your baby may need extra monitoring for a few days after they're born. This is because they may have withdrawal symptoms from gabapentin.

We do not know what the long-term effects of taking gabapentin in pregnancy may be on childhood learning and development. For safety, you'll usually be advised to take it only if the benefits of the medicine outweigh the risks. Talk to your doctor about the benefits and risks.

Find out more about how gabapentin can affect you and your baby on the Bumps (Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy) website

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking gabapentin > Gabapentin and breastfeeding
text:
If your baby is healthy, you can take gabapentin while breastfeeding, but talk to your doctor or pharmacist first.

It's important to keep taking gabapentin to keep you well. Breastfeeding will also benefit both you and your baby.

Gabapentin passes into breast milk in very small amounts. It has not been known to cause any side effects in breastfed babies. But it's important to keep monitoring your baby if you're taking any medicine while breastfeeding.

Contact your healthcare professional or call 111 as soon as possible if you notice that your baby:

- is not feeding as well as usual, or putting on weight as expected
- is more irritable than usual
- is unusually sleepy
- has a stomach upset, such as diarrhoea, constipation, or is being sick (vomiting)
- has a rash

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking gabapentin > Gabapentin and breastfeeding
text:
If your baby has any symptoms that are not listed, or if you're worried about them, you can also call 111 or contact any healthcare professional.

Carry on taking gabapentin, and keep breastfeeding as usual until you've got advice about your baby's symptoms.

It's important not to share a bed with your baby while you're taking gabapentin.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking gabapentin > Gabapentin and fertility
text:
There's no evidence that taking gabapentin affects fertility in either men or women.

However, speak to a doctor if you're trying to get pregnant. They may wish to review your medicine and prescribe a higher dose of folic acid for you to take (5mg a day) before you become pregnant.

Speak to a pharmacist or your doctor before taking gabapentin if you're trying to get pregnant.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking gabapentin > Non-urgent advice: Tell you're doctor if you're:
text:
- trying to get pregnant
- pregnant
- breastfeeding

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Taking gabapentin with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines
text:
Some medicines may affect how gabapentin works or increase the chance of you having side effects.

Antacids can reduce the amount of gabapentin that the body takes in so it does not work as well.

To stop this happening, if you need to take an antacid, take it at least 2 hours before or after your dose of gabapentin.

Check with a pharmacist or your doctor if you're taking any other medicines, including:

- strong painkillers, such as morphine – these can make you very tired and dizzy when you start taking gabapentin
- antidepressants, such as amitriptyline or fluoxetine
- antipsychotic medicines for mental health problems like schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, such as olanzapine

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Taking gabapentin with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines
text: These are not all the medicines that may cause problems if you take them with gabapentin. For a full list, see the leaflet inside your medicine packet.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Taking gabapentin with other medicines and herbal supplements > Mixing gabapentin with herbal remedies or supplements
text:
Taking herbal remedies and supplements that can make you feel dizzy or drowsy while you're taking gabapentin could make these side effects worse.

There's not enough information to say that other herbal remedies or supplements are safe to take with gabapentin. They're not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines. They're generally not tested for the effect they have on other medicines.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Taking gabapentin with other medicines and herbal supplements > Mixing gabapentin with herbal remedies or supplements > Important: Medicine safety
text: Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you're taking any other medicines, including herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Common questions about gabapentin
text:
How does gabapentin work?

In epilepsy, it's thought that gabapentin stops seizures by reducing the abnormal electrical activity in the brain.

With nerve pain, it's thought to block pain by affecting pain messages travelling through the brain and spine.

When will I feel better?

It takes a few weeks for gabapentin to work fully. You may still have seizures or pain during this time.

Are there any long-term side effects?

Some people can become addicted to gabapentin. If this happens, you'll have withdrawal symptoms after you stop taking the medicine.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Common questions about gabapentin
text:
When you stop taking gabapentin, you'll need to reduce your dose gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms. Do not stop taking gabapentin without talking to your doctor.

You can also talk to your doctor if you're concerned you are becoming physically dependent on gabapentin.

How will I know if I'm addicted to gabapentin?

If you're addicted to gabapentin, you may find it difficult to stop taking it or feel you need to take it more often than necessary.

If you stop taking gabapentin suddenly, you may get withdrawal symptoms.

These can include:

- feeling agitated or anxious
- panic attacks
- feeling your heartbeat (palpitations)
- difficulty sleeping
- shaking
- sweating
- body aches
- feeling restless

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Common questions about gabapentin
text:
Talk to your doctor if you:

- are worried about addiction
- need help with addiction
- want to stop taking gabapentin

Are there similar medicines to gabapentin?

Pregabalin (also called Lyrica) is a medicine that works in a similar way to gabapentin.

Like gabapentin, it's taken for epilepsy and nerve pain. It can also be taken for anxiety. But there are differences between pregabalin and gabapentin.

Pregabalin can be taken less often and in different doses to gabapentin.

If you need to change to pregabalin, your doctor will explain how to swap safely from gabapentin.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Common questions about gabapentin
text:
Can I get epilepsy medicines for free?

If you take medicines for epilepsy, you're entitled to free prescriptions for all the medicines you take, not just your epilepsy ones.

To claim your free prescriptions, you'll need to have a medical exemption certificate.

The application form for the medical exemption certificate is called FP92A. You can get this from your doctor's surgery.

You'll need to fill in the form, then your doctor will sign it and send it off.

Find out more about medical exemption certificates on the NHS Business Services Authority website

Is gabapentin a controlled medicine?

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Common questions about gabapentin
text:
Gabapentin is a controlled medicine. This means there are strict rules on how it's prescribed and dispensed to make sure it's not given to the wrong person or misused.

When you collect gabapentin, your pharmacist will ask for proof of identity such as your passport or driving licence. You'll also be asked to sign the back of your prescription to confirm that you've received it.

If you're collecting gabapentin for someone else, you're legally required to show the pharmacist proof of your identity if asked.

How do I collect a prescription for a controlled medicine?

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Common questions about gabapentin
text:
Your gabapentin prescription will probably need to be hand signed by a doctor. This can take longer than normal repeat prescriptions.

It's best to hand in your repeat prescription request up to 5 days before you're due to run out of gabapentin. This will give your doctor enough time to sign it.

After your prescription has been written, you'll need to collect your medicine from a pharmacist within 28 days. If you do not, your prescription will become invalid and you'll need to get a new one.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Common questions about gabapentin
text:
Sometimes your pharmacist may not be able to give you the whole amount of gabapentin prescribed to you. If this happens, you will need to go back to the pharmacy to pick up the remaining medicine within 28 days.

Again, if you do not collect your prescription within this time, it will become invalid and you will need to get a new prescription.

Do I need to stay on the same brand of gabapentin?

Most people do not have to stay on the same brand of gabapentin as there's very little difference between brands.

Talk to your doctor if you have been asked to switch to a different brand and are worried about that.

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Common questions about gabapentin
text:
If your epilepsy has been hard to control in the past and the brand you're now taking is working well for you, your doctor may recommend you stay on the same one.

Will it affect my contraception?

Gabapentin does not stop any type of contraception from working, including the combined pill, progestogen-only pill and emergency contraception.

However, if gabapentin makes you sick (vomit) or you have severe, watery diarrhoea, or any diarrhoea that lasts for more than 24 hours, your contraception may not protect you from pregnancy.

If this happens, follow the instructions in the leaflet that comes with your pills.

Find out more:

- What to do if you're sick or have diarrhoea when taking the combined pill
- What to do if you're sick or have diarrhoea when taking the progestogen-only pill

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Common questions about gabapentin
text:
Can I drive or ride a bike?

You may feel sleepy, tired or dizzy when you first start taking gabapentin. This may also happen if your dose has increased.

If this happens to you, do not drive, cycle or use machinery or tools until you feel better.

It's an offence to drive a car if your ability to drive safely is affected. It's your responsibility to decide if it's safe to drive. If you're in any doubt, do not drive.

GOV.UK has more information on the law on drugs and driving

If you have epilepsy, you're generally not allowed to drive until:

- you have not had any seizures (while awake) for 1 year
- you have only had seizures while you're asleep

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Common questions about gabapentin
text:
If you change your epilepsy medicine, your doctor will tell you whether you need to stop driving and for how long.

Epilepsy Action: driving rules if you change or withdraw your medicine

GOV.UK: epilepsy and driving information

Can I drink alcohol while taking gabapentin?

Yes, you can drink alcohol while taking gabapentin, but it may make you feel sleepy or tired.

During the first few days of taking gabapentin, it might be best to stop drinking alcohol until you see how the medicine affects you.

Is there any food or drink I need to avoid?

You can eat and drink normally while taking gabapentin.

Will recreational drugs affect gabapentin?

title: Gabapentin
section_path: Gabapentin > Common questions about gabapentin
text:
Gabapentin can intensify the highs of recreational drugs like heroin and other opioids.

If you use recreational drugs alongside gabapentin, there may be more chance of unpleasant side effects like panic attacks, anxiety and memory loss.

Find out more about the side effects of recreational drugs on the FRANK website

title: Gallbladder cancer
section_path: Gallbladder cancer
text: Find out about gallbladder cancer, including the symptoms, causes, tests, treatments, and where to get support.

title: Gallbladder cancer
section_path: Gallbladder cancer > What is gallbladder cancer?
text: - Gallbladder cancer is a cancer that's found anywhere in the gallbladder. - The gallbladder is a small organ in the top part of your tummy that helps you digest your food. - Gallbladder cancer is often found when someone is having treatment for another condition, such as gallstones. - How serious gallbladder cancer is depends on where it is in the gallbladder, how big it is, if it has spread and your general health.

title: Gallbladder cancer
section_path: Gallbladder cancer > Symptoms of gallbladder cancer > Main symptoms of gallbladder cancer
text:
Gallbladder cancer may not have any symptoms, or they might be hard to spot.

Symptoms of gallbladder cancer include:

- the whites of your eyes turning yellow or your skin turning yellow, which may be less obvious on brown or black skin (jaundice) – you may also have itchy skin, darker pee and paler poo than usual
- loss of appetite or losing weight without trying to
- a high temperature, or you feel hot, cold or shivery
- a lump in your tummy

Other symptoms can affect your digestion, such as:

- feeling or being sick
- aching pain in the right side of your tummy, sometimes described as a "dragging feeling"
- sharp pain in your tummy
- a very swollen tummy that's not related to when you eat

title: Gallbladder cancer
section_path: Gallbladder cancer > Symptoms of gallbladder cancer > Main symptoms of gallbladder cancer
text:
If you have another condition like irritable bowel syndrome you may get symptoms like these regularly.

You might find you get used to them. But it's important to be checked by a GP if your symptoms change, get worse, or do not feel normal for you.

title: Gallbladder cancer
section_path: Gallbladder cancer > Symptoms of gallbladder cancer > Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if:
text:
- the whites of your eyes or your skin turn yellow
- you're being sick for more than 2 days
- you have symptoms of gallbladder cancer that you're worried about, but are not sure where to get help

111 will tell you what to do. They can arrange a phone call from a nurse or doctor if you need one.

You can call 111 or get help from 111 online.

title: Gallbladder cancer
section_path: Gallbladder cancer > Symptoms of gallbladder cancer > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if you have:
text:
- a lump in your tummy
- lost a noticeable amount of weight
- symptoms of gallbladder cancer, such as pain or swelling in your tummy, that get worse or do not get better after 2 weeks
- a condition that causes symptoms with your digestion, and your symptoms are not getting better after 2 weeks using your usual treatments

title: Gallbladder cancer
section_path: Gallbladder cancer > Symptoms of gallbladder cancer > Important
text:
Many of these symptoms are very common and can be caused by many different conditions.

Having them does not definitely mean you have gallbladder cancer. But it's important to get them checked by a GP.

This is because if they're caused by cancer, finding it earlier makes it more treatable.

title: Gallbladder cancer
section_path: Gallbladder cancer > Symptoms of gallbladder cancer > What happens at the GP appointment
text:
The GP may feel your tummy.

They may ask you to have a blood test.

title: Gallbladder cancer
section_path: Gallbladder cancer > Symptoms of gallbladder cancer > What happens at the GP appointment > Referral to a specialist
text: You may get an urgent referral for more tests or to see a specialist in hospital if the GP thinks you have symptoms that could be cancer. This does not definitely mean you have cancer.

title: Gallbladder cancer
section_path: Gallbladder cancer > Symptoms of gallbladder cancer > What happens at the GP appointment > Find out more
text: - Cancer Research UK: seeing a GP for symptoms that could be caused by gallbladder cancer

title: Gallbladder cancer
section_path: Gallbladder cancer > Causes of gallbladder cancer > Who is more likely to get gallbladder cancer
text:
Anyone can get gallbladder cancer. It's not always clear what causes it.

You might be more likely to get it if you:

- are over the age of 75 – it's most common in people over 85
- are a woman
- have certain medical conditions, such as gallstones, growths (polyps) in your gallbladder, porcelain gallbladder, abnormal bile ducts, long-term swelling of the gallbladder or bile ducts, or diabetes
- have a brother, sister or parent who had gallbladder cancer
- have Latin American or Asian heritage

Many gallbladder cancers are linked to your lifestyle.

title: Gallbladder cancer
section_path: Gallbladder cancer > Causes of gallbladder cancer > How to lower your chance of getting gallbladder cancer
