Visit the Yellow Card website for more information about reporting side effects.

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while having hydroxocobalamin
text: Brand names: Cobalin-H, Neo-Cytamen

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while having hydroxocobalamin > Hydroxocobalamin and pregnancy
text:
Hydroxocobalamin can be used during pregnancy.

It's important that a vitamin B12 deficiency is correctly treated to make sure that you and your baby are healthy.

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while having hydroxocobalamin > Hydroxocobalamin and breastfeeding
text:
You can have hydroxocobalamin while you're breastfeeding.

Hydroxocobalamin is a natural part of breast milk. When you have hydroxocobalamin injections as a supplement or treatment, it passes into your breast milk in low amounts and helps your baby to stay healthy.

If your baby also has vitamin B12 deficiency, they will still also need treating themselves.

If you notice your baby is not feeding as well, or you have any concerns about your baby, contact your doctor, pharmacist, health visitor or midwife.

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while having hydroxocobalamin > Hydroxocobalamin and fertility
text: There's no evidence to suggest that taking hydroxocobalamin affects fertility in either men or women.

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while having hydroxocobalamin > Non-urgent advice: Tell your doctor if you're:
text:
- trying to get pregnant
- pregnant
- breastfeeding

Find out how vitamin B12 treatments such as hydroxocobalamin can affect you and your baby during pregnancy on the Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy (BUMPS) website.

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Having hydroxocobalamin with other medicines and herbal supplements
text: Brand names: Cobalin-H, Neo-Cytamen

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Having hydroxocobalamin with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines
text: Hydroxocobalamin is usually safe to have with other medicines, including painkillers.

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Having hydroxocobalamin with other medicines and herbal supplements > Mixing hydroxocobalamin with herbal remedies and supplements
text: There's not enough information to say that complementary medicines, herbal remedies and supplements are safe to take with hydroxocobalamin. They're not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines. They're generally not tested for the effect they have on other medicines.

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Having hydroxocobalamin with other medicines and herbal supplements > Important: Medicine safety
text: Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you're taking any other medicines, including herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Common questions about hydroxocobalamin
text:
Brand names: Cobalin-H, Neo-Cytamen

How does hydroxocobalamin work?

Hydroxocobalamin is a manufactured version of vitamin B12.

It works by increasing your levels of vitamin B12 so that you can make red blood cells that work properly to carry oxygen around your body.

This helps to reduce symptoms such as tiredness and lack of energy.

When will I feel better?

Hydroxocobalamin starts to work straight away. However, it may take a few days or weeks before your vitamin B12 levels and symptoms (such as extreme tiredness or lack of energy) start to improve.

Are there any long-term side effects?

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Common questions about hydroxocobalamin
text:
It's OK to have hydroxocobalamin injections for a long time. Some people will need to have them for the rest of their lives.

What will happen if I stop having the injections?

You'll be given appointments for your hydroxocobalamin injections.

If you miss having your injection, the level of vitamin B12 in your body will go down even more. This may make your health problems worse.

Talk to your doctor if you want to stop having hydroxocobalamin injections or if you are bothered by side effects.

Will it affect my contraception?

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Common questions about hydroxocobalamin
text:
Hydroxocobalamin will not stop any type of contraception working, including the combined pill, progestogen-only pill and emergency contraception.

Contraceptive pills may reduce the levels of hydroxocobalamin in your blood, but this will not affect your treatment.

However, if hydroxocobalamin makes you sick (vomit) or have severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours, your contraceptive pills may not protect you from pregnancy.

Find out more:

- What to do if you're sick or have diarrhoea when taking the combined pill
- What to do if you're sick or have diarrhoea when taking the progestogen-only pill

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Common questions about hydroxocobalamin
text:
Can I drive or ride a bike?

Hydroxocobalamin generally does not affect your ability to drive or ride a bike.

However, it can make some people feel dizzy. If you feel dizzy after having it, do not drive, cycle or use any machinery or tools until you feel OK again.

It's an offence to drive a car if your ability to drive safely is affected. It's your responsibility to decide if it's safe to drive. If you're in any doubt, do not drive.

Talk to your doctor if you're unsure whether it's safe for you to drive while having hydroxocobalamin. GOV.UK has more information on the law on drugs and driving.

title: Hydroxocobalamin
section_path: Hydroxocobalamin > Common questions about hydroxocobalamin
text:
Can I drink alcohol while having hydroxocobalamin?

Yes, you can drink alcohol while having hydroxocobalamin. Alcohol does not affect how this medicine works.

However, drinking too much on a regular basis can cause folate deficiency anaemia.

Try not to drink more than 14 units of alcohol a week. A standard glass of wine (175ml) is 2 units. A pint of lager or beer is usually 2 to 3 units of alcohol.

Is there any food or drink I need to avoid?

You can eat and drink normally while having hydroxocobalamin.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine
text: Hydroxychloroquine is a medicine used to treat conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and some skin conditions. It's only available with a prescription.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > What hydroxychloroquine is for
text:
Hydroxychloroquine is a type of medicine called a DMARD (disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug).

DMARDs work by calming your immune system or changing the way it responds. They're used to treat autoimmune conditions, where your body's natural defence system mistakenly attacks healthy parts of your body.

Hydroxychloroquine is mainly used to treat autoimmune conditions that cause inflammation, swelling and pain, such as:

- rheumatoid arthritis
- juvenile idiopathic arthritis
- lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus)

It's also used to treat skin conditions like:

- sarcoidosis
- lichen planus
- conditions that are caused or made worse by sunlight, such as porphyria cutanea tarda

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > How to take hydroxychloroquine
text:
Hydroxychloroquine usually comes as tablets that you swallow.

How much you need to take and for how long depends on why you're taking it, but some people may need to take it once or twice a day for at least 6 months.

If you're taking it to treat a skin condition caused by sunlight, you will need to take it when you know you'll spend a lot of time in the sun or be in intense sunlight, even for a short time. For example, during the summer months.

When taking hydroxychloroquine:

- swallow the tablets whole with a meal or glass of milk
- try to take it at the same time each day – if you take it twice a day, this could be once in the morning and once in the evening

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > How to take hydroxychloroquine
text: Always check the packet or leaflet that comes with your medicine. Ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice if you're not sure how to take it or have any problems taking it.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > How to take hydroxychloroquine > Important
text:
It takes several weeks for hydroxychloroquine to start working. Keep taking it unless you're told to stop.

If you've been taking it for a long time (more than 6 months) and do not feel it's helping, speak to your doctor.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > How to take hydroxychloroquine > If you miss a dose of hydroxychloroquine
text:
If you forget to take a dose, take it as soon as you remember, unless it's nearly time for your next dose.

If it is nearly time for your next dose, skip the dose you missed and take your next dose at the usual time.

Do not take 2 doses to make up for a forgotten dose.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > How to take hydroxychloroquine > If you take too much hydroxychloroquine
text: Taking too much hydroxychloroquine can be dangerous.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > How to take hydroxychloroquine > If you take too much hydroxychloroquine > Urgent advice: Get help from NHS 111 if:
text:
- you or a child have taken more than the prescribed dose of hydroxychloroquine

You can call 111 or get help from 111 online.

If you're told to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring the hydroxychloroquine packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Side effects of hydroxychloroquine
text: Like all medicines, hydroxychloroquine can cause side effects, although not everyone gets them.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Side effects of hydroxychloroquine > Common side effects
text:
Common side effects of hydroxychloroquine include:

- stomach ache
- feeling sick (nausea) and being sick (vomiting)
- loss of appetite
- diarrhoea
- headache
- an itchy rash
- mood changes

Hydroxychloroquine can sometimes cause blurred vision when you first start taking it. If this happens, do not drive, ride a bike or use machinery until your vision has gone back to normal.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Side effects of hydroxychloroquine > Common side effects > Non-urgent advice: Speak to a pharmacist or doctor if:
text:
- you have any side effects that bother you or do not go away

They may be able to give you advice about how you can reduce the side effects. Keep taking your medicine unless you're advised to stop.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Side effects of hydroxychloroquine > Serious side effects
text:
Hydroxychloroquine can sometimes cause serious side effects, although most of them are rare.

Possible serious side effects of hydroxychloroquine include:

- an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) – causing symptoms such as a swollen throat or tongue, a raised, itchy rash and difficulty breathing
- severe skin reactions – causing symptoms such as spots, sores, blisters or peeling skin, as well as a high temperature and flu-like symptoms
- vision problems (hydroxychloroquine retinopathy) – causing symptoms like constant blurred vision, changes to how you see colours or being sensitive to light
- liver problems – causing symptoms such as itchy skin, darker pee than normal, pale poo and yellowing of the skin or eyes (this may be harder to see on black or brown skin)

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Side effects of hydroxychloroquine > Serious side effects
text: If you've been taking hydroxychloroquine for a long time or are at higher risk of eye problems, you will have regular eye check-ups to look for any signs of retinopathy.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if:
text: - you're taking hydroxychloroquine and think you might be having serious side effects

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if: > More about side effects
text:
These are not all the side effects of hydroxychloroquine.

For a full list, see the leaflet that came with your medicine or search for your medicine on the electronic medicines compendium website.

You can report any side effects you get on the Yellow Card website.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Who can and cannot take hydroxychloroquine
text:
Most adults can take hydroxychloroquine. Children can take hydroxychloroquine, but they may not be prescribed it if they do not weigh enough.

Hydroxychloroquine is not suitable for some people. For example, it may not be suitable if you have:

- liver, kidney, blood or heart problems
- maculopathy or other eye problems
- diabetes
- psoriasis
- had an allergic reaction to hydroxychloroquine or related medicines, like quinine

Before taking hydroxychloroquine, tell your doctor if you have any medical conditions.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Who can and cannot take hydroxychloroquine > Breastfeeding and hydroxychloroquine
text:
Tell your doctor if you're breastfeeding.

Hydroxychloroquine can often be used while breastfeeding, but it's best to check because the medicine can pass into your breast milk in very small amounts.

If you're taking hydroxychloroquine while breastfeeding, speak to a healthcare professional or call NHS 111 if you have any concerns about your baby.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Who can and cannot take hydroxychloroquine > Pregnancy and hydroxychloroquine
text:
Hydroxychloroquine can be used during pregnancy if needed. Tell your doctor if you're pregnant or planning a pregnancy.

If you need to take hydroxychloroquine while you're pregnant, your doctor will prescribe the lowest possible effective dose.

Find out more about taking hydroxychloroquine during pregnancy on the Bumps (Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy) website

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Taking hydroxychloroquine with other medicines, food and drink
text:
There are some medicines, remedies and supplements that may not mix well with hydroxychloroquine.

This includes some types of:

- medicines to treat heart problems, such as digoxin
- epilepsy medicines
- antacids and other kinds of indigestion medicine – they may stop hydroxychloroquine from being absorbed properly
- antibiotics, such as azithromycin, clarithromycin and erythromycin
- antidepressants

Speak to a pharmacist or your doctor before taking any other medicines if you've been prescribed hydroxychloroquine.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Taking hydroxychloroquine with other medicines, food and drink
text: Before starting hydroxychloroquine, tell your doctor about any other medicines, or any herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements you take.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Taking hydroxychloroquine with other medicines, food and drink > Food, drink and alcohol with hydroxychloroquine
text: You can eat and drink normally while taking hydroxychloroquine.

title: Hydroxychloroquine
section_path: Hydroxychloroquine > Find out more about your medicine
text:
To find out more about your medicine, you can:

- check the leaflet that comes with it
- search for your medicine leaflet on the electronic medicines compendium (EMC) website
- speak to a pharmacist or doctor for advice

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide
text:
Common brands: Kwells, Kwells Kids

Hyoscine hydrobromide is a medicine that can be used to treat travel sickness, such as feeling carsick or seasick. You can buy it from a pharmacy.

This information is about hyoscine hydrobromide. There's separate information about hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan) for stomach cramps, IBS and period pain.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > What hyoscine hydrobromide is for
text:
Hyoscine hydrobromide is mainly used to treat travel sickness.

It helps with symptoms like feeling sick (nausea) and being sick (vomiting).

It works on the parts of your inner ear, nerves and brain that control balance and nausea.

It's also sometimes given as an injection as part of end-of-life care or hospital treatment.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > How to take hyoscine hydrobromide and how much to use (dose)
text:
Hyoscine hydrobromide usually comes as tablets that can be chewed, sucked or swallowed whole.

Always check the packet or leaflet that comes with your medicine. Ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice if you're not sure how to take it or have any problems taking it.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > How to take hyoscine hydrobromide and how much to use (dose) > How to take common types of hyoscine hydrobromide
text:
300 microgram tablets

For adults:

- take 1 tablet every 6 hours, as needed
- do not take more than 3 doses in 24 hours

For children aged 11 years or older:

- take half a tablet or 1 tablet every 6 hours, as needed
- do not take more than 3 doses in 24 hours

Take this medicine at least 30 minutes before you travel. This gives it time to start working.

150 microgram tablets (for children)

For children aged 11 years or older:

- take 1 or 2 tablets every 6 hours, as needed
- do not take more than 3 doses in 24 hours

For children aged 4 to 10 years:

- take half a tablet or 1 tablet every 6 hours, as needed
- do not take more than 3 doses in 24 hours

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > How to take hyoscine hydrobromide and how much to use (dose) > How to take common types of hyoscine hydrobromide
text: Take this medicine at least 30 minutes before you travel. This gives it time to start working.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > How to take hyoscine hydrobromide and how much to use (dose) > If you miss a dose of hyoscine hydrobromide
text:
If you're taking hyoscine hydrobromide for travel sickness and you miss a dose, you can take another dose if it's been at least 6 hours since your last dose.

Do not take 2 doses to make up for a missed dose.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > How to take hyoscine hydrobromide and how much to use (dose) > If you take too much hyoscine hydrobromide
text: Taking extra doses of hyoscine hydrobromide can be dangerous.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > How to take hyoscine hydrobromide and how much to use (dose) > If you take too much hyoscine hydrobromide > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if:
text:
- you've taken more hyoscine hydrobromide than it says on the packet or leaflet

If you're told to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring the hyoscine hydrobromide packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > Side effects of hyoscine hydrobromide
text: Like all medicines, hyoscine hydrobromide can cause side effects, although not everyone gets them.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > Side effects of hyoscine hydrobromide > Common side effects
text:
Common side effects of hyoscine hydrobromide include:

- blurred vision or large (dilated) pupils
- dry mouth
- feeling very tired (drowsy) or dizzy
- constipation
- skin rash or redness – redness can be harder to see on black or brown skin

If you feel drowsy, dizzy or have blurred vision after taking hyoscine hydrobromide, do not drive, ride a bike or use machinery until you no longer have these symptoms.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > Side effects of hyoscine hydrobromide > Common side effects > Non-urgent advice: Speak to a pharmacist or doctor if:
text:
- you have any side effects that bother you or do not go away

They may be able to give you advice about how you can reduce the side effects.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > Side effects of hyoscine hydrobromide > Serious side effects
text:
Hyoscine hydrobromide can sometimes cause serious side effects, although most of them are rare.

Possible serious side effects of hyoscine hydrobromide include:

- changes to your heart rate, such as a fast or irregular heartbeat
- an increased number of seizures, if you have epilepsy
- confusion, unusual behaviour, and seeing or hearing things that are not there (hallucinations), particularly in children
- an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), which can cause symptoms such as a swollen throat or tongue, a raised, itchy rash or difficulty breathing

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > Side effects of hyoscine hydrobromide > Serious side effects > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
text:
- you're taking hyoscine hydrobromide and think you might be having anaphylaxis

If you think you're having any other serious side effect, call NHS 111.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > Side effects of hyoscine hydrobromide > More about side effects
text:
These are not all the side effects of hyoscine hydrobromide.

For a full list, see the leaflet that comes with your medicine or search for your medicine leaflet on the electronic medicines compendium website.

You can report any side effects you get on the Yellow Card website

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > Who can and cannot take hyoscine hydrobromide
text:
Most adults and children aged 4 years or older can take hyoscine hydrobromide.

But hyoscine hydrobromide is not suitable for everyone. For example, it may not be suitable if:

- you've had an allergic reaction or other serious side effects from hyoscine hydrobromide
- you have epilepsy
- you have an overactive thyroid
- you have liver, kidney or prostate problems
- you have glaucoma or have been told you're at risk of glaucoma
- you have a blocked intestine or other stomach problems
- you have heart failure or a fast heartbeat
- you are aged 60 or older

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > Who can and cannot take hyoscine hydrobromide
text: Before taking hyoscine hydrobromide, tell your doctor if you have any medical conditions.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > Who can and cannot take hyoscine hydrobromide > Breastfeeding and hyoscine hydrobromide
text:
You may be able to take hyoscine hydrobromide while breastfeeding, but check with a pharmacist or doctor first. Your baby may need to be monitored for any side effects.

If you're taking hyoscine hydrobromide when breastfeeding, speak to a healthcare professional or call NHS 111 if you have any concerns about your baby.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > Who can and cannot take hyoscine hydrobromide > Pregnancy and hyoscine hydrobromide
text:
Tell your doctor if you're pregnant or trying to get pregnant. Hyoscine hydrobromide is not usually recommended during pregnancy.

However, you may be able to take it if there are no other ways to treat your travel sickness and the benefits outweigh the risks.

Find out more about taking hyoscine during pregnancy on the Bumps (Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy) website

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > Taking hyoscine hydrobromide with other medicines, food and drink
text:
There are some medicines, remedies and supplements that may not mix well with hyoscine hydrobromide.

This includes:

- antihistamines, particularly drowsy (sedating) antihistamines
- medicines for migraines and nerve pain, such as amitriptyline or nortriptyline
- some medicines for Parkinson's disease, such as amantadine
- other medicines for nausea and vomiting, such as metoclopramide and domperidone

Before taking hyoscine hydrobromide, tell the pharmacist or your doctor if you're taking any other medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > Taking hyoscine hydrobromide with other medicines, food and drink > Food, drink and alcohol with hyoscine hydrobromide
text:
You can eat and drink as normal while taking hyoscine hydrobromide.

But it's best not to drink alcohol, as it can increase the risk of side effects like feeling very sleepy.

title: Hyoscine hydrobromide
section_path: Hyoscine hydrobromide > Find out more about your medicine
text:
To find out more about your medicine, you can:

- check the leaflet that comes with it
- search for your medicine leaflet on the electronic medicines compendium website
- speak to a pharmacist for advice

title: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis)
section_path: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis)
text: Hyperacusis is when everyday sounds seem much louder to you than they should. Treatment can help. See a GP if you think you have hyperacusis.

title: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis)
section_path: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis) > Symptoms of hyperacusis
text:
You may have hyperacusis if some everyday sounds seem much louder than they should. It can sometimes be painful.

You may be affected by sounds like:

- jingling coins
- a barking dog
- a car engine
- someone chewing
- a vacuum cleaner

Hyperacusis can affect 1 or both ears. It can come on suddenly or develop over time.

Other types of hearing sensitivity include:

- some sounds triggering an upsetting emotional response like anger or disgust (misophonia)
- some sounds making you anxious (phonophobia)
- your ears having trouble adjusting between quiet and loud sounds (recruitment)

title: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis)
section_path: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis) > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
text:
- everyday noises feel too loud or painful

Your GP may refer you to a hearing specialist for further tests and treatment.

title: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis)
section_path: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis) > Treatment for hyperacusis
text:
If hyperacusis is caused by another condition, such as migraines or Lyme disease, treating the condition may help with your hyperacusis.

You can also be offered treatment to help make you less sensitive to everyday sounds.

This could be:

- sound therapy to get you used to everyday sounds again, which may involve wearing ear pieces or using a portable speaker that makes white noise
- cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) to change the way you think about your hyperacusis and reduce anxiety

If you find any sounds made during sound therapy uncomfortably loud or they cause you pain, then you should stop and contact your doctor for advice.

title: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis)
section_path: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis) > Things you can try to ease hyperacusis > Do
text: - try some relaxation techniques, such as breathing exercises

title: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis)
section_path: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis) > Things you can try to ease hyperacusis > Don't
text:
- do not wear earplugs or muffs all the time because this could make you more sensitive to noise – short-term use may help in very noisy environments
- do not avoid noise completely – this can mean you miss out on regular activities and make you more sensitive to noise

title: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis)
section_path: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis) > Causes of hyperacusis
text:
The cause of hyperacusis is unclear.

It can appear on its own or after hearing a sudden loud noise, such as fireworks.

It can also appear alongside other conditions, like:

- tinnitus
- a head injury
- Ménière's disease
- Bell's palsy
- Lyme disease
- migraines
- Williams syndrome
- autism

Children are often more sensitive to loud noises than adults. It often gets better as they get older.

But some children may become more sensitive to noise than others after having glue ear (where the ear fills up with fluid), for example, or if they have another condition, such as autism.

title: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis)
section_path: Noise sensitivity (hyperacusis) > Find out more
text:
- British Tinnitus Association: hyperacusis
- RNID

title: Hyperparathyroidism
section_path: Hyperparathyroidism
text:
Hyperparathyroidism is a condition that affects the amount of calcium in your body. This can affect different parts of your body, such as your blood, bones and kidneys. It can be treated with surgery and medicines.

There is separate information about hypoparathyroidism, which is where there is not enough calcium in the body.

title: Hyperparathyroidism
section_path: Hyperparathyroidism > Symptoms of hyperparathyroidism
text:
Many people with hyperparathyroidism have no, or very mild, symptoms. You may only find out you have it after having tests for something else.

Sometimes symptoms can have a big impact on daily life.

Symptoms of hyperparathyroidism include:

- tiredness
- aches and pains, particularly in your joints, hands, arms, feet and legs
- muscle weakness
- feeling and being sick
- loss of appetite
- constipation
- tummy pain
- feeling thirsty all the time
- peeing more than usual
- low mood and depression

title: Hyperparathyroidism
section_path: Hyperparathyroidism > When and where to get medical help
text: Treatment is usually needed for hyperparathyroidism so get checked if you have symptoms. Getting treatment can stop it getting worse and prevent complications.

title: Hyperparathyroidism
section_path: Hyperparathyroidism > When and where to get medical help > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
text: - you think you might have hyperparathyroidism

title: Hyperparathyroidism
section_path: Hyperparathyroidism > Causes of hyperparathyroidism
text:
Hyperparathyroidism happens when your body produces too much of a hormone called parathyroid hormone (PTH).

Producing too much PTH can be caused by:

- a non-cancerous growth (adenoma) on the parathyroid glands in your neck – this is called primary hyperparathyroidism
- having low levels of calcium or vitamin D in your blood, or high levels of phosphates, which may be due to an underlying condition – this is called secondary hyperparathyroidism

Too much PTH can affect the amount of calcium in your blood. Calcium helps with things like keeping your bones and teeth healthy.

title: Hyperparathyroidism
section_path: Hyperparathyroidism > Tests for hyperparathyroidism
text:
Hyperparathyroidism can be diagnosed by testing samples of your blood and pee.

Many people are first diagnosed with hyperparathyroidism when they are having blood or pee tests for something else.

If you have hyperparathyroidism, further tests and scans may then be recommended to check your general health and help plan treatment.

These can include:

- ultrasound scans
- X-rays
- bone density scans

title: Hyperparathyroidism
section_path: Hyperparathyroidism > Treatments for hyperparathyroidism
text:
If you’re diagnosed with hyperparathyroidism, you’ll be referred to a specialist for treatment.

Treatment depends on what’s causing the hyperparathyroidism.

If it’s caused by a growth on your parathyroid glands, you’ll be offered surgery to remove part or all of the glands.

If you do not want surgery, or it’s not currently a suitable option for you, the specialist may offer you medicine to help lower your calcium levels.

If hyperparathyroidism is happening because you have low calcium or vitamin D levels, treatment may include medicines and supplements.

title: Hyperparathyroidism
section_path: Hyperparathyroidism > Treatments for hyperparathyroidism > Important
text:
Do not make any changes to your diet to try to lower your calcium levels, unless you have been told to by your specialist.

A change in your usual diet could make your symptoms worse or cause more serious problems.

title: Hyperparathyroidism
section_path: Hyperparathyroidism > Complications of hyperparathyroidism
text:
If hyperparathyroidism is not treated, it can lead to complications:

These include:

- osteoporosis – where your bones become weaker and more likely to break
- kidney stones
- high blood pressure, which can increase your risk of heart disease and stroke

title: Hyperparathyroidism
section_path: Hyperparathyroidism > Find out more
text: Parathyroid UK is a charity that provides support and information for people living with parathyroid gland conditions.

title: Hypoparathyroidism
section_path: Hypoparathyroidism
text: Hypoparathyroidism (sometime called "hypopara") is a rare condition where small glands in your neck (parathyroid glands) do not work properly. It can lead to problems with your bones, muscles and nerves, but can usually be treated by taking supplements.

title: Hypoparathyroidism
section_path: Hypoparathyroidism > Hyperparathyroidism
text:
Hyperparathyroidism is a condition where there is too much calcium in the body. It is more common than hypoparathyroidism.

Find out more about hyperparathyroidism

title: Hypoparathyroidism
section_path: Hypoparathyroidism > Symptoms of hypoparathyroidism
text:
Hypoparathyroidism often starts if glands in your neck are damaged during surgery.

Symptoms include:

- a tingling or burning sensation in your fingers, toes and face
- muscle pain, stiffness and spasms
- tummy pain
- brittle nails, dry hair and dry skin
- cataracts (cloudy patches that form at the front of your eyes)

Less common and more serious symptoms include:

- confusion
- an irregular heartbeat
- seizures (fits)

title: Hypoparathyroidism
section_path: Hypoparathyroidism > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
text:
- you think you might have hypoparathyroidism

If you recently had neck or head surgery, you should have been given details of who to contact in case of complications. Try this first before talking to a GP.

title: Hypoparathyroidism
section_path: Hypoparathyroidism > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
text:
You think someone's having a seizure and:

- it's the first time it's happened
- it lasts longer than is usual for them, or longer than 5 minutes if you do not know how long their seizures usually last

Do not drive yourself to A&E.

The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

title: Hypoparathyroidism
section_path: Hypoparathyroidism > Causes of hypoparathyroidism
text:
Hypoparathyroidism happens when small glands in your neck (parathyroid glands) do not work properly.

These glands help control the level of calcium in your body. If they're not working properly, your calcium level may become too low.

Calcium is a mineral that the body needs to keep bones, muscles and nerves working properly.

Most of the time hypoparathyroidism is caused by the parathyroid glands being damaged during surgery to the neck or head.

Types of surgery that carry this risk of damage include surgery for an underactive thyroid or overactive thyroid, and surgery for head or neck cancer.

Other causes of hypoparathyroidism include:

- conditions where the body's immune system damages healthy tissue, such as Addison's disease
- some rare genetic conditions

title: Hypoparathyroidism
section_path: Hypoparathyroidism > Tests for hypoparathyroidism
text:
If there's a chance you have hypoparathyroidism, you may have a number of blood tests to measure how much calcium is in your blood and to rule out other possible causes of your symptoms.

A low level of calcium can be a sign of hypoparathyroidism.

If you're having neck or head surgery, you may have these tests soon after surgery. This is used to check if there was any damage to your parathyroid glands.

title: Hypoparathyroidism
section_path: Hypoparathyroidism > Treatments for hypoparathyroidism
text:
Hypoparathyroidism can be treated by taking:

- calcium supplements – to raise the level of calcium in your body
- vitamin D supplements – vitamin D helps your body make better use of calcium

You'll usually need to take supplements for the rest of your life.

You may be offered supplements even if you do not have any symptoms, but tests show damage to your parathyroid glands. This helps lower the risk of any serious problems.

You may also be advised to make some changes to your diet, such as:

- eating foods high in calcium, such as dairy products, green leafy vegetables, soy and tofu
- avoiding or cutting down on red meat and starchy foods, like pasta and white bread

title: Hypoparathyroidism
section_path: Hypoparathyroidism > Treatments for hypoparathyroidism
text:
You'll need regular blood tests to check your calcium levels.

If these tests show supplements are not working well, then you may need extra medicines.

title: Hypoparathyroidism
section_path: Hypoparathyroidism > Complications of hypoparathyroidism
text:
If you have hypoparathyroidism and your calcium level becomes too low, it can cause seizures and serious heart problems.

If this happens, you'll need to be treated in hospital. You'll be given calcium through a tube into a vein, until your calcium level returns to normal.

title: Hypoparathyroidism
section_path: Hypoparathyroidism > Help and support for hypoparathyroidism
text:
If you have hypoparathyroidism, health professionals will be there to support you throughout your treatment.

You can also get information and support from Parathyroid UK, a UK charity for people living with parathyroid conditions.

- Parathyroid UK: get support
- Parathyroid UK: self-help guide

title: Hypothermia
section_path: Hypothermia
text: Hypothermia is a dangerous drop in body temperature below 35C (normal body temperature is around 37C). It's a medical emergency that needs to be treated in hospital.

title: Hypothermia
section_path: Hypothermia > Symptoms of hypothermia
text:
Symptoms of hypothermia include:

- shivering
- pale, cold and dry skin – skin and lips may turn blue or grey (on black or brown skin this may be easier to see on the palms of the hands or the soles of the feet)
- slurred speech
- slow breathing
- tiredness or confusion

A baby with hypothermia may be:

- cold to touch
- floppy
- unusually quiet and sleepy and may refuse to feed

title: Hypothermia
section_path: Hypothermia > Immediate action required: Go to A&E or call 999 if:
text:
- you think you or your child have hypothermia

Find your nearest A&E

Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring any medicines you take with you.

title: Hypothermia
section_path: Hypothermia > What to do while you're waiting for help for hypothermia
text: If you think someone has hypothermia, there are things you can do while waiting for medical help.

title: Hypothermia
section_path: Hypothermia > What to do while you're waiting for help for hypothermia > Do
text:
- move the person indoors or somewhere sheltered as quickly as possible
- remove any wet clothing, wrap them in a blanket, sleeping bag or dry towel, making sure their head is covered
- give them a warm non-alcoholic drink and some sugary food like chocolate if they're fully awake
- keep them awake by talking to them until help arrives
- make sure you or someone else stays with them

There are things you should not do because they will not help and could make things worse.

title: Hypothermia
section_path: Hypothermia > What to do while you're waiting for help for hypothermia > Don’t
text:
- do not use a hot bath, hot water bottle or heat lamp to warm them up
- do not rub their arms, legs, feet or hands
- do not give them alcohol to drink

title: Hypothermia
section_path: Hypothermia > Treatment in hospital for hypothermia
text:
If you have hypothermia, you’ll usually be treated in hospital.

Your heart rate will be monitored and you may be given oxygen to help you breathe.

You may also be given warm fluids straight into a vein to help your body warm up.

Treatment in intensive care may be needed if you have severe hypothermia.

title: Hypothermia
section_path: Hypothermia > Causes of hypothermia
text:
Hypothermia happens when you get too cold and your body temperature drops below 35C.

You can get hypothermia if you:

- do not wear enough clothes in cold weather
- stay out in the cold too long
- fall into cold water
- have wet clothes and get cold
- live in a cold house – older people living alone are particularly at risk

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Brand name: Nurofen Plus

Find out how combined ibuprofen and codeine treats aches and pains and how to take it.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > About ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Brand name: Nurofen Plus

You can buy ibuprofen and codeine combined as a single medicine from pharmacies.

It's used to treat a range of aches and pains, including:

- headaches and migraine
- back pain
- period pain
- toothache
- sprains and strains
- pain from arthritis

It's usually taken when everyday painkillers, such as paracetamol, ibuprofen or aspirin, have not worked on their own.

Each tablet usually contains 200mg of ibuprofen and 12.8mg of codeine.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > About ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Ibuprofen belongs to a group of medicines called NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs). It works by reducing hormones that cause pain and swelling in the body.

Codeine is from a group of medicines called opioids. It works in the central nervous system and the brain to block pain signals to the rest of the body. It also reduces the anxiety and stress caused by pain.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > About ibuprofen and codeine > Key facts
text: - If you buy combined ibuprofen and codeine from a pharmacy and your pain is not better after 3 days, it's important to ask your doctor or pharmacist for advice about ongoing pain relief. - You can become addicted to the codeine in this medicine, if you take it for too long. Only take it when you need it for pain relief. - Do not take more than 6 combined ibuprofen and codeine tablets in 24 hours. - It's best to take your tablets with food or a drink of milk. You'll be less likely to get indigestion or stomach pain. - The most common side effects are indigestion, feeling sleepy and constipation. - It's best not to drink alcohol when you're taking combined ibuprofen and codeine. You're more likely to get side effects like feeling sleepy.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Who can and cannot take ibuprofen and codeine
text: Brand name: Nurofen Plus

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Who can and cannot take ibuprofen and codeine > Who can take ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Most adults and children aged 12 years and over can take combined ibuprofen and codeine.

However, it should only be taken if painkillers like paracetamol, ibuprofen or aspirin have not worked on their own. Do not give aspirin to anyone under 16 years old.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Who can and cannot take ibuprofen and codeine > Who may not be able to take ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Combined ibuprofen and codeine is not suitable for some people.

Never give combined ibuprofen and codeine to children aged 11 years or under.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Who can and cannot take ibuprofen and codeine > Who may not be able to take ibuprofen and codeine
text: To make sure combined ibuprofen and codeine is safe for you, tell your pharmacist or doctor if you or your child:

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Who can and cannot take ibuprofen and codeine > Who may not be able to take ibuprofen and codeine
text:
- have ever had an allergic reaction to ibuprofen, aspirin or other NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), codeine or any other medicine
- are trying to get pregnant, already pregnant, or breastfeeding
- are 18 years old or under and have recently had your tonsils or adenoids taken out to treat a sleep problem called obstructive sleep apnoea
- have asthma, breathing problems or any other lung condition
- have a head injury or a condition where there is raised pressure in your head
- have adrenal gland problems
- have a condition that causes seizures or fits
- have ever had bleeding in your stomach, a stomach ulcer, or a hole (perforation) in your stomach
- have a health problem that means you have an increased chance of bleeding, such as haemophilia or thrombocytopenia
- have liver problems such as liver fibrosis, cirrhosis or liver failure
- have high blood pressure, heart disease or severe heart failure, or have ever had a stroke
- have kidney failure
- have Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis
- regularly drink more than the maximum recommended amount of alcohol (14 units a week)
- often have constipation
- have a connective tissue disorder such as lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus)
- have low blood pressure (hypotension) or an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)
- have chickenpox

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > How and when to take ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Brand name: Nurofen Plus

Follow the instructions that come with your medicine. This is important because the codeine in combined ibuprofen and codeine can be addictive.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > How and when to take ibuprofen and codeine > Dosage and how to take combined ibuprofen and codeine > Dosage and strength
text:
Combined ibuprofen and codeine contains 200mg of ibuprofen and 12.8mg of codeine in each tablet.

Different brands have different doses, so it's important to read the instructions that come with your medicine.

However, the usual dose for adults and children aged 12 years and over is 1 or 2 tablets, taken every 4 to 6 hours.

If you're not sure how much to take, talk to your pharmacist or doctor.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > How and when to take ibuprofen and codeine > Dosage and how to take combined ibuprofen and codeine > Important
text: Do not take more than 6 combined ibuprofen and codeine tablets in 24 hours.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > How and when to take ibuprofen and codeine > Dosage and how to take combined ibuprofen and codeine > How to take it
text:
Swallow the tablets whole with a drink of water.

It's best to take it with, or just after, food or a drink of milk so it does not upset your stomach. Do not take it on an empty stomach.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > How and when to take ibuprofen and codeine > Dosage and how to take combined ibuprofen and codeine > How long to take it for
text: If you've bought combined ibuprofen and codeine from a pharmacy, do not take it for more than 3 days. If you still have pain, talk to your pharmacist or doctor. It's important to ask them for advice about ongoing pain relief.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > How and when to take ibuprofen and codeine > If you forget to take it
text:
If you forget to take a dose, check the information on the leaflet inside the packaging, or ask your pharmacist or doctor for advice on what to do.

Never take 2 doses at the same time

If you often forget doses, it may help to set an alarm to remind you. You could ask your pharmacist for advice on other ways to help you remember to take your medicines.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > How and when to take ibuprofen and codeine > If you take too much
text:
Do not take more than the recommended dose of ibuprofen and codeine, even if you think it's not enough to relieve your pain.

Taking too much combined ibuprofen and codeine can be dangerous. The amount that can lead to an overdose varies from person to person.

It's important to get medical advice if you take more than the recommended dose of ibuprofen and codeine.

It can cause side effects, such as:

- feeling very sleepy, sick or dizzy, or being sick
- stomach pain
- ringing in your ears (tinnitus)

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > How and when to take ibuprofen and codeine > If you take too much > Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E now if:
text:
You have taken more than the recommended dose of ibuprofen and codeine and you:

- are having problems with your breathing
- have chest pain or your heart rate (pulse) has slowed down or got faster
- have black poo or blood in your vomit, which are signs of bleeding in your stomach
- pass out or become unconscious
- have a fit or seizure

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > How and when to take ibuprofen and codeine > If you take too much > Urgent advice: Contact 111 for advice now if:
text:
- you take more than the recommended dose of ibuprofen and codeine, even if you do not have any symptoms

Call 111 or get help from 111 online.

If you need to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring the ibuprofen and codeine packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Brand name: Nurofen Plus

Like all medicines, combined ibuprofen and codeine can cause side effects. But because you only take it for a very short time (up to 3 days), you're unlikely to have any side effects.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Common side effects of combined ibuprofen and codeine
text:
These side effects of ibuprofen and codeine happen to more than 1 in 100 people. There are things you can do to help cope with them:

Headaches

If you get headaches after taking combined ibuprofen and codeine, do not take any more and see if the headache goes away.

It might be better to try another painkiller, like paracetamol.

Talk to your doctor if the headaches do not go away or are severe.

Feeling dizzy

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Common side effects of combined ibuprofen and codeine
text:
If you begin to feel dizzy, lie down so you do not faint. If you feel dizzy when you stand up, try getting up very slowly or stay sitting down until you feel better. Do not drive, cycle or use tools or machinery while you feel like this.

Feeling sleepy

Do not drive, cycle or use tools or machinery if you're feeling drowsy. Do not drink any alcohol as this will make you feel more tired.

Constipation

Get more fibre into your diet, such as fresh fruit and vegetables and cereals. Try to drink several glasses of water or another non-alcoholic liquid each day. If you can, it may also help to increase your level of exercise.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Common side effects of combined ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Feeling or being sick (nausea or vomiting)

Stick to simple meals and do not eat rich or spicy food. It might help to take your ibuprofen and codeine with or just after a meal or snack. Feelings of sickness normally wear off.

If you're being sick, try small, frequent sips of water to avoid dehydration. Signs of dehydration include peeing less than usual or having dark, strong-smelling pee.

Do not take any other medicines to treat vomiting without speaking to a pharmacist or doctor.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Common side effects of combined ibuprofen and codeine
text:
If you take the combined contraceptive pill or progestogen-only pill and you're being sick, your contraception may not protect you from pregnancy. Check the pill packet for advice.

Indigestion and heartburn (acid reflux)

Stop taking the medicine and see your doctor as soon as possible. If you need something to ease the discomfort, try taking an antacid, but do not put off speaking to your pharmacist or doctor if the symptoms do not go away.

Wind

Try not to eat foods that cause wind (like lentils, beans and onions). Eat smaller meals, eat and drink slowly, and exercise regularly if you can.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Common side effects of combined ibuprofen and codeine
text:
There are pharmacy medicines that can also help, such as charcoal tablets or simeticone.

Speak to a doctor or pharmacist if the advice on how to cope does not help and a side effect is still bothering you or does not go away.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Serious side effects
text:
Stop taking the medicine and call a doctor or call 111 now if you have:

- difficulty breathing
- black poo or blood in your vomit – these can be signs of bleeding in your stomach
- swollen ankles, blood in your pee, or not peeing at all – these can be signs of a kidney problem
- asthma and your symptoms are getting worse

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Serious side effects > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
text:
- you have chest pain
- you have severe stomach pain – this can be a sign of a hole in your stomach
- you have severe difficulty breathing

Do not drive yourself to A&E.

The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Serious side effects > Serious allergic reaction
text: In rare cases, it's possible to have a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to ibuprofen and codeine.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Serious side effects > Serious allergic reaction > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
text:
- your lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly become swollen
- you're breathing very fast or struggling to breathe (you may become very wheezy or feel like you're choking or gasping for air)
- your throat feels tight or you're struggling to swallow
- your skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale (if you have black or brown skin, this may be easier to see on the palms of your hands or soles of your feet)
- you suddenly become very confused, drowsy or dizzy
- someone faints and cannot be woken up
- a child is limp, floppy or not responding like they normally do (their head may fall to the side, backwards or forwards, or they may find it difficult to lift their head or focus on your face)

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Serious side effects > Serious allergic reaction > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
text:
You or the person who's unwell may also have a rash that's swollen, raised, itchy, blistered or peeling.

These can be signs of a serious allergic reaction and may need immediate treatment in hospital.

Do not drive yourself to A&E.

The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Long-term side effects
text:
The ibuprofen in this medicine can cause ulcers in your stomach or gut, especially if you take it for a long time or in big doses. However, if you take it correctly, with food, for short periods of time, the risk is very low.

If you need to take it for a long time your doctor may also prescribe a medicine to help protect your stomach.

If you buy combined ibuprofen and codeine from a pharmacy, do not use it for more than 3 days. If your pain has not gone away, talk to a pharmacist or doctor.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Long-term side effects
text:
If you need to take combined ibuprofen and codeine for a long time, your body can get used to codeine (known as tolerance). That means you need higher doses to control your pain over time.

Some people can become more sensitive to pain (hyperalgesia). If this happens, your doctor will reduce your dose gradually to help these symptoms.

It's possible to become addicted to the codeine in this medicine. For this reason, your dose will be reviewed to make sure you're only taking the amount you need to control your pain.

Speak to your doctor if you're worried about tolerance, hyperalgesia or becoming addicted.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Other side effects
text: These are not all the side effects of ibuprofen and codeine. For a full list, see the leaflet inside your medicine packet.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Side effects of ibuprofen and codeine > Reporting side effects
text:
You can report any suspected side effect using the Yellow Card safety scheme.

Visit the Yellow Card website for more information about reporting side effects.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking ibuprofen and codeine
text: Brand name: Nurofen Plus

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking ibuprofen and codeine > Ibuprofen and codeine and pregnancy
text:
While a short course of combined ibuprofen and codeine could be taken up to 20 weeks of pregnancy, other painkillers are likely to be more suitable.

Ibuprofen can affect your baby's circulation and amniotic fluid if you take it after 20 weeks, or for more than 2 to 3 days at a time.

Codeine can affect your baby, especially towards the end of pregnancy. Your baby may get used to having codeine and may have withdrawal symptoms when they're born. There is a slightly higher chance of your baby having breathing problems. These are usually temporary, but your baby may need to stay in hospital for extra monitoring.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking ibuprofen and codeine > Ibuprofen and codeine and pregnancy
text: Combined ibuprofen and codeine is not recommended during pregnancy. Other medicines are more suitable. Ask your doctor or pharmacist for advice.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking ibuprofen and codeine > Ibuprofen and codeine and breastfeeding
text:
Do not take combined ibuprofen and codeine if you're breastfeeding. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist, as they will be able to recommend a more suitable painkiller.

Small amounts of the codeine may get into breast milk and can cause breathing problems in your baby and make them feel sleepy.

However, it's OK to take ibuprofen on its own while breastfeeding.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking ibuprofen and codeine > Ibuprofen and codeine and fertility
text:
There's no evidence that taking combined ibuprofen and codeine for a maximum of 3 days will affect your fertility.

However, taking ibuprofen tablets in large doses or for a long time can affect ovulation. That might make it more difficult for you to get pregnant. You'll usually start ovulating normally again when you stop taking ibuprofen.

If you're worried about taking combined ibuprofen and codeine for longer than 3 days and how this may affect your fertility, talk to your doctor.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking ibuprofen and codeine > Non-urgent advice: Tell your doctor if you're:
text:
- trying to get pregnant
- pregnant
- breastfeeding

For more information about how ibuprofen and codeine can affect you and your baby during pregnancy, visit the Bumps (Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy) website:

- Bumps: ibuprofen
- Bumps: codeine

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Taking ibuprofen and codeine with other medicines and herbal supplements
text: Brand name: Nurofen Plus

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Taking ibuprofen and codeine with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines
text: There are some medicines that do not mix well with combined ibuprofen and codeine and can affect how well it works.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Taking ibuprofen and codeine with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines
text: Check with your pharmacist or doctor if you're taking, or have recently had, any other medicines, including:

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Taking ibuprofen and codeine with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines
text:
- anticoagulants, such as warfarin
- other anti-inflammatory painkillers, such as aspirin (including a daily low dose of 75mg), diclofenac, mefenamic acid or naproxen
- medicines for high blood pressure
- diuretic medicines, such as furosemide or spironolactone
- steroid medicines such as prednisolone
- antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, norfloxacin or ofloxacin
- antidepressants, such as citalopram, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, sertraline or venlafaxine
- other antidepressants called monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)
- methotrexate (a medicine for psoriasis and rheumatoid arthritis)
- lithium (a medicine for mental health problems)
- ciclosporin or tacrolimus, medicines used after a transplant and for the treatment of psoriasis
- zidovudine, a medicine to treat HIV
- other medicines that can make you sleepy, such as sleeping pills, tranquillisers, or medicines for anxiety
- medicines used to treat nausea and vomiting, such as domperidone or metoclopramide
- medicines for diarrhoea, such as loperamide (Imodium)
- cimetidine, a medicine used to treat stomach ulcers
- mifepristone, a medicine used for abortion

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Taking ibuprofen and codeine with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines
text: These are not all the medicines that may cause problems if you take them with combined ibuprofen and codeine. For a full list, see the leaflet inside your medicine packet.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Taking ibuprofen and codeine with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines > Taking ibuprofen and codeine with other painkillers
text:
It's safe to take combined ibuprofen and codeine with paracetamol.

Do not take combined ibuprofen and codeine with ibuprofen, aspirin or naproxen.

Ibuprofen, aspirin and naproxen belong to the same group of medicines called NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs). If you take them together, the ibuprofen plus aspirin or naproxen may increase the chance of you getting side effects, like stomach ache, or serious issues such as stomach bleeds.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Taking ibuprofen and codeine with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines > Taking ibuprofen and codeine with other painkillers
text: Many medicines you can buy from pharmacies have NSAIDs as ingredients. These include cough and cold remedies such as Nurofen Cold & Flu or Beechams Powders.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Taking ibuprofen and codeine with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines > Taking ibuprofen and codeine with other painkillers > Important
text: Before taking any other medicines, check the label to see if they contain codeine, ibuprofen, aspirin or other NSAIDs.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Taking ibuprofen and codeine with other medicines and herbal supplements > Mixing ibuprofen and codeine with herbal remedies or supplements
text: There's not enough information to say that complementary medicines and herbal remedies are safe to take with combined ibuprofen and codeine. They are not tested in the same way as other medicines. They're generally not tested for the effect they have on other medicines.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Taking ibuprofen and codeine with other medicines and herbal supplements > Important: Medicine safety
text: Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you're taking any other medicines, including herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Common questions about ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Brand name: Nurofen Plus

How does combined ibuprofen and codeine work?

Ibuprofen belongs to a group of medicines called NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs). It works by reducing hormones that cause pain and swelling in the body.

Codeine is from a group of medicines called opioids. It works in the central nervous system and the brain to block pain signals to the rest of the body. It also reduces the anxiety and stress caused by pain.

When codeine blocks the pain, there are other unwanted effects, including slow or shallow breathing. It also slows down digestion, which is why codeine can cause constipation.

When will I feel better?

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Common questions about ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Combined ibuprofen and codeine works in 30 to 60 minutes and keeps on working for about 4 to 6 hours.

Are there any long-term side effects?

The ibuprofen in this medicine can cause ulcers in your stomach or gut, especially if you take it for a long time or in big doses. However, if you take it correctly, with food, for short periods of time, the risk is very low.

If you buy combined ibuprofen and codeine from a pharmacy, do not use it for more than 3 days. If your pain has not gone away, talk to a pharmacist or doctor.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Common questions about ibuprofen and codeine
text:
If you need to take it for a long time your doctor may also prescribe a medicine to help protect your stomach.

If you need to take combined ibuprofen and codeine for a long time, your body can get used to codeine (known as tolerance). That means you need higher doses to control your pain over time.

Some people can become more sensitive to pain (hyperalgesia). If this happens, your doctor will reduce your dose gradually to help these symptoms.

It's possible to become addicted to the codeine in this medicine. For this reason, your dose will be reviewed to make sure you're only taking the amount you need to control your pain.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Common questions about ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Speak to your doctor if you're worried about tolerance, hyperalgesia or becoming addicted.

Can I become addicted to combined ibuprofen and codeine?

If you take combined ibuprofen and codeine regularly for a long time, you can become addicted to the codeine in it.

You're unlikely to become addicted if you follow your doctor's advice carefully about how long to take it for.

If you buy combined ibuprofen and codeine at a pharmacy, follow the instructions that come with the medicine and only take it for up to 3 days at a time. If your pain is not better after 3 days, it's important to ask your doctor for advice about ongoing pain relief.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Common questions about ibuprofen and codeine
text:
How will I know if I'm addicted?

If you're addicted to the codeine in combined ibuprofen and codeine, you may find it difficult to stop taking it or feel you need to take it more often than necessary.

If you stop taking codeine suddenly, you can get withdrawal symptoms.

These can include:

- feeling agitated or anxious
- panic attacks
- feeling your heartbeat (palpitations)
- difficulty sleeping
- shaking
- sweating
- body aches
- feeling restless

Talk to your doctor if you:

- are worried about addiction
- need help with addiction
- want to stop taking the medicine

Can it cause stomach ulcers?

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Common questions about ibuprofen and codeine
text:
The ibuprofen in this medicine can cause ulcers in your stomach or gut, especially if you take it for a long time or in big doses.

However, if you take it correctly, with food, for short periods of time, the risk is very low. Always follow the instructions that come with your medicine.

How does combined ibuprofen and codeine compare with other painkillers?

Some painkillers work better than others for certain types of pain. For example, the best painkiller to ease your headache may not be the best one for your backache.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Common questions about ibuprofen and codeine
text:
The ibuprofen in combined ibuprofen and codeine means it can be particularly effective for period pain, back pain, strains and sprains.

Before taking combined ibuprofen and codeine, try taking paracetamol to see if that helps your pain. Paracetamol can help relieve most types of pain.

Combined ibuprofen and codeine is meant to be taken for short periods only, of up to 3 days.

This means it may not be suitable for treating longer term conditions unless your doctor prescribes it.

If you need pain relief for a long-term condition or ongoing pain, your doctor will be able to discuss the best treatment options with you.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Common questions about ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Will combined ibuprofen and codeine affect my contraception?

Combined ibuprofen and codeine does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill, progestogen-only pill and emergency contraception.

However, if combined ibuprofen and codeine makes you vomit, your contraceptive pills may not protect you from pregnancy. Look on the pill packet to find out what to do.

Find out more:

- What to do if you're sick or have diarrhoea when taking the combined pill
- What to do if you're sick or have diarrhoea when taking the progestogen-only pill

Can I drive or ride a bike?

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Common questions about ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Combined ibuprofen and codeine can make you feel sleepy or dizzy. If this happens to you, do not drive, cycle or operate tools or machinery, until you feel better.

It's an offence to drive a car if your ability to drive safely is affected. It's your responsibility to decide if it's safe to drive. If you're in any doubt, do not drive.

Even if your ability to drive is not affected, the police have the right to request a saliva sample to check how much combined ibuprofen and codeine is in your body.

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Common questions about ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Talk to your doctor or pharmacist if you're unsure whether it's safe for you to drive while taking combined ibuprofen and codeine.

GOV.UK has more information on the law on drugs and driving.

Can I drink alcohol while taking combined ibuprofen and codeine?

Drinking alcohol while you're taking combined ibuprofen and codeine can make you feel more sleepy or increase the risk of serious side effects.

It's best to stop drinking alcohol while taking combined ibuprofen and codeine.

If you do choose to drink and you feel sleepy, stop drinking alcohol until you finish taking this medicine.

Is there any food or drink I need to avoid?

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Common questions about ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Apart from avoiding alcohol, you can eat and drink normally while taking combined ibuprofen and codeine.

In fact it's best to take ibuprofen and codeine with, or just after, a meal so it does not upset your stomach. Do not take it on an empty stomach.

Will recreational drugs affect it?

If you take recreational drugs, such as cannabis, cocaine and heroin, while you're taking combined ibuprofen and codeine, you're more likely to get side effects. This is because of the codeine in combined ibuprofen and codeine.

Side effects can include:

- breathing difficulties
- heart problems
- seizures or fits
- going into a coma
- feeling sleepy and dizzy

title: Ibuprofen and codeine
section_path: Ibuprofen and codeine > Common questions about ibuprofen and codeine
text:
Taking heroin while you're taking ibuprofen and codeine is especially dangerous. You're more likely to get all the side effects of the codeine, including addiction.

Speak to your doctor if you think you might take recreational drugs while taking ibuprofen and codeine.

Find out more about the side effects of recreational drugs on the Frank website

title: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen)
section_path: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen)
text:
Other common brands: Brufen, Calprofen, Fenbid, Ibugel, Ibuleve

Ibuprofen is a painkiller that helps relieve pain and reduce swelling (inflammation). You can buy most types from shops and pharmacies, but some types are only available with a prescription.

This information is for adults aged 18 or over. There's separate information about ibuprofen for children.

title: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen)
section_path: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen) > What ibuprofen is for
text:
Ibuprofen is a type of painkiller called a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID).

Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs can help with lots of types of pain, including:

- headaches and migraines
- joint and muscle pain
- pain after an injury
- toothache
- period pain

Ibuprofen can also help reduce a high temperature (fever).

Ibuprofen can cause more side effects than paracetamol. If you can take paracetamol, it's a good idea to try it before taking ibuprofen.

title: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen)
section_path: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen) > How to take ibuprofen and how much to take (dose)
text:
There are several different types of ibuprofen, including:

- tablets and capsules
- gels and sprays
- liquid
- granules you mix with water

How you use your medicine and how much to use depends on which type it is and how much ibuprofen it contains.

Always check the packet or leaflet that comes with your medicine. Ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice if you're not sure how to use it or have any problems using it.

If a doctor prescribes ibuprofen for you, follow the advice they give you about how to use it and how much to use.

title: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen)
section_path: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen) > How to take ibuprofen and how much to take (dose) > How to take common types of ibuprofen
text:
200mg tablets and capsules

For most 200mg tablets and capsules:

- swallow 1 or 2 tablets or capsules whole with water (ideally with or after food)
- take them up to 3 times a day if you're still in pain
- wait at least 4 hours between each dose
- do not take more than 6 tablets or capsules in 24 hours

There are also some tablets and capsules that you take in a different way, such as tablets that dissolve on your tongue or "long-lasting" capsules that should be taken less often.

Follow the instructions on the packet or leaflet that comes with your medicine to make sure you're taking it correctly.

400mg tablets and capsules

title: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen)
section_path: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen) > How to take ibuprofen and how much to take (dose) > How to take common types of ibuprofen
text:
If you're taking 400mg ibuprofen tablets or capsules:

- swallow 1 tablet or capsule whole with water (ideally with or after food)
- take it up to 3 times a day if you're still in pain
- wait at least 4 hours between each dose
- do not take more than 3 tablets or capsules in 24 hours

Gel or spray

If you're using ibuprofen gel or spray:

- apply the gel or spray to the painful area and gently rub it into your skin – check the packet or leaflet to see how much to use
- take care to avoid getting it into your eyes, mouth or on any broken skin, and wash your hands after using it
- use it up to 3 or 4 times a day if you're still in pain – check the packet or leaflet to see how many times you can use it
- wait at least 4 hours between each use
- do not use it more than 4 times in 24 hours
- do not smoke or go near naked flames, as clothes that have been in contact with ibuprofen gel or spray can burn more easily

title: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen)
section_path: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen) > How to take ibuprofen and how much to take (dose) > Important
text:
To reduce the risk of side effects, take the smallest dose you need for the shortest time you need it.

Do not take ibuprofen tablets and capsules for more than 10 days unless advised to by a doctor.

For other types of ibuprofen, check the packet or leaflet to see how long you can use it for.

See a GP if your pain gets worse or does not go away.

title: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen)
section_path: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen) > How to take ibuprofen and how much to take (dose) > If you take too much ibuprofen
text: Taking an extra dose of ibuprofen is unlikely to cause problems, but it's important to get medical advice if you take too much as it can sometimes be dangerous.

title: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen)
section_path: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen) > How to take ibuprofen and how much to take (dose) > If you take too much ibuprofen > Urgent advice: Get help from NHS 111 if:
text:
- you've taken more ibuprofen tablets, capsules, liquid or granules than it says on the packet or leaflet
- you've accidentally swallowed ibuprofen gel or spray and feel unwell

You can call 111 or get help from 111 online.

If you're told to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring the ibuprofen packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take.

title: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen)
section_path: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen) > Side effects of ibuprofen
text: Like all medicines, ibuprofen can cause side effects, although not everyone gets them.

title: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen)
section_path: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen) > Side effects of ibuprofen > Common side effects
text:
Common side effects of ibuprofen tablets, capsules, liquid and granules include:

- indigestion and stomach aches
- feeling sick (nausea) and being sick (vomiting)
- headaches
- a rash
- dizziness
- diarrhoea or constipation

You're less likely to get side effects from ibuprofen gel or spray.

Ibuprofen will not usually affect your ability to drive, ride a bike or use machinery, but if you feel dizzy after taking it, wait until the dizziness stops.

title: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen)
section_path: Ibuprofen for adults (Nurofen) > Side effects of ibuprofen > Common side effects > Non-urgent advice: Speak to a pharmacist or doctor if:
text:
