It's an offence to drive a car if your ability to drive safely is affected. It's your responsibility to decide if it's safe to drive. If you're in any doubt, do not drive.

Talk to your doctor or pharmacist if you're unsure whether it's safe for you to drive while taking letrozole. GOV.UK has more information on the law on drugs and driving.

Can I drink alcohol while taking letrozole?

There's no evidence that drinking alcohol causes any problems when taking letrozole.

Some people taking letrozole may get hot flushes or redness when they drink alcohol. In this case, avoiding alcohol may help.

title: Letrozole
section_path: Letrozole > Common questions about letrozole > Important
text:
Is there any food or drink I need to avoid?

Most people can eat and drink normally when taking letrozole.

Some people may get hot flushes or redness when they drink alcohol.

Some people find letrozole affects their appetite.

If you lose your appetite, try to make sure you have a balanced diet. Try eating smaller meals more often.

If it makes you feel hungrier and you're putting on too much weight, ask your doctor or specialist nurse to refer you to a dietitian.

title: Leukoplakia
section_path: Leukoplakia
text: Leukoplakia is a white patch or patches in the mouth. If you have a white patch in your mouth that does not go away, get it checked by a dentist or GP.

title: Leukoplakia
section_path: Leukoplakia > Symptoms of leukoplakia
text:
Leukoplakia patches:

- are white patches in the mouth
- are not usually painful
- are an irregular shape
- may be slightly raised
- may have red areas within the patch
- cannot be rubbed or scraped away (patches that can be removed could be oral thrush)

title: Leukoplakia
section_path: Leukoplakia > Symptoms of leukoplakia > Other causes of a white tongue
text: Find out about other causes of a white tongue

title: Leukoplakia
section_path: Leukoplakia > Non-urgent advice: See a dentist or GP if:
text:
- you have a white patch in your mouth that does not go away
- you have a white patch on your tongue and a weakened immune system – for example, if you have HIV or have had an organ transplant
- you have pain or discomfort in your mouth that is not going away

title: Leukoplakia
section_path: Leukoplakia > What happens at your appointment
text:
If it's thought you may have leukoplakia, the dentist or GP will look at the patch or patches in your mouth.

They will be able to rule out other possible causes, such as a fungal infection of the mouth (oral thrush) or cheek biting.

You may be referred to a specialist for a biopsy. This is where a small piece of the patch is removed and checked for abnormal cells.

title: Leukoplakia
section_path: Leukoplakia > What happens at your appointment > Important: Mouth cancer risk
text:
If you have leukoplakia, there's a small chance it could progress to mouth cancer over time.

This is why it's important to see a dentist or GP if you have a white patch or patches in your mouth.

title: Leukoplakia
section_path: Leukoplakia > Treatments for leukoplakia
text:
Treatment for leukoplakia is not always needed, but you'll have regular check-ups to make sure the patch is not getting bigger.

The patch may get smaller or go away if you:

- stop smoking
- stop drinking alcohol or reduce the amount you drink
- do not chew tobacco, paan or betel nuts

Surgery is sometimes used to remove leukoplakia patches if there's a chance that they could become cancerous.

This may be done after numbing the affected area using local anaesthetic so you do not feel any pain or discomfort. Sometimes a general anaesthetic is used.

title: Leukoplakia
section_path: Leukoplakia > Treatments for leukoplakia
text: The patch can be removed in a number of ways, including using a laser or surgical scalpel. Your mouth should heal quickly afterwards.

title: Leukoplakia
section_path: Leukoplakia > Preventing leukoplakia and mouth cancer
text:
The exact cause of leukoplakia is not known, but smoking and chewing tobacco are thought to increase your chances of getting it.

There are things you can do to reduce your chances of getting leukoplakia. These may also reduce your risk of getting mouth cancer.

title: Leukoplakia
section_path: Leukoplakia > Preventing leukoplakia and mouth cancer > Do
text:
- keep your mouth and teeth healthy by taking care of your teeth and gums
- have regular dental check-ups
- if you wear dentures, make sure they fit properly
- eat a balanced diet, including plenty of fresh fruit and vegetables

title: Leukoplakia
section_path: Leukoplakia > Preventing leukoplakia and mouth cancer > Don’t
text:
- do not smoke
- do not chew tobacco, paan or betel nuts
- do not drink more than the recommended amount of alcohol (14 units a week)

title: Leukoplakia
section_path: Leukoplakia > Hairy leukoplakia
text:
There are a number of different types of leukoplakia.

Hairy leukoplakia is caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, which also causes glandular fever.

You may have hairy leukoplakia if you have a weakened immune system – for example, if you have HIV or have had an organ transplant.

It causes fuzzy white patches, often on the sides of the tongue, that look folded or ridged. They're not painful and cannot be brushed or scraped away.

Antiviral medicines, or treatments you put onto the patch, are sometimes used to treat hairy leukoplakia.

Unlike other types, hairy leukoplakia does not carry a risk of mouth cancer.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam
text:
Common brands: Keppra

Levetiracetam is a medicine used to treat epilepsy. It's only available with a prescription.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > What levetiracetam is for
text:
Levetiracetam is used to prevent seizures caused by epilepsy.

It works by blocking the signals in your brain that can cause seizures.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > How to take levetiracetam
text:
Levetiracetam comes as tablets, granules, a liquid and that you swallow and tablets you dissolve in your mouth (orodispersible).

How much you need to take depends on what type of medicine it is. Your doctor will tell you when to take it and how much. Most people need to take it once or twice a day.

You may start on a low dose but your doctor may increase it over a few weeks until you reach a dose that works for you.

When taking levetiracetam:

- try to take it at the same time each time – if you take it twice a day, this could be once in the morning and once in the evening
- take it with or without food
- swallow tablets whole with a glass of water – do not chew or crush them
- swallow granules straight from the packet, do not chew them – drink water with the granules or afterwards
- use the syringe or spoon that comes with the liquid medicine to help you measure the right dose – you can dilute the liquid in water if you want to
- put orodispersible tablets on your tongue and leave to fully dissolve

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > How to take levetiracetam
text: Always check the packet or leaflet that comes with your medicine. Ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice if you're not sure how to take it or have any problems taking it.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > How to take levetiracetam > If you miss a dose of levetiracetam
text:
If you forget to take levetiracetam, take it as soon as you remember, unless it's nearly time for your next dose.

If it's nearly time for your next dose, skip the dose you missed and take you next dose at the usual time.

Do not take 2 doses to make up for a missed dose.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > How to take levetiracetam > If you take too much levetiracetam
text: Taking an extra dose of levetiracetam is unlikely to cause problems, but it's important to get medical advice if you take too much because it can sometimes be dangerous.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > How to take levetiracetam > If you take too much levetiracetam > Urgent advice: Speak to a pharmacist as soon as possible if:
text:
- you've taken more than your prescribed dose of levetiracetam

If you're unable to speak to a pharmacist, or you took too much of your medicine on purpose, call NHS 111 for advice.

If you're told to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring the levetiracetam packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > How to take levetiracetam > How to stop taking levetiracetam
text:
Keep taking levetiracetam for as long as your doctor advises you to.

If your doctor advises you to stop taking it, your dose will usually need to be reduced gradually. Always follow your doctor's advice.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > Side effects of levetiracetam
text: Like all medicines, levetiracetam can cause side effects, although not everyone gets them.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > Side effects of levetiracetam > Common side effects
text:
Common side effects of levetiracetam include:

- dizziness
- feeling sleepy or tired
- headaches
- difficulty controlling body movements
- feeling sick (nausea) or being sick (vomiting)
- shaking or tremors
- feeling agitated, irritable or aggressive

If you feel tired, sleepy or dizzy after taking levetiracetam, do not drive, ride a bike or use machinery until these symptoms have gone away.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > Side effects of levetiracetam > Common side effects > Non-urgent advice: Speak to a pharmacist or doctor if:
text:
- you have any side effects that bother you or do not go away

They may be able to give you advice about how to reduce any side effects. Keep taking your medicine unless you’re advised to stop.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > Side effects of levetiracetam > Serious side effects
text:
Levetiracetam can sometimes cause serious side effects, although most of them are rare.

Possible serious side effects of levetiracetam include:

- an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) – causing symptoms such as a swollen throat or tongue, a raised, itchy rash or difficulty breathing
- a skin reaction, such as a round, slightly raised rash (erythema multiforme), painful blisters (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), or peeling skin
- kidney problems – causing symptoms such as passing very little pee, feeling tired or confused, or having swollen legs, ankles or feet

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > Side effects of levetiracetam > Serious side effects > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
text:
- you're taking levetiracetam and think you're having anaphylaxis or Stevens-Johnson syndrome

If you think you're having any other serious side effect, call NHS 111.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > Side effects of levetiracetam > More about side effects
text:
These are not all the side effects of levetiracetam.

For a full list, see the leaflet that comes with your medicine or search for your medicine on the electronic medicines compendium website.

You can report any side effects you get on the Yellow Card website

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > Who can and cannot take levetiracetam
text:
Most adults and children aged 1 month old and over can take levetiracetam.

But levetiracetam is not suitable for everyone. For example, it may not be suitable if:

- you've ever had an allergic reaction to or serious side effect from levetiracetam
- you have kidney problems
- you've had low mood (depression) or thoughts of harming or killing yourself

Before taking levetiracetam, tell your doctor if you have any other medical conditions.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > Who can and cannot take levetiracetam > Breastfeeding and levetiracetam
text:
If you're breastfeeding, tell your doctor before taking levetiracetam.

Levetiracetam is not usually used while breastfeeding because the medicine can pass into your breast milk.

Your doctor will discuss it with you and may advise you to continue taking levetiracetam if the benefits to you outweigh the risks to your baby.

If you're taking levetiracetam while breastfeeding, speak to a healthcare professional or call NHS 111 if you have any concerns about your baby.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > Who can and cannot take levetiracetam > Pregnancy and levetiracetam
text:
Tell your doctor if you're planning a pregnancy or you get pregnant while taking levetiracetam.

Levetiracetam can be used during pregnancy if needed. Your doctor will discuss the risks and benefits of taking it while you're pregnant.

If you need to take levetiracetam while you're pregnant, your doctor will prescribe the lowest possible effective dose. They may also advise you to take a higher dose of folic acid.

You may be advised to give birth in hospital so you and your baby can be closely monitored after you've given birth.

Find out more about taking levetiracetam during pregnancy on the Bumps (Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy) website

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > Taking levetiracetam with other medicines, food and drink
text:
There are some medicines, herbal remedies and supplements that may not mix well with levetiracetam.

These include:

- macrogol, a laxative
- methotrexate, a medicine used to treat arthritis and other conditions

Do not use the herbal supplement St John's wort when taking levetiracetam.

Before you take levetiracetam, tell your doctor if you're taking any other medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > Taking levetiracetam with other medicines, food and drink > Food and alcohol with levetiracetam
text:
You can eat normally while taking levetiracetam.

But it's best not to drink alcohol while taking levetiracetam as it can increase the risk of side effects such as feeling sleepy.

title: Levetiracetam
section_path: Levetiracetam > Find out more about your medicine
text:
To find out more about your medicine, you can:

- check the leaflet that comes with it
- search for your medicine leaflet on the electronic medicines compendium website
- check the information about levetiracetam on the Medicines for Children website
- speak to a pharmacist or doctor for advice – if you recently started taking it, you can get help with newly prescribed medicines from a pharmacist as part of the New Medicine Service

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine
text: Levothyroxine is a medicine used to treat an underactive thyroid. It's only available with a prescription.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > What levothyroxine is for
text:
Levothyroxine is mainly used to treat an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism).

Levothyroxine can help with symptoms of an underactive thyroid including:

- tiredness
- weight gain
- low mood

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > How to take levothyroxine
text:
Levothyroxine usually comes as tablets or liquid (oral solution) that you swallow.

How much you need to take depends on your thyroid hormone levels, any other conditions you may have and your age. You'll usually take it once a day.

Your doctor may prescribe a low dose to start with and increase it gradually. This is to find the right dose to manage your condition.

You'll usually need to take the medicine for the rest of your life to prevent your symptoms returning. You should be able to live a normal life.

When taking levothyroxine:

- take it on an empty stomach 30 to 60 minutes before your first meal of the day, any drink with caffeine, such as tea or coffee, or any other medicine
- try to take it at the same time each day
- swallow tablets whole with a glass of water
- use the syringe or spoon that comes with the liquid to measure out the correct dose

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > How to take levothyroxine
text: Always check the packet or leaflet that comes with your medicine. Ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice if you're not sure how to take it or you have any problems taking it.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > How to take levothyroxine > Important
text:
You'll have regular blood tests to check you're on the right dose of levothyroxine. Being on the wrong dose can cause side effects, such as feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, headaches or problems sleeping.

If you have any side effects, talk to your GP or a pharmacist.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > How to take levothyroxine > If you miss a dose of levothyroxine
text:
If you forget to take a dose of levothyroxine, take it as soon as you remember, unless it's nearly time for your next dose.

If it's nearly time for your next dose, skip the dose you missed and take your next dose at the usual time.

Do not take 2 doses at the same time to make up for a missed dose.

If you forget to give your child a dose, talk to a doctor or pharmacist for advice.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > How to take levothyroxine > If you take too much levothyroxine
text: Taking an extra dose of levothyroxine is unlikely to cause problems, but it's important to get medical advice if you take too much as it can sometimes be dangerous.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Urgent advice: Speak to a pharmacist as soon as possible if:
text:
- you've taken more than your prescribed dose of levothyroxine

If you're unable to speak to a pharmacist, or you took too much of your medicine on purpose, call NHS 111 for advice.

If you're told to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring the levothyroxine packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Urgent advice: Speak to a pharmacist as soon as possible if: > Advice about giving medicines to children
text: - How to give different types of medicines (Medicines for Children website)

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Side effects of levothyroxine
text:
Like all medicines, levothyroxine can cause side effects, although not everyone gets them.

Most side effects usually happen when the dose is too high. They often improve when the dose is changed.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Side effects of levothyroxine > Common side effects
text:
Common side effects of levothyroxine include:

- difficulty sleeping (insomnia)
- headaches
- feeling anxious
- sweating
- hair loss

Levothyroxine will not usually affect your ability to drive, ride a bike or use machinery.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Non-urgent advice: Speak to a doctor or pharmacist if:
text:
- you have any side effects that bother you or do not go away

They may be able to give you advice about how to reduce any side effects. Keep taking your medicine unless you're advised to stop.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Non-urgent advice: Speak to a doctor or pharmacist if: > Serious side effects
text:
Levothyroxine can sometimes cause serious side effects, but most of them are rare.

Possible serious side effects of levothyroxine include:

- an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) – causing symptoms such as a swollen throat or tongue, a raised, itchy rash and difficulty breathing
- a reaction to the sudden increase in thyroid hormone levels (thyroid crisis) – causing symptoms such as a high temperature, a fast or irregular heartbeat, feeling dizzy or faint, yellowing of the eyes and skin (jaundice)

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if:
text: - you're taking levothyroxine and think you might be having serious side effects

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if: > More about side effects
text:
These are not all the side effects of levothyroxine.

For a full list, see the leaflet inside your medicines packet, or search for your medicine leaflet on the electronic medicines compendium website.

You can report any side effects you get on the Yellow Card Scheme website

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Who can and cannot take levothyroxine
text:
Most adults and children can take levothyroxine.

But levothyroxine is not suitable for everyone. For example, it may not be suitable if:

- you've had an allergic reaction or serious side effect from levothyroxine
- you have an overactive thyroid
- you have diabetes
- you have a condition that affects your adrenal glands
- you have a heart condition

Check the packet or leaflet that comes with your medicine to see if it's suitable for you. Speak to a pharmacist or doctor if you're not sure if you can use it.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Who can and cannot take levothyroxine > Breastfeeding and levothyroxine
text:
You can usually take levothyroxine while breastfeeding but check with a pharmacist or doctor first.

It's rare for breastfed babies to get any side effects from medicine you're taking, but speak to a healthcare professional if you have any concerns about your baby.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Who can and cannot take levothyroxine > Pregnancy and levothyroxine
text:
Tell your doctor if you're pregnant (or get pregnant) while taking levothyroxine.

Levothyroxine can be taken during pregnancy if needed.

If you need to take levothyroxine while you're pregnant, you may need more blood tests to check your thyroid hormone levels and make sure you're taking the right dose.

Your doctor will talk to you about the risks and benefits of taking it while pregnant.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Taking levothyroxine with other medicines, food and drink
text:
There are some medicines, remedies and supplements that may not mix well with levothyroxine.

These include:

- medicines for epilepsy, such as carbamazepine
- medicines to reduce the amount of acid in your stomach, such as omeprazole
- medicine for weight gain, such as semaglutide
- antidepressants, such as sertraline
- antacids and other indigestion treatments
- calcium and iron supplements
- some medicines for high blood pressure and heart problems, such as beta blockers and digoxin
- the herbal supplement St John's wort
- biotin (vitamin B7) as it can affect your thyroid tests

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Taking levothyroxine with other medicines, food and drink
text: Before taking levothyroxine, tell your doctor if you're taking any other medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Taking levothyroxine with other medicines, food and drink > Food, drink and alcohol with levothyroxine
text: Taking levothyroxine with some foods can affect how it works. It's best to take it 30 to 60 minutes before your first meal of the day, or any drink with caffeine, such as tea or coffee.

title: Levothyroxine
section_path: Levothyroxine > Find out more about your medicine
text:
To find out more about your medicine, you can:

- check the leaflet that comes with it
- search for your medicine leaflet on the electronic medicines compendium website
- find out about levothyroxine for hypothyroidism on the Medicines for Children website
- speak to a pharmacist or doctor

title: Lichen planus
section_path: Lichen planus
text: Lichen planus is a rash that can affect different parts of your body, including the inside of your mouth. See a GP if you think you might have it.

title: Lichen planus
section_path: Lichen planus > Symptoms of lichen planus
text:
The main symptoms of lichen planus include:

- clusters of shiny, raised, purple-red blotches on your arms, legs or body (you may see fine white lines on the blotches) – the rash may be harder to see on black or brown skin
- white patches on your gums, tongue or the insides of your cheeks
- burning and stinging in your mouth, especially when you eat or drink
- bald patches appearing on your scalp
- sore red patches on your vulva
- rough, thinning nails with grooves on
- ring-shaped purple or white patches on your penis

You may only have 1 of these symptoms.

Lichen planus on your skin can be very itchy, but not always.

title: Lichen planus
section_path: Lichen planus > Symptoms of lichen planus
text:
If you're not sure it's lichen planus

Conditions similar to lichen planus

title: Lichen planus
section_path: Lichen planus > Symptoms of lichen planus
text:
Symptoms | Possible cause
Symptoms: Red, flaky, crusty patches, often on elbows or knees | Possible cause: Psoriasis
Symptoms: Raised, red, scaly patches on the body | Possible cause: Pityriasis rosea
Symptoms: Itching and white patches on the vulva | Possible cause: Lichen sclerosus
Symptoms: Ring-like red patch anywhere on the body | Possible cause: Ringworm
Symptoms: Itchy, dry, cracked, sore and red skin | Possible cause: Eczema

title: Lichen planus
section_path: Lichen planus > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
text: - you think you have lichen planus

title: Lichen planus
section_path: Lichen planus > Treatments for lichen planus
text:
Lichen planus on your skin usually gets better on its own in about 9 to 18 months.

Creams and ointments from a GP can help control the rash and ease itching.

If creams and ointments do not work, or you have severe lichen planus, steroid tablets or treatment with a special kind of light (light therapy) can help.

Lichen planus in your mouth can last for several years. Mouthwashes and sprays from a GP can help ease symptoms like burning or sore gums.

You cannot catch lichen planus and it does not usually come back once it's cleared up.

title: Lichen planus
section_path: Lichen planus > How to ease lichen planus at home
text: There are things you can do to help ease lichen planus symptoms at home. These will depend on which area of your body is affected.

title: Lichen planus
section_path: Lichen planus > How to ease lichen planus at home > Lichen planus on the skin
text:
If you have lichen planus on your skin:

- wash with warm water – avoid soaps and body washes
- wash your hair over a sink or bath so the shampoo does not touch the rest of your skin
- a GP may prescribe a moisturising treatment for the skin (emollient) to use on the rash
- try not to scratch your skin

title: Lichen planus
section_path: Lichen planus > How to ease lichen planus at home > Lichen planus on the genitals
text:
If you have lichen planus on your genitals:

- try to have showers rather than baths
- hold a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a clean tea towel against the affected areas to ease itching and swelling
- avoid wearing tights or close-fitting clothes
- carefully dry yourself after having a pee to reduce the chances of pee getting in contact with your skin – avoid rubbing the area
- use a lubricant if sex is painful

title: Lichen planus
section_path: Lichen planus > How to ease lichen planus at home > Lichen planus in the mouth
text:
If you have lichen planus in your mouth:

- avoid salty, spicy and acidic foods, or alcohol, if they make your mouth sore
- brush your teeth carefully twice a day to keep your gums healthy
- use a mouthwash that does not contain alcohol, if it makes your mouth sore

title: Lichen sclerosus
section_path: Lichen sclerosus
text: Lichen sclerosus is a skin condition that causes itchy white patches, most commonly on the genitals. There's no cure, but treatment can help relieve the symptoms.

title: Lichen sclerosus
section_path: Lichen sclerosus > Symptoms of lichen sclerosus
text:
Lichen sclerosus affects people of all ages, including children. But it's much more common in women over 50.

People with white, brown or black skin can get lichen sclerosus.

It causes patches on the skin that are usually:

- itchy
- white
- smooth or crinkled
- easily damaged – they may bleed or hurt if rubbed or scratched

The patches can appear anywhere, but most often are on the:

- area around the opening to the vagina (vulva) and anus
- foreskin and end of the penis

Having sex can be painful because the vulva may shrink or tighten. In men, the foreskin may tighten making erections painful.

title: Lichen sclerosus
section_path: Lichen sclerosus > Symptoms of lichen sclerosus
text: See what lichen sclerosus looks like on the vulva, foreskin and anus

title: Lichen sclerosus
section_path: Lichen sclerosus > Things you can do to help with lichen sclerosus
text: If you have lichen sclerosus, there are some things you can do to help stop your skin becoming irritated or damaged.

title: Lichen sclerosus
section_path: Lichen sclerosus > Things you can do to help with lichen sclerosus > Do
text:
- wash with an emollient soap substitute instead of regular soap – ask a doctor or pharmacist about suitable products
- gently dab your genitals dry after peeing
- regularly apply a barrier cream or ointment, such as petroleum jelly, to affected areas
- wear cotton or silk underwear
- use lubricant if sex is uncomfortable

title: Lichen sclerosus
section_path: Lichen sclerosus > Things you can do to help with lichen sclerosus > Don’t
text:
- do not smoke
- do not scratch or rub the affected skin
- do not use scented soaps, bubble bath or shower gel
- do not wear tight or restrictive clothes, such as tight-fitting underwear
- do not wash your underwear with detergent – just use water
- do not wear panty liners or use fragrance-free ones if you need to use them
- do not do activities like cycling or horse riding until your symptoms have improved
- do not smoke or go near naked flames if you use an emollient – emollients are not flammable on the skin, but when they get on fabrics such as dressings, clothing and bedding they can catch fire more easily

title: Lichen sclerosus
section_path: Lichen sclerosus > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if you have:
text:
- an itchy white patch on your genitals or skin
- been diagnosed with lichen sclerosus and treatment is not helping
- been diagnosed with lichen sclerosus and have pain when going to the toilet or having sex

A GP may refer you to a specialist for tests and treatment.

title: Lichen sclerosus
section_path: Lichen sclerosus > Treatment for lichen sclerosus
text:
Lichen sclerosus cannot be cured, but using a strong prescription steroid ointment usually helps relieve the symptoms.

You may need to use the ointment regularly for a few months to get your symptoms under control. Your doctor will tell you how often you need to use the ointment.

After the initial treatment period, you may need to use other products, such as a weaker steroid ointment or a moisturising cream, to help manage your symptoms.

Follow your doctor's advice about how and when to use any medicine that's prescribed for you.

title: Lichen sclerosus
section_path: Lichen sclerosus > Treatment for lichen sclerosus > Find out more
text: Lichen sclerosus guide: for adults with vulval lichen sclerosus

title: Lichen sclerosus
section_path: Lichen sclerosus > Problems caused by lichen sclerosus
text:
Although treatment for lichen sclerosus can help, the affected skin can sometimes become scarred and tight over time.

The vulva may shrink, with the clitoris and small inner lips (labia minora) around the opening of the vagina often affected.

The scarring and tightness can cause discomfort when peeing, pooing and during sex. Having an erection can be painful.

If lichen sclerosus is severe, you might need a small operation, such as surgery to widen your vagina or remove your foreskin (circumcision).

title: Lichen sclerosus
section_path: Lichen sclerosus > Problems caused by lichen sclerosus > Cancer and lichen sclerosus
text:
Lichen sclerosus increases your risk of getting cancer on your vulva, penis or anus.

The risk is low, but it's a good idea to check yourself regularly and see a GP if you're worried.

Symptoms to look for include a lump, a change in skin texture, such as thickening, or an ulcer that does not go away.

Find out about vulval cancer, penile cancer and anal cancer.

title: Lichen sclerosus
section_path: Lichen sclerosus > Causes of lichen sclerosus
text:
The cause of lichen sclerosus is unknown.

It might be caused by your immune system, the body's defence against infection, mistakenly attacking and damaging your skin.

Lichen sclerosus is:

- not caused by an infection
- not contagious – you cannot spread it to other people through close contact, including sex
- not caused by poor personal hygiene

Rubbing or damage to the skin can trigger lichen sclerosus or make it worse.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin
text: Linagliptin is a medicine used to treat type 2 diabetes. It's only available with a prescription.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > What linagliptin is for
text:
Linagliptin is used to treat type 2 diabetes.

Type 2 diabetes happens when your body does not make enough of a hormone called insulin, or the insulin it makes does not work properly (insulin resistance). Without enough insulin, your blood sugar (glucose) can get too high.

Linagliptin works by increasing the amount of insulin your body produces and lowering your blood sugar level.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > How to take linagliptin
text:
Linagliptin comes as tablets you take once a day.

You'll usually need to take it long term. Do not stop taking it unless your doctor tells you to.

When taking linagliptin:

- swallow the tablets whole with a glass of water (do not crush or chew them)
- it's best to take it at the same time each day
- you can take it with or without food

Always check the packet or leaflet that comes with your medicine. Ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice if you’re not sure how to take it or have any problems taking it.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > How to take linagliptin > If you miss a dose of linagliptin
text:
If you forget to take a dose of linagliptin, take it as soon as you remember unless it's nearly time for your next dose.

If it's nearly time for your next dose, skip the dose you missed and take your next dose at the usual time.

Do not take 2 doses to make up for a missed dose.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > How to take linagliptin > If you take too much linagliptin
text: Taking an extra dose of linagliptin can be dangerous.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > How to take linagliptin > If you take too much linagliptin > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if:
text:
- you've taken more than your prescribed dose of linagliptin

If you're told to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring the linagliptin packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > Side effects of linagliptin
text:
Like all medicines, linagliptin can cause side effects, although not everyone gets them.

Side effects of linagliptin include:

- cold-like symptoms, such as a blocked nose
- a cough
- constipation

If you take linagliptin alongside another diabetic medicine, it may cause low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia, or a hypo). This can make you feel dizzy, feel sick (nausea), be sick (vomit), feel very hungry or feel very tired.

If you get symptoms of a hypo, eat or drink something sugary to raise your blood sugar level quickly. If this happens often, see your GP.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > Side effects of linagliptin
text: Linagliptin should not affect your ability to drive but if you have symptoms of a hypo – such as feeling sleepy, dizziness or blurred vision – do not drive, ride a bike or use machinery until you no longer have these symptoms.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > Side effects of linagliptin > Non-urgent advice: Speak to a pharmacist or doctor if:
text:
- you have any side effects that bother you or do not go away

They may be able to give you advice about how to reduce any side effects. Keep taking your medicine unless you're advised to stop.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > Side effects of linagliptin > Serious side effects
text:
Linagliptin can sometimes cause serious side effects, although most of them are rare.

Possible serious side effects of linagliptin include:

- an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) – causing symptoms such as a swollen throat or tongue, a raised, itchy rash or difficulty breathing
- severe skin reactions – causing symptoms such as a sore, itchy, raised rash, blisters or peeling skin
- swelling of your pancreas (pancreatitis) – causing symptoms such as severe pain in your stomach or your back that does not go away

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > Side effects of linagliptin > Serious side effects > Urgent advice: Call 999 if:
text:
- you're taking linagliptin and think you might be having anaphylaxis, pancreatitis or serious skin reactions

If you think you're having any other serious side effect, call NHS 111.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > Side effects of linagliptin > More about side effects
text:
These are not all the side effects of linagliptin.

For a full list, see the leaflet that comes with your medicine or search for your medicine on the electronic medicines compendium website.

You can report any side effects you get on the Yellow Card website

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > Who can and cannot take linagliptin
text:
Most adults can take linagliptin, but it's not suitable for everyone.

For example, it may not be not suitable for you if:

- you've had an allergic reaction or serious side effect from linagliptin or a similar medicine before
- you've had pancreatitis or other problems with your pancreas

Before taking linagliptin, tell your doctor if you have any medical conditions.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > Who can and cannot take linagliptin > Breastfeeding and linagliptin
text:
Tell your doctor if you're breastfeeding.

Linagliptin is usually not used if you're breastfeeding. Your doctor may suggest stopping linagliptin or switching to a different medicine.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > Who can and cannot take linagliptin > Pregnancy and linagliptin
text:
Tell your doctor if you're pregnant or get pregnant while taking linagliptin.

Linagliptin is not used during pregnancy. Your doctor may suggest stopping linagliptin or switching to a different medicine.

Find out more about taking antidiabetic drugs such as linagliptin during pregnancy on the Bumps (Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy) website

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > Taking linagliptin with other medicines, food and drink
text:
There are some medicines, remedies and supplements that may not mix well with linagliptin.

These include:

- medicines to treat epilepsy or nerve pain, such as carbamazepine
- rifampicin, a type of antibiotic
- other medicines for high blood sugar, such as insulin, metformin or gliclazide – your doctor may want to change your dose of these medicines

Before taking linagliptin, tell your doctor if you're taking any other medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > Taking linagliptin with other medicines, food and drink > Food and alcohol with linagliptin
text:
Follow your doctor's advice about diet while taking linagliptin as part of your diabetes treatment to reduce the chances of your blood sugar level getting too low. This may include eating a healthy diet and not skipping or delaying meals.

It's best not to drink alcohol while taking linagliptin because it can affect your blood sugar level.

title: Linagliptin
section_path: Linagliptin > Find out more about your medicine
text:
To find out more about your medicine, you can:

- check the leaflet that comes with it
- search for your medicine leaflet on the electronic medicines compendium website
- speak to a pharmacist or doctor for advice – if you recently started taking it, you can get help with newly prescribed medicines from a pharmacist as part of the New Medicine Service

title: Lipoedema
section_path: Lipoedema
text: Lipoedema is an abnormal build-up of fat in your legs and sometimes arms. It can be painful and affect daily life, but there are things you can do that may help.

title: Lipoedema
section_path: Lipoedema > Symptoms of lipoedema
text:
Lipoedema is more common in women. It usually affects both sides of the body equally.

Lipoedema can make your bottom, thighs, lower legs and sometimes your arms look out of proportion with the rest of the body.

You may also have pain, tenderness or heaviness in the affected limbs, and you may bruise easily.

Lipoedema affects people differently.

Some people have mild symptoms that do not affect their life. Others can struggle with physical problems, blaming themselves for the changes in their body, and have mental health problems.

title: Lipoedema
section_path: Lipoedema > Symptoms of lipoedema > Other causes of large or swollen legs
text:
There are other things that can cause large or swollen legs.

If you have swelling in all or part of a limb or another part of the body, it could be lymphoedema.

This can affect any part of the body, but usually develops in the arms or legs and develops when the lymphatic system does not work properly.

Sometimes, a build-up of fluid can cause the legs, ankles or feet to become swollen. This is called oedema. In lipoedema, the feet are not usually affected.

title: Lipoedema
section_path: Lipoedema > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
text:
- you have symptoms of lipoedema
- you have swollen legs, ankles or feet and the swelling has not improved after a few days

title: Lipoedema
section_path: Lipoedema > Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if:
text:
- your leg or legs become swollen, red, hot and painful and you have flu-like symptoms

You may have cellulitis (a skin infection) and need treatment with antibiotics.

You can call 111 or get help from 111 online.

title: Lipoedema
section_path: Lipoedema > Treatments for lipoedema
text:
If the GP thinks you have lipoedema they may refer you to a specialist for treatment.

There's currently no cure, but there are things that can help and stop it getting worse.

Your treatment will depend on how severe your symptoms are and how they're affecting you.

The main treatments are:

- eating healthily, doing more exercise and trying to maintain a healthy weight
- wearing compression stockings or bandages to reduce pain and discomfort, and make it easier for you to walk
- looking after your skin – for example, by regularly using moisturising cream (emollients) to stop your skin drying out
- counselling or cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) if you're finding it difficult to cope with your symptoms and you feel depressed
- a procedure to get rid of the fat (liposuction) if your symptoms are particularly severe – you may need more than 1 operation and it may not be available on the NHS

title: Lipoedema
section_path: Lipoedema > Treatments for lipoedema > Compression therapy
text:
Compression therapy can sometimes help manage lipoedema.

A specially trained clinician will assess you and recommend the most suitable type of compression.

Find out more about compression therapy for lipoedema on the LymphConnect website

title: Lipoedema
section_path: Lipoedema > Getting support
text:
Talking to someone and getting support can help if lipoedema is affecting your quality of life.

Lipoedema UK and Talk Lipoedema give help and advice about managing lipoedema. They can also put you in touch with other people with it.

title: Lipoedema
section_path: Lipoedema > Causes of lipoedema
text:
The exact cause of lipoedema is not clear.

It's not caused by being overweight – you can be a healthy weight and still get it.

It may be caused by changes in your hormones:

- during puberty
- when you're pregnant
- when you're going through the menopause
- when you're taking the contraceptive pill

Sometimes lipoedema runs in families.

title: Lipoma
section_path: Lipoma
text: Lipomas are soft, fatty lumps that grow under your skin. They're harmless and do not usually need any treatment, but it's important to get any lumps checked by a GP.

title: Lipoma
section_path: Lipoma > Symptoms of a lipoma
text:
Lipomas are common.

They:

- feel soft and squishy
- can be anything from the size of a pea to a few centimetres across
- may move slightly under your skin if you press them
- are not usually painful
- grow slowly
- can appear anywhere on your body

title: Lipoma
section_path: Lipoma > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
text:
- you get a lump anywhere on your body
- a lump is painful, red or hot to touch
- a lump is hard and does not move
- a lump increases in size

A GP will usually be able to tell if the lump is a lipoma.

If there's any doubt, they may refer you for a scan to check it.

In rare cases, lumps under your skin can be a sign of something more serious.

title: Lipoma
section_path: Lipoma > Getting a lipoma removed
text:
Lipomas are harmless and do not usually need to be removed. They would only be removed on the NHS if it was growing or causing symptoms because of where it is.

If you have it removed it may be sent to a laboratory to check it is a lipoma.

You can pay to have a lipoma removed at a private clinic, but it may be expensive.

A GP can give you advice about where to get treatment.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide
text:
Common brands: Saxenda, Diavic, Zegluxen

Liraglutide is a medicine used to treat obesity (called Saxenda) or manage type 2 diabetes (called Diavic and Zegluxen). It's available on the NHS or privately.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > What liraglutide is for
text:
Liraglutide is a type of medicine called a GLP-1 agonist. It can be used to manage type 2 diabetes or obesity, by helping you lose weight when you combine it with exercise and changes to your diet.

Liraglutide works for weight loss by reducing your appetite and helping you feel fuller for longer.

For type 2 diabetes it works by lowering high blood sugar levels and helps your body to make more insulin if it's needed. It also slows digestion which keeps your blood sugar levels stable after meals and can help prevent heart disease.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > What liraglutide is for
text:
Liraglutide can be prescribed for weight loss by NHS weight management services which your doctor can refer you to if your BMI meets the eligibility criteria.

If you decide to get a private prescription for liraglutide, it's important to get it from a registered pharmacy. There are some websites that sell fake weight loss medicines.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > How to use liraglutide
text:
Liraglutide comes as an injection that you give yourself once a day.

Always check the packet or leaflet that comes with your medicine. It will tell you how to get the injection ready.

Keep your injection in the fridge until you're ready to use it.

Ask a pharmacist, nurse or doctor for advice if you're not sure how to use it or you have any problems.

When using liraglutide:

- try to inject at the same time each day – you can use it at any time of day
- inject into the fatty areas of your thigh, tummy or upper arm
- change the place you inject each day – you can use the same area but do not use the exact same spot
- inject into a different place if you inject insulin as well

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > How to use liraglutide > If you miss a liraglutide injection
text:
If you forget to give yourself liraglutide and:

- it's 12 hours or less since you should have had it, give yourself the injection as soon as you remember
- it's more than 12 hours since you should have had it, skip the missed injection

Then continue as usual and give yourself your next injection the next day.

Do not give yourself 2 injections at the same time to make up for a missed one.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > How to use liraglutide > If you use too much liraglutide
text: It's important to get medical advice if you use too much liraglutide because it can sometimes be dangerous.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > How to use liraglutide > If you use too much liraglutide > Urgent advice: Get help from NHS 111 if:
text:
- you've used more than your prescribed dose of liraglutide

You can call 111 or get help from 111 online.

If you're told to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring the liraglutide packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > How to use liraglutide > How to stop taking liraglutide
text:
Talk to your doctor if you want to stop using liraglutide, and do not stop suddenly. If you have type 2 diabetes it could affect your blood sugar.

Your doctor may suggest reducing your dose gradually.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Side effects of liraglutide
text: Like all medicines, liraglutide can cause side effects, but not everyone gets them.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Side effects of liraglutide > Common side effects
text:
Common side effects of liraglutide include:

- feeling sick (nausea) or being sick (vomiting)
- constipation or diarrhoea
- headache
- feeling tired
- itchy or red skin where you inject – redness maybe harder to see on brown or black skin

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Side effects of liraglutide > Common side effects > Non-urgent advice: Speak to a pharmacist or doctor if:
text:
- you have any side effects that bother you or do not go away

They may be able to give you advice about how you can reduce the side effects. Keep taking your medicine unless you're advised not to.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Side effects of liraglutide > Serious side effects
text:
Liraglutide can sometimes cause serious side effects, but most of them are rare.

Possible serious side effects of liraglutide include:

- an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), which can cause symptoms such as a swollen throat or tongue, a raised, itchy rash or difficulty breathing
- low blood sugar (more likely if used with other diabetes medicines), which can cause symptoms such as headaches, vision problems, feeling dizzy, weak or confused, a fast heartbeat or sweating
- an inflamed pancreas (acute pancreatitis), which can cause severe pain in your stomach or back that does not go away
- gallstones or swelling of the gallbladder (cholecystitis), which can cause severe tummy pain

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Side effects of liraglutide > Serious side effects
text: If you feel dizzy or have vision problems after using liraglutide, do not drive, ride a bike or use machinery until you no longer have these side effects.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Side effects of liraglutide > Serious side effects > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if:
text: - you're taking liraglutide and think you might be having serious side effects

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Side effects of liraglutide > More about side effects
text:
These are not all the side effects of liraglutide.

For a full list, see the leaflet that comes with your medicine or search for your medicine on the electronic medicines compendium website.

You can report any side effects you get on the Yellow Card website

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Who can and cannot take liraglutide
text:
Most adults and children aged 10 years and over can use liraglutide.

Liraglutide is not suitable for some people. For example, it may not be suitable if:

- you've had an allergic reaction or serious side effect from liraglutide or another GLP-1 agonist
- you're 75 years old or over
- you have stomach or gut problems such as gastroparesis or inflammatory bowel disease
- you have or have had an inflamed pancreas (acute pancreatitis)

Before using liraglutide, tell your doctor or a pharmacist if you have any medical conditions.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Who can and cannot take liraglutide > Breastfeeding and liraglutide
text: Tell your doctor if you're breastfeeding. Liraglutide is not used while breastfeeding as it's not known if the medicine passes into breast milk.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Who can and cannot take liraglutide > Pregnancy and liraglutide
text:
Tell your doctor if you're pregnant or get pregnant while taking liraglutide.

Liraglutide is not used during pregnancy as there's not enough information to say it’s safe for your baby.

Your doctor will recommend other medicines to treat type 2 diabetes while you're pregnant.

Find out more about taking GLP-1 agonists, including liraglutide, during pregnancy on the Bumps (Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy) website

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Using liraglutide with other medicines, food and drink
text:
There are some medicines, herbal remedies and supplements that may not mix well with liraglutide.

These include:

- other diabetes medicines, such as gliclazide, glimepiride, metformin and tolbutamide
- insulin – your doctor or specialist nurse may need to adjust your dose
- other GLP-1 agonists such as semaglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide or lixisenatide
- a general anaesthetic (which puts you to sleep) or a sedative (which relaxes you) for an operation or dental procedure – tell the healthcare professional that you're using liraglutide

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Using liraglutide with other medicines, food and drink
text: Before you use liraglutide, tell your doctor or a pharmacist if you're taking any other medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Using liraglutide with other medicines, food and drink > Liraglutide and contraception
text: If there's a chance you could get pregnant, you'll need to use contraception while you’re taking liraglutide.

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Using liraglutide with other medicines, food and drink > Food, drink and alcohol with liraglutide
text:
You'll need to eat a healthy, balanced diet while using liraglutide.

It's best to avoid drinking alcohol while taking liraglutide because it can increase side effects like feeling or being sick (nausea or vomiting).

Find out more about eating a healthy, balanced diet

title: Liraglutide
section_path: Liraglutide > Find out more about your medicine
text:
To find out more about your medicine, you can:

- check the leaflet that comes with it
- search for your medicine leaflet on the electronic medicines compendium website
- speak to a pharmacist or doctor for advice – if you recently started taking it for type 2 diabetes, you can get help with newly prescribed medicines from a pharmacist as part of the New Medicine Service

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril
text: Lisinopril is a medicine to manage high blood pressure. It’s only available with a prescription.

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > What lisinopril is for
text:
Lisinopril is a type of medicine called an ACE inhibitor which makes your blood vessels relax and widen. This helps to lower your blood pressure and makes it easier for your heart to pump blood around your body.

Lisinopril is used to treat:

- high blood pressure (hypertension)
- a recent heart attack
- kidney problems caused by diabetes

It’s also used, along with other medicines, to treat heart failure.

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > How to take lisinopril
text:
Lisinopril comes as tablets you swallow with water, or as a liquid.

Your doctor may prescribe a low dose to start with and gradually increase it over a few days or weeks. This reduces the chances of side effects.

You may have regular blood tests or other checks while you're taking lisinopril.

Some people take it for a few weeks while others take it for several months or more.

When taking lisinopril:

- try to take it at the same time each day
- swallow the tablets whole with a glass of water

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > How to take lisinopril
text: Always check the packet or leaflet that comes with your medicine. Ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice if you're not sure how to take it or have any problems taking it.

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > How to take lisinopril > If you miss a dose of lisinopril
text:
If you forget to take a dose of lisinopril, take it as soon as you remember, unless it's nearly time for your next dose.

If it’s nearly time for your next dose, skip the dose you missed and take your next dose at the usual time.

Do not take 2 doses to make up for a missed dose.

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > How to take lisinopril > If you take too much lisinopril
text: Taking an extra dose of lisinopril can be dangerous.

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > How to take lisinopril > Urgent advice: Get help from NHS 111 if:
text:
- you've taken more than your prescribed dose of lisinopril

You can call 111 or get help from 111 online.

If you're told to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring the lisinopril packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take.

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > Side effects of lisinopril
text: Like all medicines, lisinopril can cause side effects, although not everyone gets them.

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > Side effects of lisinopril > Common side effects
text:
Common side effects of lisinopril include:

- headaches
- feeling or being sick (nausea or vomiting)
- diarrhoea
- feeling dizzy, especially if you stand up quickly
- a dry cough that does not go away
- kidney problems (you'll have blood tests to check for this)

If you feel dizzy or drowsy after taking lisinopril, do not drive, ride a bike or use machinery until you no longer have these symptoms.

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > Side effects of lisinopril > Non-urgent advice: Speak to a pharmacist or doctor if:
text:
- you have any side effects that bother you or do not go away

They may be able to give you advice about how you can reduce the side effects. Keep taking your medicine unless you're advised to stop.

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > Side effects of lisinopril > Serious side effects
text:
Lisinopril can sometimes cause serious side effects, although most of them are uncommon or rare.

Possible serious side effects of lisinopril include:

- an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) – causing symptoms such as a swollen throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash and difficulty breathing
- kidney failure – which may cause symptoms such as blood in your pee, passing less pee than usual, and pain in your lower back
- angioedema – which causes swelling in areas such as your lips, tongue and face (you have a higher chance of getting angioedema if you have black skin)

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > Side effects of lisinopril > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if:
text: - you're taking lisinopril and think you might be having serious side effects

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > Side effects of lisinopril > More about side effects
text:
These are not all the side effects of lisinopril.

For a full list, see the leaflet that came with your medicine or search for your medicine leaflet on the electronic medicines compendium website.

You can report any side effects you get on the Yellow Card website

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > Who can and cannot take lisinopril
text:
Lisinopril is a medicine for adults and children over 6 years old.

Lisinopril is not suitable for some people. For example, it may not be suitable if you’ve had an allergic reaction to lisinopril or another ACE inhibitor.

It also may not be suitable if you have:

- a condition called angioedema that causes swelling in areas such as your face, hands and feet, mouth or throat
- kidney problems
- liver problems
- treatment to prevent allergy symptoms, such as desensitisation therapy

Before taking lisinopril, tell your doctor if you have any medical conditions.

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > Who can and cannot take lisinopril > Breastfeeding and lisinopril
text:
Tell your doctor if you're breastfeeding.

Lisinopril may be taken while breastfeeding, but it's best to check because the medicine may pass into your breast milk in small amounts.

A doctor may recommend you try a different ACE inhibitor, called enalapril, while you’re breastfeeding.

If you’re taking lisinopril while breastfeeding, speak to a healthcare professional or call NHS 111 if you have any concerns about your baby.

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > Who can and cannot take lisinopril > Pregnancy and lisinopril
text:
Tell your doctor if you're pregnant or become pregnant.

Lisinopril is not usually used during pregnancy because it can:

- affect how your baby’s kidneys, skull, lungs and joints develop
- reduce the level of amniotic fluid that protects them in the womb
- increase the risk of stillbirth

A doctor will recommend an alternative medicine that’s safer to take during pregnancy.

Find out more about taking lisinopril and other ACE inhibitors during pregnancy on the Bumps (Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy) website

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > Taking lisinopril with other medicines, food and drink
text:
There are some medicines, remedies and supplements that may not mix well with lisinopril.

This includes:

- other medicines for high blood pressure and heart problems
- medicines for asthma
- antiviral medicines, such as aciclovir
- antidepressants, such as amitriptyline
- antibiotics, such as cefalexin
- diuretics, such as bendroflumethiazide
- anticoagulants, such as heparin
- the medicine lithium, used to treat some mental health problems
- painkillers, such as ibuprofen

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > Taking lisinopril with other medicines, food and drink
text: This is not the full list of medicines that may not mix well with lisinopril. Before taking lisinopril, tell your doctor if you’re taking any other medicines, remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > Taking lisinopril with other medicines, food and drink > Food, drink and alcohol with lisinopril
text: You can eat as normal while taking lisinopril, but it may be best to avoid drinking alcohol because it can increase the risk of low blood pressure (hypotension).

title: Lisinopril
section_path: Lisinopril > Find out more about your medicine
text:
To find out more about your medicine, you can:

- check the leaflet that comes with it
- search for your medicine leaflet on the electronic medicines compendium website
- speak to a pharmacist or doctor for advice

title: Listeriosis
section_path: Listeriosis
text: Listeriosis is a rare infection caused by bacteria called listeria. It usually goes away on its own, but it can make some people seriously ill.

title: Listeriosis
section_path: Listeriosis > How you get listeriosis
text:
Listeriosis is usually caused by eating food contaminated with listeria bacteria.

Listeria can contaminate a wide range of foods, but most infections are caused by eating chilled, ready-to-eat foods, such as:

- cold, cooked sliced meats and cured meats
- smoked and cured fish – including in sushi
- cooked shellfish
- soft mould-ripened cheeses (such as camembert and brie) and blue-veined cheeses
- pâté
- pre-prepared sandwiches and salads
- pre-cut fruit (such as pre-packed melon slices)
- unpasteurised milk
- dairy products made from unpasteurised milk

title: Listeriosis
section_path: Listeriosis > How you get listeriosis
text:
These foods do not always contain listeria. If you have eaten them recently, you do not need to do anything unless you get symptoms of the infection.

Although it's less common, you can also catch listeriosis from:

- someone else who has it – for example, if you eat food they've handled when they've not washed their hands
- close contact with farm animals – especially sheep and cows that are giving birth

title: Listeriosis
section_path: Listeriosis > Symptoms of listeriosis
text:
In most people, listeriosis has no symptoms or only causes mild symptoms for a few days, such as:

- a high temperature
- aches and pains
- chills
- feeling or being sick
- diarrhoea

If you're pregnant, you may also have a stomach ache or notice your baby moving less than usual.

Babies with listeriosis may also be irritable and feed less than usual.

title: Listeriosis
section_path: Listeriosis > Risks of listeriosis
text:
Listeriosis is not usually serious for most people.

But some people have a higher risk of serious problems, including:

- anyone who is pregnant
- newborn babies
- people with a condition that weakens their immune system, such as cancer, diabetes, liver disease or kidney disease
- people having treatment that weakens their immune system, such as chemotherapy or steroid tablets

Older people are also at higher risk of getting seriously ill from listeriosis, and this risk increases with age.

If you get listeriosis while you're pregnant, there is a risk it could cause miscarriage or stillbirth.

title: Listeriosis
section_path: Listeriosis > Risks of listeriosis
text: In babies and people with a weakened immune system, listeriosis can sometimes lead to serious and life-threatening problems such as sepsis or meningitis.

title: Listeriosis
section_path: Listeriosis > Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if:
text:
- you're pregnant and think you have listeriosis
- you have a condition that weakens your immune system (like cancer or kidney disease) and think you have listeriosis
- you're having treatment that weakens your immune system (like chemotherapy or steroid tablets) and think you have listeriosis
- you think your baby might have listeriosis

You can call NHS 111 or get help from 111 online.

If you're pregnant, you can also call your midwife for advice.

title: Listeriosis
section_path: Listeriosis > Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if you or your child:
text:
- have a severe headache and stiff neck
- find it uncomfortable to look at bright lights
- have a fit (seizure)
- feel suddenly confused
- feel very sleepy or are difficult to wake
- have a rash that does not fade when a glass is rolled over it – the rash may be blotchy, like bruises or small red pinpricks

These could be symptoms of meningitis caused by listeriosis, which needs to be treated in hospital straight away.

Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring any medicines you take with you.

title: Listeriosis
section_path: Listeriosis > Treatment for listeriosis
text:
For most people, listeriosis is mild and gets better in a few days.

You can usually look after yourself at home by resting and drinking plenty of fluids.

If you're at a higher risk of getting seriously ill (for example, you're pregnant or have a weakened immune system), you may need antibiotics.

Find out how to treat diarrhoea and vomiting

title: Listeriosis
section_path: Listeriosis > How to avoid listeriosis
text: There are some simple things you can do to reduce your risk of getting listeriosis.

title: Listeriosis
section_path: Listeriosis > How to avoid listeriosis > Do
text:
- keep chilled, ready-to-eat foods cold – try to make sure your fridge is working properly and is set to 5C or below
- eat ready-to-eat foods within 4 hours of taking them out of the fridge
- eat, cook or freeze foods by their use-by date
- follow storage instructions on food labels and use opened food within 2 days (unless the packaging says otherwise)
- keep raw and ready-to-eat foods separate
- follow any cooking instructions on packaging, and cook or reheat (including frozen vegetables) until they're steaming hot right through
- wash your hands regularly with soap and water

title: Listeriosis
section_path: Listeriosis > How to avoid listeriosis > Foods to avoid if you're at risk
text:
If you're pregnant or have a weakened immune system, you should avoid eating ready-to-eat cold-smoked or cured fish products, such as smoked salmon or gravlax (unless cooked until steaming hot).

If you're pregnant, you should also avoid eating other foods that have the highest risk of causing listeriosis.

These include:

- some soft cheeses (including brie and camembert) – unless cooked until steaming hot
- all types of pâté – including vegetable pâté
- unpasteurised milk or dairy products
- any undercooked food

If you're pregnant, you should also avoid close contact with farm animals that are giving birth or have recently given birth.

title: Listeriosis
section_path: Listeriosis > How to avoid listeriosis > Foods to avoid if you're at risk
text: Find out which foods to avoid during pregnancy

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium
text:
Brand names: Priadel, Camcolit, Liskonum, Li-Liquid

Find out how lithium treats mood disorders such as mania and bipolar disorder, and how to take it.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > About lithium
text:
Brand names: Priadel, Camcolit, Liskonum, Li-Liquid

Lithium is a type of medicine known as a mood stabiliser. It's used to treat mood disorders such as:

- mania (feeling highly excited, overactive or distracted)
- hypo-mania (similar to mania, but less severe)
- regular periods of depression, where treatment with other medicines has not worked
- bipolar disorder, where your mood changes between feeling very high (mania) and very low (depression)

Lithium can also help reduce aggressive or self-harming behaviour.

Lithium is available on prescription.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > About lithium
text: It comes as regular tablets or slow-release tablets (lithium carbonate). Brand names for the tablets include Priadel, Camcolit and Liskonum. It also comes as a liquid that you swallow (lithium citrate). Common brands of lithium liquid are Priadel and Li-liquid.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > About lithium > Key facts
text: - Lithium may take several weeks or months to work. - Common side effects of lithium are feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, a dry mouth and a metallic taste in the mouth. - You'll have regular blood tests to check how much lithium is in your blood. These results will be recorded in your lithium record book. - You'll be given a lithium alert card to keep with you at all times. In an emergency, this will let health professionals know you're taking lithium. - Try to avoid a low-sodium (low-salt) diet as this can increase the levels of lithium in your blood and increase the chance of getting side effects.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > Who can and cannot take lithium
text: Brand names: Priadel, Camcolit, Liskonum, Li-Liquid

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > Who can and cannot take lithium > Who can take lithium
text: Most adults and children aged 12 years old and over can take lithium.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > Who can and cannot take lithium > Who may not be able to take lithium
text:
Lithium may not be suitable for some people. To make sure it's safe for you, tell your doctor before starting to take it if you:

- have ever had an allergic reaction to lithium or other medicine
- have heart disease
- have severe kidney problems
- have an underactive thyroid gland (hypothyroidism) that is not being treated
- have low levels of sodium in your body – this can happen if you're dehydrated or if you're on a low-sodium (low-salt) diet
- have Addison's disease, a rare disorder of the adrenal glands
- have a rare heart condition called Brugada syndrome, or someone in your family has this condition
- need to have surgery
- are trying to get pregnant, or are already pregnant or breastfeeding

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > Who can and cannot take lithium > Who may not be able to take lithium
text:
Before prescribing lithium, your doctor will do some blood tests to check your kidneys and thyroid are OK. They'll also check your weight and continue to check it throughout your treatment.

If you have a heart condition, the doctor may also do a test that measures the electrical activity of your heart (electrocardiogram).

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium
text:
Brand names: Priadel, Camcolit, Liskonum, Li-Liquid

Always take lithium as your doctor tells you to.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > Dosage
text:
There are 2 different types of lithium – lithium carbonate and lithium citrate. It's important not to change to a different type unless your doctor has recommended it. This is because different types are absorbed differently in the body.

Lithium carbonate comes as standard tablets and slow-release tablets (the medicine is released into your body more slowly).

Standard tablets come as 250mg strength tablets. Slow-release tablets come as 200mg, 400mg and 450mg strength tablets.

Lithium citrate comes as a liquid. This is usually only prescribed for people who have trouble swallowing tablets.

Starting doses vary depending on your age, why you're taking it and the type of lithium your doctor recommends.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > Dosage
text: If you have kidney problems your doctor will monitor the level of lithium in your blood even more closely and change your dose if necessary.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > Changes to your dose
text:
When you start your treatment, you'll need to have a blood test every week to make sure the level of lithium in your blood is not too high or too low. Your doctor may change your dose depending on the results of your blood test.

Once the doctor is happy, you'll have a blood test every 3 to 6 months to check your levels are stable.

Once you find a dose that suits you, it usually stays the same, unless your condition changes, or your doctor prescribes another medicine that may affect the way lithium works.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > How to take it
text:
Swallow tablets whole with a drink of water or juice. Do not chew them.

You can take lithium with or without food.

If you're taking liquid, use the plastic syringe or spoon that comes with your medicine to measure the correct dose. If you do not have one, ask your pharmacist. Do not use a kitchen teaspoon as it will not measure the right amount.

You'll usually take your lithium once a day, at night. This is because when you have your regular blood test, you need to have it 12 hours after taking your medicine. You can choose when you take your lithium – just try to keep to the same time every day.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > How long to take it for
text: As long as it's working well to control your condition, you'll generally take lithium for a long time. Some people need to take it for many years.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > How long to take it for > Important
text: Do not stop taking lithium suddenly or change your dose without speaking to your doctor first. It's important to keep taking it, even if you feel better. If you suddenly stop, it you could become unwell again very quickly.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > Stopping lithium
text:
If you or your doctor decide to stop your lithium, it must be reduced gradually over a number of weeks or months.

Do not stop taking lithium suddenly even if you feel better, or because you think the dose is too little or too much. The symptoms of your condition are likely to come back.

However, you must stop taking it if you have symptoms such as loss of appetite, problems with your eyesight or feeling very thirsty. These could be signs of lithium toxicity or an allergic reaction. If this happens it's important to stop taking lithium straight away and get medical help.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > If you have an infection or illness
text: If you feel unwell or become unwell while you're taking lithium, it can affect your medicine.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > If you have an infection or illness > Urgent advice: Call 111 now if you:
text:
- have an illness that causes severe diarrhoea, vomiting, a high temperature or sweating
- have a urinary tract infection (UTI)
- are not eating and drinking much

Get help from 111 online or call 111

Infections and illnesses like colds and flu can also make you dehydrated. This can affect the levels of lithium in your blood.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > Information about your lithium treatment
text:
When you start taking lithium, you'll get a lithium treatment pack (usually a purple folder or book) with a record booklet. You need to show your record booklet every time you see your doctor, go to hospital, or collect your prescription.

When you go to the doctor for blood tests, you or your doctor will write in the record booklet:

- your dose of lithium
- your lithium blood levels
- any other blood test results
- your weight

The treatment pack also has a lithium alert card. You'll need to carry this card with you all the time. It tells healthcare professionals that you're taking lithium. This can be useful for them to know in an emergency.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > Information about your lithium treatment
text: Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you've lost your treatment pack or did not get one.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > If you forget to take it
text:
If you usually take tablets or slow-release tablets and it's less than 6 hours since you were supposed to take your medicine, take it as soon as you remember. If it's more than 6 hours, just skip the missed dose and take your next one at the usual time.

If you forget to take a dose of lithium liquid, just skip the missed dose and take your next one at the usual time.

Never take 2 doses at the same time. Never take an extra dose to make up for a forgotten one.

If you forget doses often, it may help to set an alarm to remind you. You could also ask your pharmacist for advice on other ways to help you remember to take your medicine.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > If you take too much
text:
Taking too much lithium can be dangerous. This is because very high amounts of lithium can cause problems with your kidneys and other organs. It can cause symptoms such as:

- feeling or being sick
- problems with your eyesight (blurred vision)
- increased need to pee, lack of control over pee or poo
- feeling faint, lightheaded or sleepy
- confusion and blackouts
- shaking or muscle weakness, muscle twitches, jerks or spasms affecting the face, tongue, eyes or neck

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > How and when to take lithium > If you take too much > Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if:
text:
you take more than your prescribed dose of lithium, even if you do not feel any different

If you need to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring the lithium packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take.

title: Lithium
section_path: Lithium > Side effects of lithium
text:
Brand names: Priadel, Camcolit, Liskonum, Li-Liquid

If you're on the right dose and the level of lithium in your blood is right, you may not have any side effects.
