title: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage)
section_path: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage)
text: A meniscus tear is a common type of damage to cartilage in the knee. The cartilage is found between the bones in the knee joint and protects them when you move. It usually gets damaged because of an injury.

title: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage)
section_path: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage) > Symptoms of a meniscus tear
text:
A meniscus tear usually happens when you twist your knee while playing sport. But it can also happen from more minor injuries such as twisting when standing up.

Symptoms of a meniscus tear include:

- knee pain or tenderness
- stiffness or swelling around your knee – the swelling may not start for a few hours or days
- difficulty bending, straightening or moving your knee
- your knee giving way when you try to stand
- a crunching or clicking feeling when you move your knee

The symptoms can be similar to sprains.

title: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage)
section_path: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage) > How to ease symptoms of a meniscus tear
text: There are some things you can do to ease symptoms of a meniscus tear.

title: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage)
section_path: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage) > How to ease symptoms of a meniscus tear > Do
text:
- stop any exercise or activities and rest your knee when you can during the first few days
- put an ice pack (or bag of frozen peas) wrapped in a towel on your knee for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours
- wrap a bandage around your knee or wear a knee support – remove it when you sleep
- keep your leg raised on a pillow as much as possible
- take paracetamol or ibuprofen gel or tablets to ease pain

title: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage)
section_path: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage) > How to ease symptoms of a meniscus tear > Don’t
text:
- do not use heat packs and avoid hot baths
- do not drink alcohol
- do not massage your knee
- do not carry anything heavy
- do not completely stop moving your knee – after a few days of resting, try to do some gentle movements

title: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage)
section_path: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage) > How to ease symptoms of a meniscus tear > A pharmacist can help with a meniscus tear
text: You can ask a pharmacist about painkillers and the types of knee supports you can get.

title: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage)
section_path: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage) > When and where to get medical help
text: Most symptoms of a meniscus tear are not serious, but sometimes you may need medical help.

title: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage)
section_path: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage) > When and where to get medical help > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
text:
- knee pain is stopping you doing normal activities or affecting your sleep
- the pain is getting worse or keeps coming back
- your symptoms have not improved after treating it at home
- your knee is stiff for more than 30 minutes after waking up

title: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage)
section_path: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage) > When and where to get medical help > Refer yourself for back or joint help
text:
In many areas you may be able to get help, such as physiotherapy, from NHS community musculoskeletal (MSK) services without needing a referral from a GP.

Get NHS help for back or joint problems

title: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage)
section_path: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage) > When and where to get medical help > Urgent advice: Get an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111 if:
text:
- you have very bad knee pain after a fall or injury
- you're unable to walk or put weight on your knee
- the skin around your knee is swollen and feels hot
- you have knee pain and a high temperature, or you feel hot, cold or shivery
- you cannot bend or straighten your leg

You can call 111 or get help from 111 online.

title: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage)
section_path: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage) > When and where to get medical help > Immediate action required: Go to A&E if:
text:
- your knee has moved out of place, changed shape or is pointing at an odd angle
- you have any tingling or you have no feeling in your knee, leg or toes

Do not drive to A&E. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring any medicines you take with you.

title: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage)
section_path: Meniscus tear (knee cartilage damage) > Treatments for a meniscus tear
text:
A meniscus tear can get better on its own without treatment, but it can take a while to heal.

Sometimes, physiotherapy may be recommended to help reduce pain and improve movement and strength in the knee.

If the damage is severe, you may need arthroscopy surgery to repair or remove the damaged cartilage.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause
text: Menopause and perimenopause are a natural part of life. This happens when your periods change and eventually stop due to lower hormone levels. It usually affects women between 45 and 55 but it can happen earlier. It affects anyone who has periods.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > What are menopause and perimenopause?
text:
- Perimenopause happens when your periods become irregular and menopause is when your periods stop altogether. - Menopause is caused by a fall in hormone levels and usually affects women between the ages of 45 and 55, but it can happen earlier. - Menopause and perimenopause can affect anyone who has periods. - Menopause itself is defined as not having a period for 12 months and you're not using hormonal contraception. - Common symptoms include hot flushes, low mood, sleep problems and memory problems. - There's no routine test for perimenopause and menopause. A doctor may diagnose it based on your age and symptoms
- Early menopause or premature ovarian insufficiency can happen before the age of 45. It can be caused by surgery to remove the ovaries (oophorectomy). Sometimes the reason is unknown.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Menopause and perimenopause symptoms
text:
Perimenopause and menopause are different for everyone.

You may get symptoms that have a big impact on your daily life, including relationships, social life, family life and work, or you may hardly have any symptoms at all.

Symptoms can happen during perimenopause and menopause. They can also happen after your menopause has ended (post menopause).

Sometimes, ethnic background can affect symptoms of perimenopause and menopause, how severe they are and how long they last. For example, women from a Black ethnic background are more likely to have hot flushes that are severe and continue longer.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Changes to your periods
text: One of the first signs of perimenopause is usually a change to your periods. They may happen more often or less often, and bleeding may get heavier or lighter. Eventually, you stop having periods altogether.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Hot flushes and night sweats
text: Hot flushes are when your face, neck and chest suddenly feel very hot or cold. It can make you sweat a lot, cause palpitations or anxiety, or make you feel dizzy. It can happen during the day or night (night sweats) and last for several minutes.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Sleep problems
text: Not being able to get to sleep or stay asleep can affect your daily life. It can make you feel irritable, stressed and anxious. Sleep problems may be worse if you also have night sweats.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Mood changes, poor memory and brain fog
text: You may have mood swings, low mood or depression. You may also notice problems with your memory or concentration. These symptoms may feel worse if you have sleep problems and feel very tired.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Weight gain
text: Weight gain during perimenopause and menopause is common. It often happens around the stomach and upper body.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Vaginal problems
text: You may get symptoms such as dryness, a burning feeling, irritation or itching in and around the vagina. These symptoms can also make sex feel painful.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Menopause and perimenopause symptoms > UTIs (urinary tract infections)
text: You may get more UTIs (urinary tract infections) or symptoms that feel like a UTI. This includes feeling pain or a burning sensation when you pee and needing to pee more often than usual, including at night.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Other symptoms of menopause and perimenopause
text:
Menopause and perimenopause may affect you in other ways, including:

- a faster, slower or more noticeable heartbeat (palpitations)
- weakening bones (loss of bone density), which can lead to osteoporosis
- feeling the need to pee more or not being able to control when you pee (urinary incontinence)
- headaches and migraines that are worse than usual
- muscle aches and joint pains
- hair thinning or hair loss
- skin changes, including dry and itchy skin
- reduced sex drive (loss of libido)
- sensitive teeth, painful gums or other mouth problems

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Non-urgent advice: Contact your GP if:
text:
- you think you have symptoms of menopause or perimenopause and want to know what your options are
- you have symptoms like a fast heartbeat (palpitations)
- you still have periods but your bleeding pattern has changed and you're bleeding more, not less, than before
- you have not had a period for 12 months or more, and you have any vaginal bleeding

Early advice can help reduce the effects of menopause and perimenopause on your health, relationships and work.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Non-urgent advice: Contact your GP if: > Find out more:
text:
- Menopause in ethnic minority women on the British Menopause Society website (PDF only, 129KB)
- Menopause symptoms and symptoms tracker on the Rock My Menopause website

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > How long menopause and perimenopause symptoms last
text:
Perimenopause ends when you reach menopause. Menopause is when you have not had a period for 12 months. After this it's called postmenopause.

Symptoms usually last for 7 to 9 years, sometimes longer, and during this time they can change.

For example, you may get hot flushes and night sweats for a while, but they may improve and be replaced by other symptoms such as low mood and anxiety.

You may also get symptoms that continue after menopause, such as joint pain and vaginal dryness.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Menopause and perimenopause symptoms if you're using hormonal contraception
text:
Using hormonal contraception can make it harder to tell if you've reached perimenopause or menopause. This is because hormonal contraception can affect your periods.

Some types of hormonal contraception can make periods irregular or stop completely. These include the:

- progestogen-only pill
- IUS (hormonal coil)
- contraceptive implant
- contraceptive injection

The combined pill causes monthly bleeds like a period for as long as you take it.

Talk to a GP about the best contraception for you. Depending on your age and whether you're in perimenopause or menopause, they may want to change it.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Menopause and perimenopause symptoms if you're using hormonal contraception
text:
The combined pill is not recommended if you're aged 50 or over as the risks of taking it generally outweigh the benefits. A GP may recommend a progestogen-only contraception instead.

It's possible to get pregnant during perimenopause. You still need contraception:

- for 1 year after your final period, if you're 50 or over
- for 2 years after your final period, if you're aged 40 to 49 years old

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Bleeding before and after menopause > Bleeding before menopause
text:
During perimenopause, your periods may become irregular, lighter or heavier.

Taking hormone replacement therapy (HRT) during perimenopause can make your periods more regular. You may have some irregular bleeding or spotting but this should settle within 6 months.

Talk to your GP if you're taking HRT and still having irregular or heavier bleeding or spotting after 6 months.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Bleeding before and after menopause > Bleeding after menopause
text: If you have not had a period for more than 12 months and you get any vaginal bleeding (postmenopausal bleeding), this needs to be checked.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Symptoms of menopause and perimenopause > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
text:
You have postmenopausal bleeding, even if:

- it's only happened once
- there's only a small amount of blood, spotting, or pink or brown discharge
- you do not have any other symptoms
- you're not sure if it's blood

Postmenopausal bleeding is not usually serious but can be a sign of cancer. Cancer may be easier to treat if it's found early.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Treatment for menopause and perimenopause > Hormonal replacement therapy (HRT)
text:
If you have symptoms of perimenopause or menopause, talk to a doctor, nurse or pharmacist about HRT and other options available.

The type of HRT you're offered will depend on whether you still have periods or not, or if you have had your womb removed (hysterectomy).

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Treatment for menopause and perimenopause > Hormonal replacement therapy (HRT) > Oestrogen
text:
Oestrogen is the main type of HRT and can help manage your symptoms. It can be taken as tablets or used as patches, spray or gel.

It's sometimes used as a cream or pessary to treat vaginal dryness and soreness, or urinary symptoms, after the menopause.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Treatment for menopause and perimenopause > Hormonal replacement therapy (HRT) > Progestogen
text:
If you're taking oestrogen and have not had a hysterectomy, it's important to take progestogen to protect your womb.

Progestogen can be taken as tablets, as part of a combined patch or as the hormonal coil (intrauterine system, or IUS).

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Treatment for menopause and perimenopause > Hormonal replacement therapy (HRT) > Testosterone
text:
Testosterone gel or cream can help to improve low libido (sex drive) for some.

There are many reasons why you may have low libido around the menopause, including relationship difficulties, how you feel about yourself, and physical discomfort. You may be able to get testosterone on prescription from a menopause specialist.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Treatment for menopause and perimenopause > Hormonal replacement therapy (HRT) > Testosterone > More information
text: Find out more about hormone replacement therapy (HRT).

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Treatment for menopause and perimenopause > Non-hormonal treatments
text:
If HRT does not work for your symptoms, you cannot take it for some reason or you do not want to take it, other types of treatment are available.

If you have low mood, depression or anxiety caused by perimenopause or menopause, you may be offered antidepressants.

If you have hot flushes and night sweats, there are other medicines or treatments that can help. You may be offered cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), or if that does not help a doctor may suggest clonidine, or an antidepressant.

Talk to a GP about how to improve your symptoms and what medicines may be suitable for you.

Find out more about other medicines for menopause symptoms

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Treatment for menopause and perimenopause > Non-hormonal treatments > Herbal remedies and complementary medicines
text:
Herbal remedies and complementary medicines such as red clover and black cohosh are sometimes sold for symptoms of menopause or perimenopause. But there is very little evidence to show how well they work, or how safe they are.

Some herbal remedies and complementary medicines may also cause serious side effects when taken with other medicines.

Find out more about herbal remedies and complementary medicines for menopause symptoms

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Things you can do to help menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Lifestyle changes for perimenopause and menopause
text:
Eating well, exercising and looking after your mental wellbeing can help with symptoms during perimenopause and menopause.

It can also help you keep as well as possible in the future.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Things you can do to help menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Lifestyle changes for perimenopause and menopause > Do
text:
- try to get plenty of rest, including keeping to regular sleep routines
- try to eat a healthy, balanced diet
- eat calcium-rich food like milk, yoghurt and kale, if you can, to keep your bones healthy
- exercise regularly, with focus on weight-bearing exercises to build strength as this can help protect against weakening bones
- try relaxing things such as yoga, tai chi or meditation
- talk to other people going through the same thing, like family, friends or colleagues
- talk to a doctor before taking herbal supplements or complementary medicines
- talk to a doctor about hormonal contraception if you need to – HRT is not contraception

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Things you can do to help menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Lifestyle changes for perimenopause and menopause > Don’t
text:
- do not smoke as this can make menopause symptoms worse
- try not to drink more than the recommended alcohol limit – it may affect your symptoms

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Things you can do to help menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Other ways to help perimenopause and menopause symptoms > How to ease mood changes
text:
It's common to have mood swings, low mood and anxiety around the time of the menopause and perimenopause.

Try to:

- get as much rest as you can
- exercise regularly
- do relaxing activities

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is a type of talking therapy that can help with a low mood and feelings of anxiety. It can also help with sleep problems.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Things you can do to help menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Other ways to help perimenopause and menopause symptoms > How to ease hot flushes and night sweats
text:
You can try:

- wearing lightweight clothing
- keeping your bedroom cool at night
- taking a cool shower, using a fan or having a cold drink
- finding ways to reduce your stress level
- to avoid or reduce potential triggers, such as spicy food, caffeine, hot drinks**,** smoking and alcohol
- to exercise regularly
- to keep to a healthy weight

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) can also help manage hot flushes.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Things you can do to help menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Other ways to help perimenopause and menopause symptoms > How to ease vaginal dryness
text:
There are vaginal moisturisers or lubricants you can get without a prescription at a pharmacy.

You can talk to a pharmacist, in private, if you'd like help to decide which moisturiser is right for you.

If you're having sex and using condoms, do not use an oil-based lubricant as this can damage condoms. Water-based lubricants are available**.**

There are other treatments for vaginal dryness that a doctor can prescribe, such as HRT (hormone replacement therapy) or hormonal treatment (creams, pessaries, gel or vaginal rings).

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Things you can do to help menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Other ways to help perimenopause and menopause symptoms > How to ease vaginal dryness
text: Find out about treatment for vaginal dryness.

title: Menopause and perimenopause
section_path: Menopause and perimenopause > Things you can do to help menopause and perimenopause symptoms > Other ways to help perimenopause and menopause symptoms > Protecting against weak bones
text:
You can try to:

- exercise regularly, particularly focusing on strength exercises, where your feet and legs support your weight (like walking, running or dancing) and resistance exercises (for example, using weights)
- eat a healthy diet that includes plenty of fruit, vegetables and sources of calcium, such as milk, yoghurt and kale
- get some sunlight on your skin as this triggers the production of vitamin D, which can help keep your bones healthy
- take vitamin D supplements
- stop smoking and cut down on alcohol

Taking HRT can also reduce the risk of osteoporosis.

Find out more about preventing osteoporosis

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine
text:
Brand names: Asacol, Mezavant, Octasa, Pentasa, Salofalk, Zintasa

Find out how mesalazine treats inflammatory bowel conditions and how to take it.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > About mesalazine
text:
Brand names: Asacol, Mezavant, Octasa, Pentasa, Salofalk, Zintasa

Mesalazine is used to treat ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease and other types of inflammatory bowel disease.

Mesalazine works by helping to reduce swelling (inflammation). It can also help with healing.

Some people take mesalazine together with steroids to improve their symptoms.

Mesalazine is only available on prescription. It comes as:

- tablets
- granules
- rectal foam
- suppositories
- enemas

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > About mesalazine > Key facts
text:
- Different types and brands of mesalazine tablets and granules work on different parts of your gut. Rectal foam, suppositories or enemas are prescribed for the lower part of your gut. If you find one that works for you, it’s usually best to stick to the same one
- You’ll usually need blood tests, liver tests and kidney tests before you start treatment with mesalazine, and then regular monitoring tests. - Mesalazine starts working straight away, but it may take up to a few months to work fully. - Common side effects of mesalazine include stomach pain, indigestion, farting (flatulence), and feeling or being sick,
- Drink plenty of fluids, such as water, while you’re taking or using mesalazine to help prevent kidney problems.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Who can and cannot take mesalazine
text: Brand names: Asacol, Mezavant, Octasa, Pentasa, Salofalk, Zintasa

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Who can and cannot take mesalazine > Who can take mesalazine
text: Most adults and children aged 5 years old and older over can take mesalazine.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Who can and cannot take mesalazine > Who may not be able to take or use mesalazine
text:
Although most adults and children aged 5 years old and older over can take mesalazine, it may not be suitable for some people. To make sure it's safe for you, tell a doctor before taking if you:

- have ever had an allergic reaction to mesalazine, aspirin, or any other medicines like it, such as methylsalicylate or choline salicylate
- have ever had an allergic reaction to any other medicine
- have ever had kidney problems while taking other medicines such as sulfasalazine
- have ever developed a severe skin rash, skin peeling, blistering or mouth sores after using mesalazine
- have problems with your kidneys or liver
- are trying to get pregnant, already pregnant, or breastfeeding

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine
text: Brand names: Asacol, Mezavant, Octasa, Pentasa, Salofalk, Zintasa

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > Dosage
text:
Always follow the instructions from a pharmacist, doctor or on the leaflet that comes with your medicine.

Your dose of mesalazine will depend on why you need it, and the brand you’re using. It also depends on whether you're taking it for a short or long time.

Once your symptoms start to get better, it's likely that your dose will be reduced. This lower dose is sometimes called a maintenance dose. If your symptoms return, your doctor may increase your dose again.

Your child's dose may be lower. Doctors usually prescribe child doses based on their weight.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > How to take mesalazine > Tablets and granules
text:
You’ll either take mesalazine tablets or granules once a day, or as 2 or 3 smaller doses throughout the day.

Swallow the tablets whole with a drink of water. Do not break, chew or crush them. This is because some tablets have a special coating to protect the medicine from the acids in your stomach.

For granules, open the sachet and tip the granules onto your tongue. Swallow them whole with a drink of water or squash. Do not chew them, as some granules have a special coating.

Drink plenty of fluids when taking this medicine to help prevent dehydration and possible kidney problems. You can take some brands with food. Check the leaflet that comes with your medicine.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > How to take mesalazine > Tablets and granules
text: If you're also taking indigestion medicines or remedies, leave a 2-hour gap before and after taking mesalazine. Indigestion treatments can affect how well the medicine works.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > How to take mesalazine > Suppositories
text:
Your doctor or pharmacist will tell you how many mesalazine suppositories to use each day. You can use some brands once a day before you go to bed, and use other brands several times a day with the last dose before you go to bed.

To use a suppository:

- Wash your hands before using the suppository. Also clean around your bottom (anus) with mild soap and water, rinse and pat dry. - Unwrap the suppository. - Gently push the suppository into your anus with the pointed end first. - Sit or lie down. It should be left in place for as long as possible, so inserting it before going to sleep helps. The suppository will start to soften, as it melts with your body heat. This is normal. - Wash your hands again.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > How to take mesalazine > Suppositories
text:
If the suppository comes out within 10 minutes of putting it in, you can insert another one.

Try not to do a poo for at least an hour after using a suppository. This gives the medicine time to work.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > How to take mesalazine > Enemas
text:
There are 2 types of mesalazine enema with slightly different ways to use them. Read the instructions that come with your medicine before you start.

You’ll usually use mesalazine enemas once a day before you go to bed.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > How to take mesalazine > Enemas
text: Before you use an enema:

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > How to take mesalazine > Enemas
text:
- Try to do a poo. The medicine works best when your bowels are empty. - Wash your hands. - Lie on your side, with your bottom slightly higher than the rest of your body. You can use a pillow to lift your bottom up. You may want to lie on a towel. - Put one of the disposable plastic bags provided over your hand (like a glove) and pick up the bottle. - Shake the bottle well. - Break the seal on the nozzle, or remove the protective cap. - Gently push the nozzle into your bottom (anus) as far as is comfortable. - Squeeze the bottle steadily to allow the liquid to empty into your anus quite quickly. This should take no more than 30 to 40 seconds. It's normal for some liquid to be left in the bottle afterwards. - Remove the nozzle from your bottom. - Peel the disposable plastic bag off your hand and use it to cover the bottle, ready to throw away. - Lie on your side This will stop any liquid coming out of your bottom. - Wash your hands. - For sleeping, find a comfortable position that keeps the liquid in your bottom for as long as possible. The longer it stays there, the better it will
- work.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > How to take mesalazine > Rectal foam
text:
You’ll usually use mesalazine rectal foam once a day before you go to bed. The dose is 2 full applicators.

Read the instruction leaflet first. The pictures show you exactly how to use the foam.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > How to take mesalazine > Rectal foam
text: To use rectal foam:

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > How to take mesalazine > Rectal foam
text: - If you need to do a poo, do it before using the rectal foam. This is because the medicine works best when your bowels are empty. - Wash your hands. - Remove the plastic flap (or safety lock) from underneath the dome-shaped pump at the top of the can, if you’re using it for the first time. - Push a new applicator onto the nozzle. This nozzle sticks out beneath the dome at the top of the can. - Shake the can for about 20 seconds. - There is a rounded gap at the base of the dome. Twist the dome until the gap lines up with the nozzle. - Put your finger on top of the dome and turn the can upside down. The spray will only work properly if you hold the can with the dome pointing straight down. - Either stand with one leg raised and resting on a chair, or lie down on your side with your lower leg stretched out and upper leg bent. - Gently put the tip of the applicator into your bottom (anus) as far as possible. You may want to use a lubricating jelly on the tip of the applicator. - Push the dome down. This fills the applicator with a dose of foam. - Release the dome very slowly, to push the foam out. - Wait 10 to 15 seconds and then slowly remove the applicator from your bottom. Do this slowly to prevent the foam coming out.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > How to take mesalazine > Rectal foam
text:
Remove the applicator from the nozzle. Put it in the plastic bag provided and throw the bag away (with your normal household rubbish).

After using the foam, try not to poo until the next morning. For the medicine to work properly it needs to stay inside your bowel as long as possible.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > How long to take it for
text:
If you’re having a flare up, your doctor may prescribe you a higher dose of mesalazine for a short time. This should help control your symptoms.

You can also take it long term to keep inflammation under control and prevent symptoms from flaring up again. How long you use it for will depend on your condition and how severe it is.

Do not stop using mesalazine unless your doctor tells you to.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > If you forget to take it
text:
If you miss a dose of mesalazine, take or use it as soon as you remember, unless it's almost time for your next dose. In this case, skip the missed one and take the next dose at the usual time.

Do not take or use 2 doses together to make up for a forgotten dose.

If you often forget doses, it may help to set an alarm to remind you. You could also ask your pharmacist for advice on other ways to help you remember to take your medicine.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > If you take too much
text: Taking up to 1 extra dose of mesalazine is unlikely to cause problems.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > How and when to take mesalazine > If you take too much > Urgent advice: Contact 111 for advice now if:
text:
- you've taken or used up to 1 extra dose of mesalazine and you feel unwell
- you've taken or used more than 1 extra dose of mesalazine, even if you feel well

Go to 111 online.nhs.uk or call 111

If you need to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring all the mesalazine packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine
text:
Brand names: Asacol, Mezavant, Octasa, Pentasa, Salofalk, Zintasa

Like all medicines, mesalazine can cause side effects in some people, but many people have no side effects or only minor ones.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Common side effects of mesalazine
text:
Side effects of mesalazine can vary depending on the type (such as tablets or granules), and the size of your dose. Check the leaflet that comes with your medicine before taking or using.

These common side effects happen in more than 1 in 100 people. There are things you can do to help cope with them:

Indigestion or wind

Try not to eat foods that cause wind (like lentils, peas, beans and onions). Eat smaller meals, and eat and drink slowly.

Stomach pain

Putting a heat pad or covered hot water bottle on your stomach may help the pain. Contact a doctor if the pain is severe or does not go away.

Feeling or being sick (nausea or vomiting)

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Common side effects of mesalazine
text:
Stick to simple meals and do not eat rich or spicy food. Check the instructions that come with your medicine to see if you can take it after you've eaten. If you're being sick, try having small, frequent sips of water or squash to avoid dehydration. Do not take any other medicines to treat vomiting without speaking to a pharmacist or doctor.

If you take the combined contraceptive pill or the progestogen-only pill and you’re being sick, your contraception may not protect you from pregnancy. Check the pill packet for advice.

Diarrhoea

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Common side effects of mesalazine
text:
Drink plenty of fluids, such as water or squash, to avoid dehydration. Speak to a pharmacist if you have signs of dehydration such as peeing less than usual or having dark strong-smelling pee. Do not take any other medicines to treat diarrhoea without speaking to a pharmacist or doctor. If you take the combined contraceptive pill or the progestogen-only pill and you have severe, watery diarrhoea or any diarrhoea that lasts for more than 24 hours, your contraception may not protect you from pregnancy. Check the pill packet for advice.

Headaches

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Common side effects of mesalazine
text:
Drink plenty of water and ask your pharmacist to recommend a suitable painkiller. Tell your doctor if the aches continue despite taking painkillers or if they last for more than a few days.

Speak to a doctor or pharmacist if this advice on how to cope does not help and a side effect is still bothering you or does not go away.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Serious side effects
text: Serious side effects are rare and happen in less than 1 in 1,000 people

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Serious side effects > Skin rashes
text:
Severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome are a rare side effect of mesalazine.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome causes flu-like symptoms, followed by a rash made up of circular patches that are darker in the middle and lighter around the outside (this may not be as obvious on black or brown skin). The affect skin eventually dies and peels off.

This is more likely to happen in the first month of taking mesalazine.

You’re more likely to get Stevens-Johnson syndrome if:

- You’ve had it before after taking mesalazine or certain other medicines
- You have a weakened immune system, for example, from having a condition like HIV or AIDS, or treatment like chemotherapy
- a close family member has had Stevens-Johnson syndrome

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Serious side effects > Skin rashes
text:
To help reduce the chance of you getting a rash that could be confused with Stevens-Johnson syndrome, it’s best not to try any new medicines or food during the first 3 months of your treatment.

It's also best to not start taking mesalazine within 2 weeks of a viral infection, vaccination, or rash caused by something else.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Serious side effects > Skin rashes > Immediate action required: Go to A&E now if:
text:
- you get a severe rash with flushing, blisters or ulcers, these can be signs of Stevens-Johnson syndrome or other severe skin reactions

Stop taking mesalazine straight away if this happens.

Find your nearest A&E

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Serious side effects > Other serious side effects
text: Tell your doctor or call 111 straight away if you get:

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Serious side effects > Other serious side effects
text:
- unexplained bleeding, an unexplained sore throat or high temperature, bruising, red or purple marks on your skin (these may be less obvious on black or brown skin), or if you feel generally unwell during the treatment – these can be signs of problems with your blood
- a high temperature, chills, a sore throat, ear or sinus pain, a cough, pain when peeing, mouth sores or a wound that will not heal – these can be signs of an infection
- a change in the colour of your pee or the amount you pee, or a sudden pain in the side of your tummy (abdomen)– these can be signs of kidney problems, including kidney stones
- yellowing of the whites of your eyes or your skin (this may be less obvious on black or brown skin), dark pee, stomach pain, high temperature, feeling tired or feeling sick – these can be signs of liver problems
- back or stomach pain, fever, feeling sick or being sick – these can be signs of an inflamed pancreas
- increasingly severe or frequent headaches, changes to your vision, ringing or buzzing in your ears (tinnitus), dizziness, back pain or neck pain – these can be signs of a build-up of pressure around the brain

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Serious side effects > Other serious side effects > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
text:
- you get chest pain, this can be a sign of heart problems

Do not drive yourself to A&E.

The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Serious allergic reaction
text: In rare cases, it's possible to have a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to meslazine.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Serious allergic reaction > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
text:
- your lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly become swollen
- you're breathing very fast or struggling to breathe (you may become very wheezy or feel like you're choking or gasping for air)
- your throat feels tight or you're struggling to swallow
- your skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale (if you have black or brown skin, this may be easier to see on the palms of your hands or soles of your feet)
- you suddenly become very confused, drowsy or dizzy
- someone faints and cannot be woken up
- a child is limp, floppy or not responding like they normally do (their head may fall to the side, backwards or forwards, or they may find it difficult to lift their head or focus on your face)

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Serious allergic reaction > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
text:
You or the person who's unwell may also have a rash that's swollen, raised, itchy, blistered or peeling.

These can be signs of a serious allergic reaction and may need immediate treatment in hospital.

Do not drive yourself to A&E.

The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Other side effects
text: These are not all the side effects of mesalazine. For a full list, see the leaflet inside your medicines packet.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Side effects of mesalazine > Reporting side effects
text:
You can report any suspected side effect using the Yellow Card safety scheme.

Visit the Yellow Card website for more information about reporting side effects.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking mesalazine
text: Brand names: Asacol, Mezavant, Octasa, Pentasa, Salofalk, Zintasa

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking mesalazine > Mesalazine and pregnancy
text:
If you’re already taking mesalazine, you can continue to take it during pregnancy. It’s important to make sure that your inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is well controlled. There's no evidence that taking mesalazine in pregnancy harms your baby.

If you become pregnant while taking mesalazine, speak to your doctor. Do not stop taking your medicine unless your doctor tells you to.

Your doctor can explain the risks and benefits of taking mesalazine and will help you choose the best treatment for you and your baby.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking mesalazine > Mesalazine and breastfeeding
text:
If your baby is healthy, then it's usually OK to take or use mesalazine while breastfeeding, but talk to your doctor first.

The small amounts of mesalazine that pass into breast milk should not cause any side effects in your baby. Many people have taken mesalazine while breastfeeding without any problems, although there have been some rare cases of diarrhoea in babies.

It's very rare for breastfed babies to have side effects from medicines you're taking. But it's important to keep monitoring your baby if you're taking any medicine while breastfeeding

Contact your healthcare professional or call 111 as soon as possible if you notice your baby is:

- not feeding as well as usual
- has diarrhoea
- is being sick (vomiting)
- has a rash
- is being irritable

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking mesalazine > Mesalazine and breastfeeding
text:
If your baby has any symptoms that are not listed, or if you're worried about them, you can also call 111 or contact any healthcare professional.

Carry on taking the medicine, and keep breastfeeding as usual until you've got advice about your baby's symptoms

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking mesalazine > Mesalazine and fertility
text:
There's no evidence to suggest that taking mesalazine will reduce fertility in either men or women.

Speak to your doctor if you're trying to get pregnant. They may want to review your treatment.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility while taking mesalazine > Non-urgent advice: Tell your doctor if you're:
text:
- trying to get pregnant
- pregnant
- breastfeeding

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Taking mesalazine with other medicines and herbal supplements
text: Brand names: Asacol, Mezavant, Octasa, Pentasa, Salofalk, Zintasa

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Taking mesalazine with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines
text:
Some medicines affect the way mesalazine works and increase the chances of you having side effects. Tell a pharmacist or doctor before starting to take mesalazine if you're taking any other medicines, including:

- laxatives, such as lactulose for constipation
- medicines that affect the way your kidneys work, such as azathioprine, mercaptopurine or thioquanine, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as aspirin or ibuprofen
- certain medicines that help to prevent blood clots, like warfarin

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Taking mesalazine with other medicines and herbal supplements > Cautions with other medicines
text: These are not all the medicines that may cause problems if you take them with mesalazine. For a full list, see the leaflet inside your medicine packet.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Taking mesalazine with other medicines and herbal supplements > Mixing mesalazine with herbal remedies and supplements
text: There's not enough information to say that complementary medicines, herbal remedies and supplements are safe to take with mesalazine. They’re not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines. They’re generally not tested for the effect they have on other medicines.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Taking mesalazine with other medicines and herbal supplements > Important: Medicine safety
text: Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you're taking any other medicines, including herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Common questions about mesalazine
text:
Brand names: Asacol, Mezavant, Octasa, Pentasa, Salofalk, Zintasa

How does mesalazine work?

Mesalazine works by reducing swelling (inflammation). This helps reduce the symptoms of inflammatory conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease

When will I feel better?

Mesalazine starts to work straight away but it may take around a week for symptoms to improve. Depending on how bad your symptoms are, it may take longer to start improving.

It may take a few months for your symptoms to go away.

Are there any long term side effects?

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Common questions about mesalazine
text:
Mesalazine can be taken long term. However, your doctor will want to check how your kidneys are working during treatment. In rare cases, mesalazine can cause kidney problems.

You’ll usually need blood tests, liver tests and kidney tests before you start treatment with mesalazine, and then regular monitoring tests.

These checks usually happen once every 3 months for the first year. They’ll usually be once a year after that or as often as your doctor recommends.

Can I take painkillers with mesalazine?

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Common questions about mesalazine
text:
You can take paracetamol with mesalazine. However, you should to avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as aspirin or ibuprofen.

Like mesalazine, NSAIDs can cause problems with the way your kidneys work. They can also irritate the gut and increase the risk of ulceration and bleeding.

Ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice if paracetamol is not working for you.

Are there any other treatments for Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis?

Other medicines used to treat Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis include:

- immunosuppressants, such as azathioprine and methotrexate
- steroids, such as prednisolone and budesonide
- biological medicines, such as adalimumab and infliximab

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Common questions about mesalazine
text:
Why is it important to stick to the same brand?

Different brands and forms of mesalazine (tablets, granules, rectal foam, suppositories and enemas) work on different parts of your gut. Your doctor will prescribe the brand that releases mesalazine in the part of your gut that needs it most.

You'll usually stay on the same brand and type of mesalazine, if it's working to control your symptoms. If it does not help your symptoms, your doctor may try you on a different one.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Common questions about mesalazine
text:
Always use the brand that your doctor has prescribed for you. It's important to make sure the pharmacist gives you the right brand when you collect your prescription.

Can I stop taking mesalazine?

If you’re thinking of stopping mesalazine, talk to your doctor first. If you stop, your symptoms may come back.

If you want to stop because of any side effects, your doctor may be able to review your treatment and prescribe something else.

Do not stop taking or using mesalazine unless your doctor tells you to.

Can I take mesalazine before surgery?

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Common questions about mesalazine
text:
Tell the specialists who are going to carry out your surgery that you’re taking mesalazine. They will tell you if you need to stop taking it.

Will it affect my contraception?

Mesalazine does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill, the progestogen-only pill and emergency contraception.

However, if taking or using mesalazine makes you vomit or have severe, watery diarrhoea, or any diarrhoea that lasts for more than 24 hours, your contraceptive pills may not protect you from pregnancy. Look on the pill packet to find out what to do.

Find out more:

- What to do if you’re sick or have diarrhoea when taking the combined pill
- What to do if you’re sick or have diarrhoea when taking the progestogen-only pill

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Common questions about mesalazine
text:
Can I drive or ride a bike?

Mesalazine is unlikely to affect your ability to drive, ride a bike or operate tools and machinery.

Can I drink alcohol while taking mesalazine?

You can drink alcohol while taking mesalazine. However, alcohol can irritate your gut so may make symptoms worse.

It's best to stick to the national guidelines of no more than 14 units a week

Is there any food or drink I need to avoid?

You can usually eat and drink normally while taking or using mesalazine. If you have indigestion or feel sick, it's best to stick to simple meals, and avoid alcohol and spicy foods.

title: Mesalazine
section_path: Mesalazine > Common questions about mesalazine
text: For inflammatory bowel disease, your doctor may advise you to make some changes to your diet as part of your treatment. This can include following a special diet or adding a nutritional supplement.

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma
text: Mesothelioma is a rare type of cancer that can develop in the lining of the body's organs. It's usually caused by exposure to asbestos.

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > What is mesothelioma?
text: - Mesothelioma is a rare type of cancer that starts in the lining of the body's organs (mesothelium). - Mesothelioma usually affects the lining of the lungs. It can sometimes affect the lining of the tummy (abdomen). - Being in close contact with, and breathing in, asbestos (a material used in some buildings) over a long period of time is the most common cause of mesothelioma. - How serious mesothelioma is depends on the area of your body affected, how big the cancer is, if it has spread and your general health.

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Symptoms of mesothelioma > Main symptoms of mesothelioma
text:
The symptoms of mesothelioma vary depending on the type you have and the area of your body affected.

In most people, mesothelioma affects the lining of their lungs (pleural mesothelioma). In some people, it affects the lining of their tummy (peritoneal mesothelioma).

Symptoms of pleural mesothelioma include:

- chest pain
- shortness of breath
- a cough that does not go away
- difficulty swallowing
- a hoarse voice
- a high temperature
- sweating heavily at night
- feeling very tired (fatigue)
- loss of appetite or losing weight without trying
- curved nails over rounded fingertips (clubbing)

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Symptoms of mesothelioma > Main symptoms of mesothelioma
text:
Symptoms of peritoneal mesothelioma include:

- tummy pain
- a swollen tummy
- feeling sick (nausea) or being sick (vomiting)
- loss of appetite or losing weight without trying
- diarrhoea or constipation

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Symptoms of mesothelioma > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
text: - you have the symptoms of mesothelioma and think you've come into contact with and breathed in asbestos over a long period of time.

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Symptoms of mesothelioma > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if: > Important
text:
Some of these symptoms are very common and can be caused by other conditions.

Having the symptoms does not definitely mean you have mesothelioma, but it's important to get checked by a GP.

If your symptoms are caused by cancer, finding it early may mean it's easier to treat.

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Symptoms of mesothelioma > What happens at your GP appointment
text: The GP will ask about your symptoms and work history. They may gently feel any areas that are painful or swollen, and listen to your lungs.

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Symptoms of mesothelioma > What happens at your GP appointment > Referral to a specialist
text:
You may get an urgent referral for more tests or to see a specialist in hospital if the GP thinks you have symptoms that could be cancer. This does not definitely mean you have cancer.

The specialist you see will depend on your symptoms. If your lungs are affected, you'll see a respiratory specialist. If you have abdominal symptoms, you'll see a gastroenterologist.

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Symptoms of mesothelioma > What happens at your GP appointment > Find out more
text:
- Seeing a GP when you have symptoms of mesothelioma (Cancer Research UK)
- Referral to a specialist for symptoms of mesothelioma (Cancer Research UK)

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Causes of mesothelioma > Main causes of mesothelioma
text:
The main cause of mesothelioma is breathing in asbestos fibres over a long period of time.

Asbestos is a building material that was used in the UK from the 1950s until it was banned in 1999.

You may have been exposed to asbestos if you work, or used to work, in the building industry in a job such as:

- an electrician, carpenter or plumber
- a heating and ventilation engineer
- a construction or demolition worker

It can take a long time (15 to 60 years) for mesothelioma to develop after being exposed to asbestos.

title: Mesothelioma

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Tests and next steps for mesothelioma > Main tests for mesothelioma
text:
The tests for mesothelioma depend on your symptoms and the area of your body that's affected.

The GP may arrange for you to have an X-ray of your chest or tummy depending on the symptoms you have.

Other tests you may have after being referred to a specialist include:

- scans, like a CT scan, an ultrasound scan or a PET-CT scan
- fluid may be drained from your lungs or tummy using a small tube and checked for cancer cells
- an operation where a small cut is made in your chest or abdomen and a long, thin tube with a camera at the end used to look inside your lungs or tummy

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Tests and next steps for mesothelioma > Main tests for mesothelioma > Find out more
text: - Tests for mesothelioma (Cancer Research UK)

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Tests and next steps for mesothelioma > Getting your results
text:
It can take several weeks to get the results of your tests.

You may be asked to go to the hospital to get your results, or they may be sent to you in the post.

Try not to worry if your results are taking a long time to get to you. It does not definitely mean anything is wrong.

You can call the hospital or GP if you're worried. They should be able to update you.

A specialist will explain what the results mean and what will happen next. You may want to bring someone with you for support.

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Tests and next steps for mesothelioma > Getting your results > If you're told you have mesothelioma
text:
Being told you have mesothelioma can feel overwhelming. You may be feeling anxious about what will happen next.

It can help to bring someone with you to any appointments you have.

A group of specialists will look after you throughout your diagnosis, treatment and beyond.

This will include a clinical nurse specialist, who will be your main point of contact during and after treatment.

You can ask them any questions you have.

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Tests and next steps for mesothelioma > Getting your results > Get support
text:
Macmillan Cancer Support has a free helpline that's open every day from 8am to 8pm.

They're there to listen if you have anything you want to talk about.

Call 0808 808 00 00

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Tests and next steps for mesothelioma > Next steps
text:
If you've been told you have mesothelioma, you may need more tests. These can include:

- a small operation to remove a tiny piece of affected lining from your lungs or tummy to check it for cancer cells (biopsy)
- different, more specialised types of ultrasound scan

You may not have all these tests.

The results of these tests will help show if the cancer has spread and how far (called the stage).

The specialists will use the results of these tests and work with you to decide on the best treatment plan for you.

title: Mesothelioma

text: - Stages of mesothelioma (Cancer Research UK)

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Treatment for mesothelioma > Main treatments for mesothelioma
text:
Mesothelioma can be difficult to treat.

The treatment you have will depend on:

- the type of mesothelioma
- where it is
- if it has spread
- your general health

Immunotherapy, where medicines are used to help your immune system fight the cancer, is the most common treatment for mesothelioma.

Chemotherapy, radiotherapy and supportive treatments may also be used to help control symptoms.

Surgery is rarely used to treat mesothelioma, but may be if the cancer is found early.

The specialist care team looking after you will:

- explain the treatments, benefits and side effects
- work with you to create a treatment plan that's best for you
- help you prepare for treatment and manage any side effects

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Treatment for mesothelioma > Main treatments for mesothelioma
text:
You'll have regular check-ups during and after any treatments. Depending on the stage of your mesothelioma, you may have tests and scans.

If you have any symptoms or side effects you're worried about, talk to your specialists. You do not need to wait for your next check-up.

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Treatment for mesothelioma > Immunotherapy
text:
Immunotherapy is where medicines are used to help your immune system kill the cancer.

You may have immunotherapy for mesothelioma if:

- you're unable to have surgery
- before other treatments like chemotherapy

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Treatment for mesothelioma > Immunotherapy > Find out more
text: - Immunotherapy for mesothelioma (Cancer Research UK)

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Treatment for mesothelioma > Chemotherapy
text:
Chemotherapy uses medicines to kill cancer cells.

You may have chemotherapy for mesothelioma:

- to treat it if it's found early
- at the same time as other treatments, such as surgery or radiotherapy, to help make them more effective
- to help make the cancer smaller or control and improve symptoms

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Treatment for mesothelioma > Chemotherapy > Find out more
text:
- Chemotherapy for pleural mesothelioma (Cancer Research UK)
- Chemotherapy for peritoneal mesothelioma (Cancer Research UK)

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Treatment for mesothelioma > Radiotherapy
text:
Radiotherapy uses high-energy rays of radiation to kill cancer cells.

You may have radiotherapy for mesothelioma:

- after surgery to help stop the cancer coming back
- to help slow the growth of the cancer and control the symptoms

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Treatment for mesothelioma > Radiotherapy > Find out more
text: - Radiotherapy for pleural mesothelioma (Cancer Research UK)

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Treatment for mesothelioma > Surgery
text:
Surgery is not often used to treat mesothelioma because removing all the cancer can be difficult.

You may have surgery if mesothelioma is found early or to help relieve your symptoms.

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Treatment for mesothelioma > Surgery > Find out more

title: Mesothelioma
section_path: Mesothelioma > Treatment for mesothelioma > What happens if you've been told your cancer cannot be cured
text:
If you've been diagnosed with advanced mesothelioma, it might be very hard to treat. It may not be possible to cure the cancer.

In this situation, the aim of your treatment will be to limit the cancer and its symptoms, and help you live longer.

Finding out the cancer cannot be cured can be very hard news to take in. You'll be referred to a special team of doctors and nurses called the palliative care team or symptom control team.

They'll work with you to help manage your symptoms and make you feel more comfortable.

The clinical nurse specialist or palliative care team can also help you and your loved ones get any support you need.

text:

There are also national cancer charities that can offer support and information about mesothelioma.

title: Metabolic syndrome
section_path: Metabolic syndrome
text: Metabolic syndrome is the name for a group of health problems that put you at risk of type 2 diabetes or conditions that affect your heart or blood vessels. It's different from metabolic disorders which are rare genetic conditions.

title: Metabolic syndrome
section_path: Metabolic syndrome > Symptoms of metabolic syndrome
text:
You may not have any symptoms of metabolic syndrome.

You usually find out you have it after a blood test or check-up.

title: Metabolic syndrome
section_path: Metabolic syndrome > Check if you're at risk of metabolic syndrome
text:
Metabolic syndrome is very common. It's not known what causes it.

It is linked to insulin resistance. This is when your body does not respond to the hormone insulin properly. It may also be linked to having too much fat around your tummy.

You are more likely to get metabolic syndrome if you:

- are living with obesity
- eat a high-saturated-fat diet
- do not exercise much
- have a Hispanic or South Asian background
- smoke
- drink a lot of alcohol

Your risk of getting metabolic syndrome also increases as you get older.

title: Metabolic syndrome
section_path: Metabolic syndrome > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
text: - you think you are at risk of metabolic syndrome

title: Metabolic syndrome
section_path: Metabolic syndrome > Tests for metabolic syndrome
text:
If your GP or hospital specialist thinks you have metabolic syndrome, they will:

- ask about medical conditions you or family members have
- check your body mass index (BMI) and waist measurement
- check your blood pressure
- ask about any symptoms you have

They will usually arrange some blood tests to check your blood glucose and the fats in your blood, such as cholesterol. They may tell you not to eat or drink anything apart from water for up to 12 hours before the test.

title: Metabolic syndrome
section_path: Metabolic syndrome > Treatments for metabolic syndrome
text:
Treatment for metabolic syndrome usually involves making changes to your lifestyle.

You may also be offered medicines to help you:

- lose weight
- improve your insulin resistance and blood glucose levels
- improve your cholesterol
- lower your blood pressure

title: Metabolic syndrome
section_path: Metabolic syndrome > How to prevent metabolic syndrome
text: The best way to prevent metabolic syndrome, to treat it and prevent complications is through a healthy lifestyle.

title: Metabolic syndrome
section_path: Metabolic syndrome > How to prevent metabolic syndrome > Do
text:
- try to lose weight if you're overweight
- eat less saturated fat and meat and dairy products and have more fruit, vegetables and whole grains
- do at least 150 minutes of moderate to intense exercise a week, spread over at least 4 or 5 days
- try to cut down or quit smoking if you smoke

title: Metabolic syndrome
section_path: Metabolic syndrome > How to prevent metabolic syndrome > Don’t
text: - do not sit for long periods of time

title: Metabolic syndrome
section_path: Metabolic syndrome > Complications of metabolic syndrome
text:
Metabolic syndrome increases your chances of having cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.

It may also increase your chances of getting:

- non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
- osteoarthritis
- gout
- some cancers

It can sometimes affect fertility.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin
text: Metformin is a medicine that can be used to treat type 2 diabetes, gestational diabetes and the hormone condition polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). It’s only available with a prescription.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > What metformin is for
text:
Metformin is used as a treatment for:

- type 2 diabetes (either on its own or combined with other diabetes medicines)
- diabetes that can develop during pregnancy (gestational diabetes)
- symptoms of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), previously called polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
- type 1 diabetes (when combined with insulin)

Type 2 diabetes is a condition where the body does not make enough insulin, or the insulin it makes does not work properly.

This can cause high blood sugar (glucose) levels. Metformin works by lowering your blood sugar level.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > How to take metformin
text:
Metformin usually comes as tablets, a liquid (oral solution) you swallow, or a powder that you mix with water.

How much you need to take depends on why you’re taking it and your age. Most people take it 1 to 3 times a day with food. Your doctor may prescribe a lower dose to start with.

When taking metformin:

- tablets – swallow tablets whole with some water, do not crush or chew them)
- powder – mix powder with 150ml of water before drinking the mixture
- liquid – use the spoon or syringe that comes with the liquid to measure the right dose

Depending on why you're taking it, you may need to take it long term.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > How to take metformin
text:
Your health care professional will monitor your treatment to make sure it's suitable for you. You can also ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice if you’re not sure how to take it or have any problems taking it.

Always check the packet or leaflet that comes with your medicine.

If you get ill with vomiting, diarrhoea or a high temperature (fever) when taking metformin, there's a risk you'll get dehydrated.

Talk to a pharmacist or doctor for advice, or follow the advice they've already given you.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > How to take metformin > Important
text: It's important to keep taking your medicine. If you stop, your blood sugar level may start to rise again. Talk to your doctor if you're having problems with your medicine.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > How to take metformin > If you miss a dose of metformin
text:
If you take metformin once a day and forget to take it, take it as soon as you remember, unless it’s nearly time for your next dose.

If you take it more than once a day and it’s nearly time for your next dose, skip the dose you missed. Take your next dose at the usual time.

Do not take 2 doses to make up for a missed dose.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > How to take metformin > If you take too much metformin
text: Taking an extra dose of metformin can be dangerous.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > How to take metformin > If you take too much metformin > Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if:
text:
- you've taken more than your prescribed dose of metformin

If you're told to go to A&E, do not drive. Ask someone to drive you or call 999 and ask for an ambulance.

Bring the metformin packet or leaflet inside it, any remaining medicine, and any other medicines you take.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > Side effects of metformin
text:
Like all medicines, metformin can cause side effects, although not everyone gets them.

Most side effects should ease after a couple of weeks as your body gets used to the medicine, but some can last longer.

You may be more at risk of side effects if you take more than one medicine for lowering blood sugar levels, such as metformin and insulin.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > Side effects of metformin > Common side effects
text:
Common side effects of metformin include:

- feeling sick (nausea) or being sick (vomiting)
- diarrhoea
- tummy pain
- loss of appetite
- a change to the way things taste
- vitamin B12 deficiency, which can make you feel very tired

Metformin on its own (without another diabetes medicine), will not usually affect your ability to drive, ride a bike or use machinery, but if you feel dizzy after taking it, wait until the dizziness stops.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > Side effects of metformin > Non-urgent advice: Speak to a pharmacist or doctor if:
text:
- you have any side effects that bother you or do not go away

They may be able to give you advice about how to reduce any side effects. Keep your medicine unless you’re advised to stop.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > Side effects of metformin > Serious side effects
text:
Metformin can sometimes cause serious side effects, although most of them are rare.

Possible serious side effects of metformin include:

- too much acid in your blood (lactic acidosis) – causing symptoms such as being sick (vomiting), stomach pain and muscle cramps, and breathing problems, it can also make you feel severely tired
- an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) – causing symptoms such as a swollen throat or tongue, a raised, itchy rash and difficulty breathing
- inflammation of the liver (hepatitis), which can cause yellowing of your skin and the whites of your eyes – yellowed skin may be less noticeable on brown or black skin

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > Side effects of metformin > Serious side effects > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
text:
- you're taking metformin and think you might be experiencing lactic acidosis or anaphylaxis

If you think you're having any other serious side effect, call NHS 111.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > Side effects of metformin > More about side effects
text:
These are not all the side effects of metformin.

For a full list, see the leaflet that comes with your medicine or search for your medicine on the electronic medicines compendium website.

You can report any side effects you get on the Yellow Card website

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > Who can and cannot take metformin
text:
Metformin can be taken by most adults and children aged 10 years old and over, but it’s not suitable for everyone.

For example, it may not be suitable if:

- you've ever had an allergic reaction to or serious side effect from metformin
- you have liver and kidney problems
- you have a severe infection, such as a lung or kidney infection
- you have heart failure
- you drink a lot of alcohol (more than the recommended amount)

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > Who can and cannot take metformin > Breastfeeding and metformin
text:
Tell your doctor if you’re breastfeeding. You can usually take metformin while breastfeeding because it only passes into breast milk in tiny amounts. But check with a doctor first.

It's rare for breastfed babies to get any side effects from a medicine you're taking, but speak to a healthcare professional or call NHS 111 if you have any concerns about your baby.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > Who can and cannot take metformin > Pregnancy and metformin
text:
Tell your doctor if you're pregnant or get pregnant while taking metformin.

You can take metformin during pregnancy, but check with a doctor first.

It's important to control diabetes if you're pregnant. Poorly controlled diabetes can increase the risk of problems such as miscarriage.

Find out more about taking metformin during pregnancy on the Bumps (Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy) website.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > Taking metformin with other medicines, food and drink
text:
There are some medicines, herbal remedies and supplements that may not mix well with metformin.

These include:

- medicines to treat fluid build-up in the body (diuretics)
- anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen and diclofenac
- some medicines to treat high blood pressure

Before you take metformin, tell your doctor or pharmacist if you’re taking any other medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > Taking metformin with other medicines, food and drink > Food and alcohol with metformin
text:
You can eat as normal while taking metformin.

Try to limit how much alcohol you drink while taking metformin because it can increase the risk of serious side effects.

title: Metformin
section_path: Metformin > Find out more about your medicine
text:
To find out more about your medicine, you can:

- check the leaflet that comes with it
- search for your medicine leaflet on the electronic medicines compendium website
- speak to a pharmacist or doctor for advice – if you recently started taking it, you can get help with newly prescribed medicines from a pharmacist as part of the New Medicine Service

title: Methadone
section_path: Methadone
text:
Brand name: Physeptone

Find out how methadone treats heroin dependence, and how to take it.

title: Methadone
section_path: Methadone > About methadone
text:
Brand name: Physeptone

Methadone is an opioid medicine. Other opioids include codeine, morphine, fentanyl and oxycodone.

Methadone is one of the medicines that can be used to help you stop taking heroin. It works by reducing heroin withdrawal symptoms, such as feeling restless or anxious, a runny nose, sweating, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, shaking and muscle cramps. It also helps stop cravings for heroin.

It can also be used to treat dependence on other opioids.

There are 2 main ways to use methadone to treat heroin dependence:

- maintenance therapy – you switch from heroin to methadone, then stay on it, usually long term
- detox (detoxification) – you switch from heroin to methadone, before gradually withdrawing from methadone until you're completely free from both

title: Methadone
section_path: Methadone > About methadone
text:
Some people start with maintenance therapy and go on to detox to help stop them using both heroin and methadone.

Methadone for heroin dependence is available on prescription only. It usually comes as a green liquid you swallow or an injection. It also comes as tablets but these are not given often.

You'll get your prescription from a prescriber at a local drug treatment service, or your GP.

Methadone is also used for end of life care and severe pain. This is usually prescribed by a specialist and comes as liquid, tablets or injections. It's also available as a cough medicine for end of life care.

title: Methadone
section_path: Methadone > About methadone
text:
If you use heroin and want to stop, ask a GP or local drug treatment service for help with heroin addiction. You're entitled to the same confidential care as anyone else.

Find your local drug treatment service

title: Methadone
section_path: Methadone > About methadone > Key facts
text: - The most common side effects of methadone, if you're not used to opioids, are constipation, feeling or being sick, and feeling cold and sweaty. - It's best to avoid alcohol while taking methadone, as it can cause very serious side effects. It's important to tell your prescriber how much you drink. - You may have a regular urine or saliva test at your local drug treatment service or GP surgery. This is to check for heroin, methadone and other drugs. - Methadone is addictive, so you'll need to reduce your dose slowly if you want to stop taking it to prevent withdrawal symptoms. Talk to your GP or prescriber first. - Grapefruit and grapefruit juice can affect how your methadone works. It may make side effects worse.

title: Methadone
section_path: Methadone > Who can and cannot take methadone
text: Brand name: Physeptone

title: Methadone
section_path: Methadone > Who can and cannot take methadone > Who can take methadone
text: Most adults aged 18 years and over, and occasionally younger people, can take methadone for heroin dependence.

title: Methadone
section_path: Methadone > Who can and cannot take methadone > Who may not be able to take methadone
text:
Methadone may not be suitable for some people. To make sure it's safe for you, tell your doctor or prescriber before starting methadone treatment if you:

- have ever had an allergic reaction to methadone or any other medicine
- have a lung condition, or breathing difficulties
- have ever abused or been dependent on alcohol, prescription medicines or illegal drugs
- have a head injury or get bad headaches
- have ulcerative colitis
- have seizures or fits
- have heart disease, heart rhythm problems (arrhythmia) or low blood pressure
